If the **original reviewer is unavailable, the team should request a fresh review through the normal review channel rather than waiting for that same person**.

- **For a data-plane specs PR:** after you address all feedback and get CI green, use the **re-review** control in the PR’s **Reviewers** pane (the circle icon next to the reviewer’s name), then **ping the Azure API Stewardship Board General Channel** so another reviewer sees it: [API Stewardship Board General Channel]([internal Teams link omitted]). If the board asked for a follow-up review, use the same offline review path described here: [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).\
- **If sign-off is still needed and no reviewer is responding,** reach out to the review board core alias with the PR link: [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).\
- **For an ARM specs PR:** follow the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** guidance and use the ARM review help path rather than trying to find the original reviewer. If you need reviewer help, use **ARM API Review Office Hours**: [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review). If the PR is not getting picked up again, verify it has re-entered the ARM queue per that guidance.

So the short answer is: **request re-review on the PR, then escalate through the board/on-call channel for that review path; you do not need the exact original reviewer to come back.**

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Work around npm ci package resolution failures in azure-rest-api-specs caused by the default proxy/feed

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If running npm ci in azure-rest-api-specs fails because package resolution goes through Microsoft's default proxy/feed and returns 404 not found or permission errors for packages, what local workaround can be used?

**Historical ground truth**

A local workaround is to use the Azure SDK public Azure DevOps npm registry instead of the default proxied registry. You can either set your user .npmrc registry to:

registry=https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/public/_packaging/azure-sdk-for-js/npm/registry/

or run:

npm ci --registry=https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/public/_packaging/azure-sdk-for-js/npm/registry/

If you change your user .npmrc, change it back when working in unrelated repositories.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes. The historical local workaround was to bypass Microsoft’s default proxy/feed by forcing `npm ci` to use the internal CFS registry directly:

```bash
npm ci --registry=https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/public/_packaging/azure-sdk-for-js/npm/registry/
```

That was the documented short-term fix when `npm ci` in `azure-rest-api-specs` failed with `404 Not Found` or permission errors because package resolution went through the default proxy/feed instead of resolving first-party packages correctly.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to rerun SDK validation checks and obtain ARM sign-off for a spec PR

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

For a public Azure REST API spec PR whose merge guidance says it is in ARM review purview, must receive the ARMSignedOff label from an ARM reviewer, and is currently marked WaitForARMFeedback, how do you rerun SDK validation checks, and how do you get ARM sign-off?

**Historical ground truth**

To rerun SDK validation checks on a spec PR, push another commit to the PR; an empty commit is sufficient to trigger the checks again. For ARM sign-off, follow the PR's merge guidance: when the PR is in ARM review purview, it must receive the ARMSignedOff label from an ARM reviewer. If it is marked WaitForARMFeedback, it is waiting in the ARM review queue, and the ARM review queue guidance explains when it will be reviewed.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes. For a **public ARM spec PR** in **`WaitForARMFeedback`** that says it needs **`ARMSignedOff`**, the reusable process is:

- **Rerun SDK validation** by commenting ``/azp run SDK Validation - {Language}`` on the PR, for example ``/azp run SDK Validation - Go``. Re-running any language-specific SDK validation check also re-evaluates **`SDK Validation Status`**. See the SDK validation guide: [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- **Get ARM sign-off** through the **ARM review step**, not by rerunning SDK checks. If the PR has **`ARMReview`**, it must be reviewed by an ARM reviewer and receive **`ARMSignedOff`**. If it is already **`WaitForARMFeedback`**, that means it is in the ARM review queue. Follow the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** guidance and the ARM review process: [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).

**Process details**

- **Authoritative source:** always follow the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** comment for the exact blocker order and required actions. The general PR workflow is documented here: [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).
- **How to rerun SDK checks:** use a PR comment in this form:
  ```text
  /azp run SDK Validation - Go
  ```
  Replace `Go` with the language shown on your PR. The command syntax and the note about `SDK Validation Status` are in [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- **If the SDK Validation checks do not appear:** that usually means you lack the permission to trigger them. Use the access instructions referenced from [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- **How ARM sign-off happens:** a PR with **`ARMReview`** must be reviewed by ARM; the expected progression is effectively **`ARMReview` → ARM reviewer approval → `ARMSignedOff`**. The ARM review overview is here: [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).
- **What `WaitForARMFeedback` means:** it indicates the PR is in the ARM review flow/queue. If step 1 blockers were addressed and the PR is in this state, the next needed action is typically ARM review rather than more SDK reruns. Queue behavior is described in [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).
- **If you need help from ARM:** use the support path described in the ARM review guide, including **ARM API Review Office Hours** from [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review). That guide also notes that if the PR has breaking changes, those should be resolved before asking the on-call ARM reviewer for help.

</details>

### spec-review-0083: Whether to merge a GA spec PR before TypeSpec SDK-generation changes are complete

**Dataset:** `versioning.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0093](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0093) | **GT basis:** expert | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-07-10T22:33:04.109Z

**Assessment:** The answer correctly distinguishes contract-preserving post-merge TypeSpec/SDK-only follow-up work from changes that affect the published REST API. It is well supported by retrieved guidance that main is a production branch, merging publishes to customers, and once an API version is published it cannot be changed in place except approved spec-to-implementation bug fixes; compatible or breaking later API-affecting changes require the normal versioning/breaking-change path and typically a new API version.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that for a GA PR targeting public main, merge should wait until the API version is final if remaining work might change the published API contract.; Allow a follow-up PR only when the deferred TypeSpec/configuration work is genuinely contract-preserving and does not alter the emitted REST/OpenAPI surface.; Explain that main is a production/publishing branch, so merging there publishes the spec for customer consumption.; Explain that once an API version is published, it must not be modified in place except for the narrow approved bug-fix path to align spec with actual implementation.; State that if deferred changes later affect the API, they trigger versioning/breaking-change review considerations and generally require a new API version rather than editing the existing GA version in place.; Acknowledge that automation may surface labels such as VersioningReviewRequired or BreakingChangeReviewRequired on such later PRs and that the PR's merge guidance should then be followed.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [review-process-07-004](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-07-004), [versioning-01-008](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-008)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Whether to merge a GA spec PR before TypeSpec SDK-generation changes are complete

question: For a GA API spec PR targeting main, if the API surface is finalized but additional TypeSpec decorations or configuration are still needed for SDK generation, should those changes be included before merging, or can they be added in a follow-up PR after merge? What are the versioning or breaking-change implications if the later changes end up affecting the API?

**Historical ground truth**

For a PR targeting main, the safer approach is to wait until everything is complete before merging, because main is not intended for iterative development. If the remaining TypeSpec changes are truly limited to SDK-generation configuration and will not require any API change, it can be acceptable to merge first and add those configurations later. But if the later changes turn out to require an API change or create a breaking change, they may need additional approval and could require publishing a new API version.

**Cached dev answer**

Short answer: **include the remaining TypeSpec work before merging if there is any chance it changes the published API contract.** A GA spec PR to public `main` is treated as a **production/publish** event, not a staging checkpoint, so you should merge only when the GA API version is final and ready to release.

- **What can wait until after merge?**\
  Only changes that are **truly contract-preserving**. By implication from the versioning policy, a follow-up PR is reasonable only if the remaining TypeSpec decorations/config affect SDK generation mechanics but **do not change the emitted REST/OpenAPI surface at all**. Before merging, validate that with the [TypeSpec / tooling guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs/api-typespec).

- **Why this matters for a GA PR on `main`:**\
  Public `main` is a **production branch**; merging there publishes the spec for customers, and the PR guidance says you should open/merge that PR only when you are **ready to release** the features in it. See [PR guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr) and [branch/versioning guidance](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/swaggeronboarding.html).

- **If the later TypeSpec change does affect the API:**\
  - If it is a **compatible / non-breaking** change to the already-published GA version, automation can label it **`VersioningReviewRequired`**. The rule is: **even compatible changes are not allowed in-place in an existing published API version**; you should create a **new API version** instead. See [breaking/versioning guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).\
  - If it is a **breaking** change, it can trigger **`BreakingChangeReviewRequired`** and go through the breaking-change review path, again as a **new version**, not as an in-place edit to the GA version. See the same [guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).

- **Very narrow exception:**\
  The docs note an exception for fixing the spec to match the **actual implementation**; that is a special approved-bugfix path, not a general way to finish deferred SDK-related API changes after GA. See [breaking/versioning guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).

- **Practical recommendation:**\
  Use the [Azure SDK Tools Agent / TypeSpec workflow](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs/api-tooling) to finish validation and SDK-generation checks **before** merging the GA PR. If you intentionally split work, keep the post-merge PR limited to **non-contract** SDK customization only.

</details>

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

### spec-review-0086: Handling breaking-change flags for spec corrections that match shipped service behavior

**Dataset:** `versioning.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0096](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0096) | **GT basis:** bot_fallback | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-07-09T00:09:57.507Z

**Assessment:** The answer matches the historical guidance: an in-place update is allowed when it only corrects the published spec to reflect already-shipped behavior, but the PR must still follow the breaking-change review path and justify that service behavior and wire contract are unchanged. It also correctly distinguishes real customer-visible behavior changes as requiring a new API version.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that published API versions are normally immutable, with a narrow exception for correcting the spec to match already-deployed implementation.; Require that the exception applies only when the actual wire contract/service behavior is already shipped and unchanged by the PR.; Acknowledge that automation may still flag the diff as a breaking change because it compares published spec artifacts rather than live service behavior.; Require the author to complete the applicable breaking-change/versioning review workflow rather than bypassing review solely because the change is a spec correction.; Require explicit PR justification/evidence that the prior spec was inaccurate and that customers do not need to change what they send, receive, or do.; State that if the change would alter customer-visible behavior or contract, it is not a spec-correction exception and must use a new API version.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [versioning-01-008](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-008), [review-process-05-006](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-05-006)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Handling breaking-change flags for spec corrections that match shipped service behavior

question: If a published API version's spec is wrong and a PR only corrects the spec to match already-shipped service behavior without changing the wire contract, how should that be handled when tooling flags it as a breaking change?

**Historical ground truth**

A published API version may be corrected in place when the change only fixes the specification to match already-shipped service behavior and does not change the actual wire contract. If automated tooling flags that update as a breaking change, it can still be treated as a spec correction rather than a service behavior change. However, that does not remove the need to complete the breaking-change review process and provide justification that the service behavior is unchanged and the spec was inaccurate. If the change would alter actual customer-visible service behavior, then it is not a spec-correction exception and a new API version is required instead.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — handle it as a **spec bug fix**, not as a normal service-breaking change, **if** the PR truly only makes the published spec match the behavior that is already shipped on the wire.

- **What to do:** keep the correction narrowly scoped, clearly explain in the PR that the service behavior is already live and the spec was inaccurate, and follow the spec PR breaking-change guidance at [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).
- **Why tooling still flags it:** the automation compares published spec artifacts, so an in-place correction to an already published version can still look like a breaking diff even when customer-observed behavior is unchanged.
- **Expected path:** the docs explicitly allow one exception to “no changes after publish”: **fixing the spec to match actual implementation**. That exception is handled through the **`-Approved-BugFix`** path described in the breaking-change guidance, rather than treating it as a standard customer-breaking service change. See [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).
- **Do not use this exception** if the correction would change what existing clients can actually send or receive, or would require customer action. In that case, it is a real contract change and should go through a **new API version** and, if applicable, the normal breaking-change review process described in [Azure REST API versioning](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs/api-versioning) and [Azure Breaking Change Process](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/azurebreakingchangeplaybook).

**Practical PR wording to include**
- “This PR does not change shipped service behavior or the wire contract.”
- “It corrects the published specification to match the already deployed implementation.”
- “Please evaluate under the bug-fix exception for published API versions.”

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Handling a non-blocking JS SDK validation failure caused by stale tsp-location.yaml configuration

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a specs PR has a JS SDK validation failure caused by a stale tsp-location.yaml path, and that validation is not listed among the PR's merge-blocking checks, should the check be skipped, and what is the recommended way to handle it?

**Historical ground truth**

If the JS SDK validation failure is not listed among the PR's merge-blocking checks, it does not need to be skipped in order to merge. The recommended approach is to leave the failure in place, document in the PR why it is failing, and correct the stale tsp-location.yaml configuration in the appropriate follow-up or migration work. After the configuration is fixed, rerun the validation with `/azp run SDK Validation - JS`. No standard per-PR skip label for this JS SDK validation scenario was identified in the cited guidance. If temporary suppression is truly necessary, request it through the PR suppression process with justification.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **from a merge-process standpoint, it can be skipped as a blocker**, because a check that is **not** listed among the PR’s merge-blocking checks is non-required and does not prevent merge. But **it should not be ignored as a technical issue**: the recommended handling is to **fix the stale `tsp-location.yaml` configuration and rerun the JS SDK validation**, rather than trying to suppress or “paper over” the failure.

- **Process rule:** Per [Understanding required vs non-required checks](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr), non-required failures do **not** block merge, even if they are red.
- **Do not treat this as a suppression case by default:** Per [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions), general `SDK azure-sdk-for-js` generation-failure suppressions are **not** supported except for SDK **breaking-change** suppression cases. A stale path/config issue does not fit that pattern.
- **Recommended fix:** update the stale `tsp-location.yaml` so it points to the correct spec/`tspconfig.yaml` source, then rerun the JS SDK validation check using the documented [SDK Validation rerun flow](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation), i.e. the `/azp run SDK Validation - {Language}` pattern using the exact check name shown on the PR.
- **Practical takeaway:** **skip it as a merge blocker, not as a defect**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Does moving common types to TypeSpec avoid breaking-change approval for new versions?

question: Under the breaking-change process described here, does moving common types from JSON-based specs to TypeSpec exempt new common-type versions from breaking-change approval? If not, what durable process options can reduce repeated approvals?

**Historical ground truth**

No. Under the process described here, moving common types to TypeSpec does not by itself exempt new versions from breaking-change review. If a change narrows accepted input values, it is still considered a breaking change and requires review. To reduce repeated approvals, one option is to remove an older preview version when it does not need to be kept, so breaking-change comparison is only against the previous stable version. Previously approved breaking changes should not need to be re-approved.

**Cached dev answer**

No. Moving ARM Common Types from JSON-authored specs to TypeSpec does **not** by itself avoid breaking-change approval for new common-type versions.

- The retrieved guidance defines breaking changes by **customer impact / contract change**, not by authoring format. If a change alters API behavior, contract, versioning, or otherwise requires customer action, it still falls under the breaking-change process.\
- The TypeSpec assessment guidance is explicit that TypeSpec-based analysis **does not replace** official ARM API, Stewardship, or Azure Breaking Change reviews.\
- So the format change from JSON to TypeSpec is not an exemption; if the new common-type version introduces a breaking contract change, review is still required.

**Durable options to reduce repeated approvals**

- **Prefer additive common-types evolution.** If you can add new shared shapes without changing or removing existing ones, you avoid creating a breaking change in the first place.\
- **Do not change published versions in place.** For preview APIs, the guidance says to create a **new preview api-version** instead of making breaking changes in the same published preview version. If the newer preview or GA replaces the older preview, that replacement path does not require the full Azure Breaking Change / Retirement process unless it also breaks against the latest GA.\
- **Batch unavoidable breaks.** If breaking changes are truly necessary, make fewer, larger common-types version transitions rather than frequent small breaking revisions, so you do not re-enter approval repeatedly. This is an inference from the process: approvals are triggered by the breaking change itself, so reducing the number of breaking transitions reduces repeated approvals.\
- **Standardize on one common-types version per spec.** The common-types guidance says to use the **latest single version that contains all required types** and not mix versions. That reduces churn from repeated version hopping across specs.\
- **Start review early when a break is unavoidable.** The process guidance says to classify early and submit the intake before customer communications or enforcement, using the breaking-change intake flow at [https://aka.ms/breakingchangeintake](https://aka.ms/breakingchangeintake).

So the practical answer is:

- **TypeSpec migration alone:** no exemption.\
- **Best long-term reduction strategy:** keep common-types changes non-breaking where possible, roll breaking changes into new service/api versions instead of mutating published ones, and minimize how often you introduce a new breaking common-types version.

</details>

**Assessment:** The answer matches the retrieved versioning guidance and the historical ground truth: it treats ServiceName as the independently versioned customer-consumable contract boundary, explains that an RP namespace can contain multiple services, makes branding secondary, and uses docs/SDK/version cadence as the split test. It also reasonably says TypeSpec @service should generally align without overstating that branding or internal modeling should control the folder boundary.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that ServiceName should primarily represent a customer-consumable API contract/service boundary that versions uniformly over time.; Explain that an RP namespace is not itself the service boundary and may contain one or more independently versioned services.; Tie one ServiceName to its own contract, documentation/examples, and typically SDK package/lifecycle for each version.; Advise using a single ServiceName when APIs ship, version, document, and are consumed together; split only when areas can evolve or retire independently.; Treat external branding as a secondary naming influence rather than the primary determinant when it conflicts with versioning/contract boundaries.; Acknowledge that TypeSpec service boundaries are an important technical signal and should generally align with the chosen ServiceName boundary, especially for a single uniformly versioned API surface.; Note that ServiceName does not need to equal the RP namespace exactly.; If discussing shared sources across services, preserve the rule that each service must own its copied contract artifacts on its own timeline rather than sharing one live source.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [versioning-01-030](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-030), [versioning-01-031](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-031)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to choose ServiceName for platform-style resource providers

question: When choosing ServiceName in azure-rest-api-specs for a resource provider that is more of a platform/foundation than a standalone branded Azure service, should the service folder primarily represent the documentation/SDK/versioning boundary, the TypeSpec @service boundary, or external product branding? How should teams decide the appropriate ServiceName?

**Historical ground truth**

Choose ServiceName primarily as the boundary for a customer-consumable API contract that versions uniformly. In practice, the service folder is the unit that owns the TypeSpec sources, emitted stable and preview OpenAPI, documentation grouping, and typically the SDK and versioning lifecycle. A TypeSpec @service boundary is usually the strongest technical signal for that folder boundary, especially when there is a single main.tsp with one @service and one uniformly versioned API surface. External branding can influence the chosen name, but it should not override the versioning and contract boundary. A useful decision test is whether the operations version uniformly, should ship together as one documentation set and SDK package line, can evolve independently from sibling areas, and have a stable customer-facing name for that slice. The ServiceName does not need to match the RP namespace exactly.

**Cached dev answer**

Use **ServiceName primarily as the Azure service/versioning boundary**, not as an internal platform boundary and not purely as a branding label.

- The repo guidance defines an Azure service as a set of operations that **version uniformly over time**.
- For one `ServiceName`, the service version has a **1:1 relationship** with its contract, documentation, examples, and SDK package/lifecycle.
- The **RP namespace** (`Microsoft.X`) is the provider boundary; it can contain **one or more services**. The RP namespace itself does **not** version, but each service under it does.

So for a platform/foundation RP, the decision test should be:

- **Use one `ServiceName`** if the APIs are intended to ship, version, document, and produce SDKs **together**.
- **Split into multiple `ServiceName` folders** only when the areas are truly **independent customer-facing services** with their own version cadence, contract ownership, docs, and SDK lifecycle.
- Treat **branding as secondary**: the docs call `ServiceName` a **customer-facing service name**, but the stronger rule is the **independent versioning/contract boundary**. Branding alone should not force a split if the APIs are one uniformly versioned service.
- Treat the TypeSpec `@service` boundary as something that should **generally align** with that service boundary, but the repo folder decision is driven by the **service/versioning contract**, not by whatever internal modeling split happens to exist in TypeSpec.

A practical way to choose the name:

- Ask: **Would customers reasonably think of this as one service with one API/version story?**
- Ask: **Will docs and SDK be published/consumed together?**
- Ask: **Could one area need to rev or retire independently from another?**
- If the answers are “together,” use one `ServiceName`.
- If the answers are “independently,” use sibling service folders under the same RP namespace.

One more important implication from the repo rules:

- If two services share files, they should **not** point at the same TypeSpec/OpenAPI source in-place; each service must own its contract copy on its own timeline. That’s another sign that `ServiceName` is about **independent contract ownership**, not just folder cosmetics.

If you want, I can turn this into a **concrete naming recommendation** for your RP by evaluating your current capability areas against the split-vs-single-service test.

</details>

It also appropriately distinguishes release-* as feature branches and notes RPSaaSCanary only for validation, not manifest rollout.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that for RPaaS-based ARM APIs in private preview, limited iteration within the same published preview api-version is allowed only for some non-breaking changes.; State that breaking on-the-wire changes to a published preview must use a newer dated preview api-version rather than editing the existing version in place.; State that RPaaS private-preview / limited-subscription Canary rollout is supported from private RPSaaSMaster behind AFEC.; Reject using private release-* branches as the manifest target for RPaaS private-preview or customer Canary rollout, while allowing them as development/feature branches.; If mentioning alternatives, distinguish validation-only branches such as RPSaaSCanary from supported rollout branches.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can the same private-preview API version be updated iteratively for Canary testing in an RPaaS-based RP?

question: For an RPaaS-based RP in private preview, can teams iteratively update the same API version over time for Canary testing, and can the RPaaS manifest point to a private-repo release-* branch instead of RPSaaSMaster?

**Historical ground truth**

Yes, teams can continue iterating on the same private-preview API version over time, including for Canary testing, but there is no supported path to have the RPaaS manifest roll out from a private-repo release-* branch instead of RPSaaSMaster. The supported approach is to do day-to-day integration on release-* or other non-master development branches as appropriate, then merge customer-testable, non-breaking updates for that same private-preview API version into RPSaaSMaster for rollout behind AFEC. If the work is still internal and not yet for private-preview customers, it should remain on development or release branches until it is ready to be promoted. During private preview, non-breaking changes within the same API version are allowed, with the documented approval path used when required.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes, with an important limit: for an **RPaaS-based ARM RP in private preview**, you may keep iterating on the **same preview `api-version` only for some non-breaking changes** while it remains private preview. If you introduce a **breaking on-the-wire change** to that published preview, you should create a **newer dated preview `api-version`** instead of changing the existing one in place.

- **Same private-preview version for Canary?**
  - **Allowed in a narrow sense:** private preview is the main exception where **some non-breaking changes** can stay in the same `api-version`.
  - **Not for breaking changes:** if the Canary iteration changes the published wire contract incompatibly, treat it as a **new preview version** and follow the breaking-change guidance in [CPEX Breaking Changes FAQs](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/faq_breaking_changes).

- **Can the RPaaS manifest point to `release-*` instead of `RPSaaSMaster`?**
  - **No for private-preview/customer Canary rollout.** The documented branch for **RPaaS-based ARM private preview** is **private `RPSaaSMaster`**, with AFEC gating. The rollout matrix for **Canary (limited subscriptions)** also points to **private `RPSaaSMaster`**.
  - `release-*` is documented as a **feature branch**, not the supported lifecycle branch for RPaaS private-preview rollout. Use the branch guidance in [API versions and branches](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches) and [Supported GitHub repos/branches](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/swaggeronboarding.html).
  - **Adjacent case:** if you mean **validation only**, the ARM wiki notes `RPSaaSCanary` can be used for Canary validation; that is different from saying the private-preview manifest should target `release-*`.

**Practical rule**
- **Private preview + RPaaS ARM** → keep the live/private-preview spec on **`RPSaaSMaster`**.
- **Iterative Canary fixes** → reuse the same version only for **non-breaking** changes.
- **Breaking iteration** → mint a **new preview `api-version`**.

</details>

**Acceptance criteria:** State that a crash during Python breaking-change checking while importing the newly generated package is not, by itself, evidence of an API spec breaking change.; Prefer classifying missing generated types/AttributeError during import as a Python emitter/generator/tooling defect unless there is concrete evidence the spec or generation config is invalid.; Recommend routing the issue to the Python emitter/tooling owners rather than asking the spec author to fix the API definition.; Do not suggest using approved-breaking-change labels or suppressions to bypass a generator crash, since this is not a normal reviewed breaking-change diff.; Allow the conditional exception that if investigation shows the spec/config directly causes an unsupported shape and the generator is behaving as designed, then it can be treated as a spec/config issue.

**Frozen facts:** The checker crashed during detect_breaking_changes.; The crash occurred while importing the freshly generated Python package.; The observed errors included missing generated types such as CacheUpdate and AccountEncryption members.; Investigation concluded the problem was an emitter bug.; A linked fix PR was described as fixing TypedDict rendering for template-instantiated models.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [sdk-review-01-016](expert-knowledge-report.md#sdk-review-01-016)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Python breaking-change checker crash due to missing generated types should be routed as an emitter bug

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If the Python breaking-change checker crashes during detect_breaking_changes while importing the freshly generated package and reports AttributeError for missing generated types, should this be treated as a spec issue to fix in the API definition, or as a Python emitter/tooling bug to route to the generator owners?

**Historical ground truth**

A Python breaking-change check failure of this form should be treated as a Python emitter/tooling bug, not as an API spec issue for the author to fix. The key signal is that the checker crashes while importing the freshly generated package and references missing generated types such as CacheUpdate. In the historical case, investigation concluded it was an emitter issue, and the identified fix area was TypedDict rendering for template-instantiated models. The appropriate action is to route the problem to the Python emitter/tooling owners rather than trying to resolve it through spec changes or the approved-breaking-change label.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **treat that first as a Python emitter/generator bug, not automatically as a spec bug**.

- An import-time crash in `detect_breaking_changes` against the **freshly generated package** means the validation step could not even load the generated SDK surface. That is different from a normal reported breaking-change diff; it points to a failure in generation/output assembly unless you can show the spec/config itself is invalid.
- The Python guidance says to **distinguish incorrect spec/configuration from an emitter/generator defect** by regenerating with the identified inputs and inspecting the unpatched output, and to **fix/report generator-wide defects upstream instead of masking them in one SDK**.\
  - Python customization guidance: [Grow Up Story for Generated SDKs](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-python/blob/main/doc/dev/customize_code/how-to-patch-sdk-code.md)
- The Python breaking-change migration guide also treats many SDK-surface mismatches as **emitter changes**, resolved with Python client customizations or generator/config changes rather than by changing the service API contract itself.\
  - Guide: [Azure Python SDK Breaking Changes Review and Resolution Guide for TypeSpec Migration](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-python/blob/main/doc/dev/mgmt/sdk-breaking-changes-guide.md)

**Practical rule**
- **Route to Python generator owners** if the checker crashes with `AttributeError` for missing generated types while importing newly generated code.
- **Treat as a spec issue only if** you can show the spec/config directly produces an unsupported or conflicting shape and the generator is behaving as designed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Common causes when required checks do not start on an API spec PR

question: In azure-rest-api-specs, what are common causes and workarounds when required Azure DevOps checks remain stuck in "waiting for status to be reported" instead of starting?

**Historical ground truth**

Two likely causes were identified when required checks did not start on an API spec PR. First, the GitHub account associated with the PR might not have the required Azure SDK access configured correctly; the recommended fix is to follow the Azure SDK access setup steps carefully, including making the organization's membership public if required by that process. Second, PRs opened through Copilot collaboration may be unable to trigger Azure DevOps pipelines on their own; a practical workaround is to open a new PR directly from the contributor's own account instead of via Copilot.

**Cached dev answer**

The most common causes are: **a missed Azure DevOps PR trigger**, **permissions/membership problems that prevent SDK validation checks from materializing**, and **stale branch infrastructure on protected or release branches**. Also, first verify whether the stuck check is actually merge-blocking: in specs PRs, the real gate is **`Automated merging requirements met`**, and some checks can appear pending without blocking merge.

- **Missed PR trigger:** Azure DevOps can occasionally miss the PR event, which leaves a required build stuck at **“Expected / Waiting for status to be reported.”** In that case, retrigger the check; if you need to refresh all checks after branch maintenance, the documented workaround is to **close and reopen the PR**. See the branch-update guidance here: [Create a PR against main | Update your branch with changes from main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish).

- **`SDK Validation Status` stuck pending:** If you **do not see any `SDK Validation - {Language}` checks at all**, that usually means the PR author is missing required permissions. The documented fixes are to get the needed write access, make Azure org membership **public**, and ensure the required partner-group access is in place; once a language-specific SDK validation is rerun, `SDK Validation Status` is re-evaluated. See: [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).

- **Out-of-date protected/release branch infrastructure:** The docs explicitly note that old branches can reach a state where PR checks do not function correctly until the branch is refreshed from `main`. For unprotected branches, merge `main`; for protected `release-*` branches, use the documented helper flow here: [Create a PR against main | Update your branch with changes from main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish).

- **Check may not actually be required on that branch:** Required checks differ by branch. Before spending time on a stuck check, confirm the branch’s required-check matrix here: [API versions and branches](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches). If `Automated merging requirements met` is green, the PR is not blocked by required automation; see: [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

- **If the workflow automation itself is broken:** The guidance for SDK validation is to have **azure-rest-api-specs maintainers rerun or repair the workflow**, then rerun SDK validation from the PR. Start from: [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).

</details>

question: If an Azure REST API specs PR appears blocked in the merge or check workflow, what contributor access and permissions should the PR author verify first to rule out repository permission-related blocking issues?

First verify that the PR author has completed the required Azure SDK access setup. They should follow the instructions at aka.ms/azsdk/access. Missing this setup should be treated as an early thing to fix when a PR is unexpectedly blocked.

**Cached dev answer**

First, confirm the PR is **actually blocked by required checks**: if **`Automated merging requirements met`** is green, the PR is **not** blocked by automation, even if some non-required checks are failing. After that, the first permission checks for the PR author are:

- **Verify your GitHub account is linked to your Microsoft account** using the [access setup guide](https://aka.ms/azsdk/access). The specs PR docs explicitly require a linked GitHub/Microsoft account plus repo permissions before PR workflows work.
- **Verify you have access to the correct repo**:
  - Public work: [Azure/azure-rest-api-specs](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs)
  - Private work: [Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr)
- **Make your membership in the `Azure` GitHub organization public** on the [Azure org people page](https://github.com/orgs/Azure/people?query=). The specs guidance specifically calls out private org membership as a common cause when PR gateway pipelines do not start or SDK validation checks do not appear.
- **Ensure you have the required write/partner access** from the [access setup guide](https://aka.ms/azsdk/access) — especially if expected `SDK Validation - {Language}` checks are missing. The SDK validation guidance says missing SDK validation checks usually means the author lacks the permission required to trigger them.
- **If this is an RPaaS/private-branch workflow**, also verify membership in the [RP platform Users group](https://repos.opensource.microsoft.com/orgs/Azure/teams/rpaas-users), because that group is required for some private-repo merge paths.

**Adjacent case to rule out:** if your PR targets **`main` in `azure-rest-api-specs-pr`**, that branch is **read-only by design**. In that case, inability to merge is not a personal permission problem.

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Should teams bypass the Python PyPI package-name check to unblock a release?

question: When a spec PR fails Python SDK validation because the intended Python package name has not yet been registered on PyPI, should the team bypass or suppress that check to release sooner, or should they complete package-name registration instead?

**Historical ground truth**

Teams generally should not bypass this Python package-name check just to accelerate a release. The check is intended to prevent the desired package name from being maliciously claimed on PyPI; if that happens, reclaiming the name can take much longer or require choosing a different package name. If registration can proceed in parallel, that is the preferred approach rather than relying on a bypass.

**Cached dev answer**

No — the team should **not bypass or suppress** that check to ship sooner, and they also should **not try to register/reserve the name on PyPI** as a workaround.

- If Python SDK validation says the **package-name review is incomplete**, and your spec PR already has the Python package settings but is missing the expected package-name review comment/labels/blocking status, treat that as an **automation/workflow issue**, not as a signal to suppress validation. Follow the guidance in [Review SDK package names | Troubleshoot a missing package-name review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/develop/namespace-review): ask `azure-rest-api-specs` maintainers to rerun/fix the package-name review workflow, then rerun SDK validation.
- The same guidance explicitly says **don’t open a separate manual review request** and **don’t register or reserve the package on PyPI or another registry** just to clear this failure. So between your two options, **“complete package-name registration on PyPI” is also not the right fix**.
- For Python releases, publication to PyPI happens through the supported Azure DevOps/ESRP release flow described in [Release process | Python Package Index](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-python/blob/main/doc/dev/release.md) and [ESRP Release Process](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-python/blob/main/doc/esrp_release.md), not by manual pre-registration/upload.
- Practically: the fastest supported path is **fix/rerun the package-name review workflow**, not bypass it.

</details>

**Historical ground truth**

No. For a public preview service, completing a beta SDK release is part of the preview requirement, and reserving the Python package name is a prerequisite for that process. The package name should be reviewed and reserved during spec PR review so it is not claimed by attackers and to avoid the effort and delays of reclaiming an occupied PyPI name later.

No — for a **public preview** spec PR, you should **not treat the Python package-name check as something to skip just because the SDK name is still undecided**. But the guidance also says **do not reserve a registry package as a workaround** for validation automation. Instead, the PR needs the **required package-name review/approval signals** completed, using the exact intended Python package name in the PR metadata/Required Artifacts.\

- The SDK validation guidance says the PR can be blocked when **required package-name review signals or approvals are missing**. It also explicitly says that if the automation failed, you should have the workflow rerun/repaired and complete the approvals — **not reserve a registry package as a workaround**.
- The Required Artifacts guidance also expects an **exact Python package name** value.
- Since **public preview** PRs go to public `main`, and that branch is for finished specs released to customers, the practical takeaway is: if the Python package name is not settled enough to supply the required review/approval inputs, the PR is **not really ready for public-preview merge yet**.

**What to do**
- **Do not try to bypass it by reserving on PyPI first** just to make validation happy.
- **Choose the intended Python package name now**, put it into the PR’s Required Artifacts exactly as required, and complete the package-name review/approval flow.
- If the validation workflow is stuck or misfired, have it rerun and then rerun **SDK Validation - Python** from the PR checks guidance at [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- If the team truly cannot decide the package name yet, the safest answer is to **hold the public preview PR** until that naming decision is made, because public `main` is for customer-ready public-preview/GA specs as described in [API versions and branches](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches).

It correctly states conversion must be horizontal, with no API changes and no version rev, and recommends converting the latest existing version first, then adding the new version separately. Its added rationale about reducing APIView noise is consistent with retrieved review guidance and does not contradict the core recommendation.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that TypeSpec conversion and adding a new API version should be split into separate PRs, not combined.; Explain that OpenAPI-to-TypeSpec conversion is a horizontal migration that must not change the API contract.; Explain that the conversion PR must not rev or introduce a new api-version.; Recommend first converting the latest existing approved/current version to TypeSpec in one PR.; Recommend adding the new API version in a follow-up PR after conversion, using TypeSpec.; Ground the recommendation in durable process/validation concerns, such as PR checks/review difficulty when conversion and versioning are mixed.

**Frozen facts:** The scenario combined a new stable API version with conversion from handwritten Swagger to TypeSpec.; The author stated there were zero intended API surface changes from the prior approved version.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [repository-workflow-02-001](expert-knowledge-report.md#repository-workflow-02-001), [review-process-02-028](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-02-028)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Should TypeSpec conversion and a new API version be combined in one PR?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

Historical context: a service needed a new API version, had zero intended behavioral API changes from the prior approved version, and also converted the spec from handwritten Swagger/OpenAPI to TypeSpec in the same PR. What process is recommended: combine both changes in one PR or split them?

**Historical ground truth**

Do not combine a TypeSpec conversion with adding a new API version in the same PR. That pattern is a diagonal conversion, and it is not the recommended approach. Instead, first convert the latest existing API version from Swagger/OpenAPI to TypeSpec in one PR without revving the version. Then add the new API version in a second PR using TypeSpec. TypeSpec conversion guidance says the conversion scope should be horizontal: it should not introduce API changes and should not rev the API version. PR checks are not designed to handle a diagonal conversion well, so splitting the work avoids that problem.

**Cached dev answer**

**Recommended process:** **split them into separate PRs**.

- **PR 1: TypeSpec conversion only.** The documented conversion scope is explicitly **horizontal**: it **must not change the API** and **must not rev the API version**. That means the conversion PR should preserve the existing approved contract rather than introduce a new `api-version`.
- **PR 2: new API version only, if still needed.** Handle the version bump as a separate change so review/validation can assess the versioned delta on its own.
- **Why split:** review guidance says a new-version PR should show the actual changes **without extra “noise”** in APIView. A Swagger→TypeSpec rewrite adds a lot of representation noise even when behavior is unchanged, so combining it with a new version makes review and breaking-change analysis harder.

So the reusable answer is: **do not combine a brownfield TypeSpec migration with a new API version in one PR unless you have a very unusual, explicitly approved exception**. Convert first, keep the contract unchanged, then do the versioned change separately.

</details>

title: How should a horizontal TypeSpec conversion be structured?

Yes. A horizontal TypeSpec conversion should be done against the existing API version rather than by creating a new version. Yes — for a **horizontal** handwritten OpenAPI → TypeSpec migration, you should convert the **existing API version**, not create a new API version just for the conversion.

- The guidance explicitly says **no API version revving occurs during conversion**.
- The recommended target is the **newest existing version** for which SDKs have been generated, whether that version is **stable or preview**.
- After conversion, compile and compare the emitted OpenAPI with the original spec to confirm they are functionally equivalent.

If you want to make **real API changes**, treat that as a **separate versioning exercise**. In other words:
- **Conversion PR**: same API version, no contract changes.
- **Feature/breaking-change PR**: new API version if required by versioning policy.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: What are best practices for minimizing differences when converting OpenAPI to TypeSpec?

question: What are best practices for converting a handwritten OpenAPI specification to TypeSpec while minimizing unnecessary differences from the original spec and keeping SDK shape as similar as practical?

**Historical ground truth**

Focus on making the TypeSpec correct and aligned with repository best practices rather than trying to force the emitted OpenAPI to match handwritten Swagger exactly. For SDK generation, use the current language-specific TypeSpec guidance and the latest DPG emitters. Some differences between AutoRest-based output and DPG-emitter output are expected, but method signatures and models can often remain similar. Prefer native TypeSpec constructs and decorators, such as the proper paging decorators, instead of carrying forward OpenAPI-specific extensions into the TypeSpec source.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — the best practice is to treat this as a **brownfield compatibility exercise, not a redesign**. The converted TypeSpec should preserve the released OpenAPI contract and SDK-facing shape as much as practical, and you should only keep differences that reflect a real service change or a required TypeSpec/Azure convention.

- **Use a horizontal-conversion mindset.** Follow the scope in [Convert OpenAPI specs to TypeSpec](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs/api-typespec-conversion): do **not** introduce API changes or rev the version just because you are moving to TypeSpec.

- **Continuously compare generated OpenAPI to the handwritten OpenAPI.** The migration guidance in [Getting started with TypeSpec migration](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/01-get-started) recommends compiling TypeSpec, diffing the emitted OpenAPI against the original, and iterating. Fix differences in this order:
  1. routes/paths
  2. model/definition names
  3. lower-level detail differences

- **Preserve the contract with the simplest TypeSpec construct.** Per [Fixing Converted TypeSpec](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/faq/conversionfix), don’t keep OpenAPI-only constructs unless necessary. For example, if SDK grouping/name drift comes from `operationId`, prefer TypeSpec client metadata such as `@clientLocation` / `@clientName` over retaining raw OpenAPI annotations.

- **Prefer compatibility over linter purity for older specs.** If the original OpenAPI is effectively “grandfathered,” the equivalent TypeSpec may violate current lints. In that case, use **targeted suppressions** instead of reshaping the API and risking breaks, as described in [Fixing Converted TypeSpec](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/faq/conversionfix).

- **Accept only the differences that are truly required.** [Understanding the OpenAPI Changes](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/faq/mustread) calls out some changes that can be expected when aligning to Azure conventions, such as common ARM resource bases or standard paging forms. Those are acceptable when they are convention-driven and harmless; otherwise preserve the original shape.

- **Use SDK generation as a validation signal, not as permission to drift.** The conversion process document says SDKs generated from the TypeSpec during migration are for **validation**, so use them to detect accidental shape changes early rather than to justify broad refactoring.

- **Watch the common drift areas first.** The conversion docs specifically call out:
  - route/path differences
  - model naming differences
  - casing differences
  - datetime-format differences

If you want a one-line rule: **preserve the released OpenAPI shape first, then use TypeSpec-native/customization mechanisms to recover SDK compatibility, and only accept differences that are required by Azure conventions or true service behavior.**

</details>

**Replay question**

title: What SDK generation strategy is recommended during or after TypeSpec migration?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

When migrating a service from handwritten Swagger/OpenAPI to TypeSpec, what SDK generation strategy is recommended if the team expects either very few future SDK changes or continued SDK evolution?

**Historical ground truth**

Do not plan on generating shipping SDKs from Swagger emitted by TypeSpec as a long-term strategy. If very little SDK change is expected going forward, a practical option is to stop generating and update the SDK manually. If the SDK is expected to continue evolving for months or years, invest in moving to direct TypeSpec-based generation and rebase the current generated code onto TypeSpec-generated code. Time spent trying to patch TypeSpec solely to reproduce a preferred emitted Swagger shape is generally not a good long-term investment.

**Cached dev answer**

Short answer: treat the **migration itself** as a **horizontal conversion**, not an SDK-refresh event. The migration guidance says converted TypeSpec should not change the API or rev versions, and any SDKs produced from the converted TypeSpec are **for validation only, not production release**.

- **If you expect very few future SDK changes:** the practical recommendation is to **keep the existing released SDK path** and use TypeSpec-generated SDKs only to validate that the migration preserved the existing contract. That follows from the conversion guidance that generated SDKs during migration are validation-only.
- **If you expect continued SDK evolution:** migrate the service to **TypeSpec-based SDK generation** and make TypeSpec the ongoing source for SDK output. Configure language emitters in [`tspconfig.yaml`](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-spec-gen-sdk-config) and use the [Azure SDK Tools Agent](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/develop/sdk-develop) as the primary workflow for generation, validation, and release.
- **Do not run both generation paths at once:** the SDK generation config guidance says you **cannot enable both OpenAPI and TypeSpec generation simultaneously**; disable one before enabling the other at [SDK generation configuration](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-spec-gen-sdk-config).

</details>

title: How to proceed when ARM review blocks a PR and you need ARMChangesRequested cleared

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If ARM review blocks a PR over GET-shape concerns and the author wants to continue the review or argue for their design, what is the correct process in the PR, and what should they do if they cannot remove the ARMChangesRequested label themselves?

**Historical ground truth**

Use the ARM review workflow in the PR itself. Reply directly to the ARM reviewers' comments to discuss the design, then remove the ARMChangesRequested label so ARM review can continue, following the documented next steps for the PR. If you do not have permission to remove that label, you likely also do not have permission to merge. In that case, follow the repository access process, or have the PR author or another teammate with the necessary permissions remove the label.

**Cached dev answer**

The correct path is to keep the discussion **in the PR** and follow the PR automation’s **Next Steps to Merge** instructions for ARM review. If ARM has concerns about the GET shape and you want to continue the review or defend the design, respond on the PR, address the feedback there, and then get the PR back into the ARM review flow rather than trying to bypass it.

- **In the PR, continue the discussion and resolve/respond to the ARM feedback there.** The spec PR process is driven by the PR template/comments and the ARM review step. See [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review) and [Create a PR against a specs repo](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).
- **To resume ARM review, `ARMChangesRequested` must be removed.** The ARM review guidance says that once that label is removed, `WaitForARMFeedback` should be added and the PR can re-enter the ARM queue. See [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).
- **If you can’t remove `ARMChangesRequested` yourself, ask in the PR / prescribed “Getting help” path for someone with permission to remove it.** The docs do not state a separate self-service fallback; they point you to the PR’s help path and ARM reviewer help/office hours when you need assistance. See [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to evaluate many TypeSpec suppressions in a new preview ARM API PR

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

Historical context: for a new preview ARM API version authored in TypeSpec, the spec under review had many suppressions in .tsp sources, and reviewers also discussed direct OpenAPI decoration for long-running operations, hand-authored x-ms-examples, and repetitive custom operations for resources exposed at multiple endpoints. In that situation, how should reviewers evaluate which suppressions are acceptable versus signs that the TypeSpec should be refactored instead, and what authoring patterns are preferred?

**Historical ground truth**

For a new preview ARM API version authored in TypeSpec, a large number of suppressions should be treated as a warning sign. The default expectation is to fix the TypeSpec and follow Azure ARM and SDK-friendly authoring patterns, not to rely on broad or permanent suppressions.

Suppressions are generally acceptable only when they are narrow and well-justified, such as:
- brownfield or migration cases affecting older OpenAPI artifacts that have not yet been migrated,
- narrowly scoped `SdkTspConfigValidation` suppressions for specific necessary `tspconfig.yaml` deviations, or
- confirmed tooling bugs or approved exceptions.

For a brand-new preview surface, reviewers should usually expect the spec to be fixed instead of suppressing issues such as:
- ARM or Azure Resource Manager rule violations,
- anonymous types or anonymous parameters in resource-manager specs,
- missing integer formats, and
- broad `TypeSpecRequirement` or `TypeSpecValidation` suppressions against the new generated preview API.

The preferred remedy is to refactor the TypeSpec to use standard Azure Resource Manager templates, named models, and correct schema details directly in source. Directly applying OpenAPI decorations for long-running operations is a poor pattern, and hand-authoring `x-ms-examples` is brittle and likely to fail on later API versioning. When resources are exposed at multiple endpoints, `LegacyOperations` is preferable to repetitive custom operations because it reuses parameter definitions and template operation definitions, reducing boilerplate and improving maintainability and reviewability.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — in that kind of **new preview ARM TypeSpec PR**, reviewers should usually treat suppressions as **exceptions with a specific justification**, not as the default authoring strategy. If the code needs many suppressions because it is bypassing ARM/TypeSpec templates, repeating the same workaround across endpoints, or patching emitted Swagger directly, that is a strong sign the spec should be **refactored toward native TypeSpec ARM patterns** instead.

- **Accept a suppression** when it is:
  - a **false positive**,
  - a **known library limitation / legacy constraint**, or
  - an **ARM-reviewed exception** with a clear reason.\
  The expected pattern is a narrow `#suppress` on the violating declaration, using the **fully qualified rule name plus a reason**, per [ARM Rules, TypeSpec Linting, and Suppression](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/arm-rules).

- **Prefer refactoring over suppression** when:
  - the warning points to a rule that already has a native ARM TypeSpec fix,
  - the same suppression appears repeatedly across similar operations,
  - authors are adding **OpenAPI-only decorations** to force the generated Swagger shape,
  - or the suppressions are compensating for copy/pasted operation patterns that should be reusable.\
  That is especially important because the repo guidance for TypeSpec-generated Swagger says not to use OpenAPI-only workarounds that change only emitted OpenAPI while leaving the TypeSpec semantic model different; use a scoped Swagger suppression only for genuine validator/emitter issues, per [Swagger LintDiff](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-LintDiff).

- **For long-running operations**, the preferred pattern is to model them with **ARM/Azure TypeSpec templates and helpers**, not by directly decorating OpenAPI:
  - use ARM operation templates such as `ArmCustomPatchAsync` or the action templates in [ARM Resource Operations](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/resource-operations),
  - and use the Azure/Core LRO model so emitters can derive LRO metadata such as `final-state-via`, as described in [Deep Dive: Long-running (Asynchronous) Operations](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/azure-core/long-running-operations).\
  For a **new preview** API, reviewers should generally push authors away from direct `@typespec/openapi` / `@extension(...)` fixes for LRO behavior unless they are preserving an already-published contract and there is no equivalent TypeSpec expression.

- **For `x-ms-examples`**, the preferred pattern is **example files**, not inline OpenAPI extension decoration.\
  The TypeSpec guidance explicitly says **do not use** `@extension("x-ms-examples", ...)`; instead keep examples in the versioned examples folder and let the emitter wire them up, per [x-ms-examples example files](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/faq/x-ms-examples).

- **For repetitive custom operations on resources exposed at multiple endpoints/scopes**, prefer **reusable operation aliases or generic interfaces** over duplicating bespoke operations:
  - TypeSpec ARM guidance recommends operation/interface templates first, then lower-level custom building blocks only when templates do not fit, in [ARM Resource Operations](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/resource-operations).
  - The docs also show reusing the same operation alias across multiple resource interfaces/scopes, which is the cleaner pattern reviewers should prefer over cloning equivalent custom ops, in [Using Private Endpoints with Child Resources](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/private-endpoints) and the extension-scope examples in [Modeling Resources in TypeSpec](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/resource-type).

- **A practical review heuristic**:
  - **Good suppression**: narrow, explained, and tied to a known false positive or library quirk.
  - **Bad suppression smell**: broad, repeated, or used to keep an OpenAPI-centric design alive in TypeSpec.
  - **Preferred authoring**: ARM templates, reusable interfaces/aliases, file-based examples, and semantic TypeSpec LRO modeling.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Choose GET for a read-only paginated query without side effects

question: For an Azure API, should a read-only paginated query with no side effects use GET even if the endpoint is not a tracked resource?

**Historical ground truth**

Yes. A read-only retrieval or list operation with no side effects should use GET, even if the endpoint is not a tracked resource. POST is better reserved for actions or body-driven bulk operations rather than standard read or list semantics. For pagination, return a nextLink and have clients follow that URL with GET. For a new API, prefer a regular query parameter name such as skipToken instead of $skiptoken unless legacy compatibility requires the dollar-prefixed form. Also avoid action-like naming for a collection-style read operation when it can be modeled as a collection.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **use `GET`** for a read-only paginated query with no side effects, even if the endpoint is **not** a tracked resource.

- **Why:** Azure guidance treats `GET` as the normal verb for reads and paged list/query operations. ARM guidance also says collection `GET`s use paging (`nextLink` / pageable), and the TypeSpec guidance notes that standard automated paging expects `GET`; if you use another verb, SDKs typically need custom paging code.
- **Important distinction:** **“not a tracked resource” does not mean “don’t use GET.”** The tracked-resource rules mostly affect **which list operations are required** at certain scopes, not whether a side-effect-free read should be modeled as `GET`.
- **When `POST` is the adjacent valid variant:** use `POST` only if this is really an **action** endpoint or you need a request body for complex inputs that cannot reasonably fit query parameters. ARM does allow some read-only `POST` actions at subscription/tenant scope, but that is a special-case action pattern, not the default for normal paginated reads.

If you’re authoring this in TypeSpec/ARM, the safest pattern is a normal paged **GET** list/query operation, not a `POST` action.

</details>

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [review-process-01-021](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-01-021)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Why does WaitForARMFeedback get removed from a PR, and can it be manually restored?

question: In Azure REST API specs PR workflow, why might the WaitForARMFeedback label be removed automatically, and can contributors restore it manually?

**Historical ground truth**

WaitForARMFeedback is managed by automation, so manually re-adding it will not persist. If a PR still has ARMChangesRequested, the path forward is to have ARM review updated so that ARMChangesRequested is cleared; the label behavior reflects review state rather than being the root cause of the block.

**Cached dev answer**

`WaitForARMFeedback` is an automation-managed **queue state** for ARM review, not a “sticky” label contributors should treat as permanent.

- **Why it gets removed automatically**
  - If the ARM review workflow finds **Critic-verified blocking findings**, the workflow adds `ARMChangesRequested` and removes `WaitForARMFeedback`.
  - If the PR has already reached **`ARMSignedOff`**, automation treats `WaitForARMFeedback` as invalid in that state and removes it.
  - Separately, the documented path into the ARM queue is: once `ARMChangesRequested` is cleared, automation should add `WaitForARMFeedback` again.

- **Can contributors manually restore it?**
  - I could verify that the **documented** way to get the label back is **not** “manually restore it,” but to put the PR back into the correct state so automation re-adds it.
  - In practice: if `ARMChangesRequested` is on the PR, fix the blocking feedback and then follow the PR instructions in [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).
  - If you’re unsure why the label disappeared, check the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** comment first, then use [PR getting help](https://aka.ms/azsdk/pr-getting-help).

So the short answer is: **it is usually removed because the PR moved out of the “waiting for ARM” state, and contributors should rely on automation to re-add it rather than treating it as a manual label to restore.**

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Who should modify ARM lease files in a spec PR

question: If a spec PR triggers ARM lease-related checks, should the PR author add or modify lease.yaml themselves, or is that handled by Modeling reviewers?

**Historical ground truth**

PR authors should not add or modify the ARM lease file themselves. Lease files are owned by Modeling reviewers, who have the necessary access and handle adding or deleting lease entries. Contributors do not need to take action on that file.

**Cached dev answer**

No — a normal spec PR author generally should **not** add or modify `lease.yaml` just because an ARM lease-related check showed up.

- The ARM lease guidance says **only Product Managers (PMs)** are authorized to add or modify lease files, and that this happens **after office hours discussions with the RP owner**.
- So if your PR needs an ARM lease/design-discussion period, the right path is to work with the **ARM modeling/PM reviewers**, not to self-edit `.github/arm-leases/.../lease.yaml` in your spec PR.
- One important detail: ARM leases are read from **`main` in the public `azure-rest-api-specs` repo**, and lease files present only in your PR branch are **ignored**. So adding one in your branch usually does not solve the check.

**Exception:** if your PR is already the one intentionally changing a lease file and the **ARM Lease Validation** check fails, then that lease file change itself needs to be corrected per the lease rules in the ARM lease guidance at [ARM Leases README](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/main/.github/arm-leases/README.md).

</details>
