**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [versioning-01-052](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-052)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: When a new scenario justifies making a required property optional

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

In an ARM/TypeSpec API, a property is currently required because it is needed for one product mode, but a new mode has no meaningful value for that property. In the historical scenario, a Cluster rack definition required networkRackId for managed clusters, while a bring-your-own network fabric mode had no associated network rack; the property also participated in linked access checks when present. Is making that property optional in a new API version a reasonable breaking change, and what alternatives should be considered first?

**Historical ground truth**

Changing a property from required to optional is a breaking change. If this change is made, it should be introduced only in a new API version and handled through the normal breaking-change approval process.

The preferred design approach is to first consider additive alternatives that keep the existing contract stable, such as:
- adding an explicit mode property for the new scenario while keeping the existing property shape stable, with scenario-specific validation enforced by the service, or
- introducing a separate model or resource shape if the scenarios are materially different.

Those alternatives have trade-offs. Keeping a property required when it is not meaningful in one mode can produce an awkward contract if callers must send a placeholder value. Changing an existing model into a discriminated union is also a breaking change and is typically more invasive for clients and SDKs than making a single property optional.

A required-to-optional change can be a reasonable breaking-change proposal when the property genuinely does not apply in the new scenario, older API versions remain unchanged, runtime validation still enforces the property where it is logically required, and the proposal clearly explains customer impact, alternatives considered, and versioning behavior.

If proceeding in TypeSpec, keep older versions unchanged and make the property optional only in the new version using versioning decorators such as @madeOptional; a new mode field can be added separately if it improves clarity.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **in a new API version**, making that property optional can be a **reasonable way to unblock a genuinely new mode** where the old required contract no longer makes sense. But it should be treated as a **breaking change decision**, not as a routine additive change: TypeSpec supports `@madeOptional(...)`, yet making a property optional is still considered breaking when that property appears in responses, and Azure guidance says any on-the-wire change belongs in a **new dated API version**, not an in-place edit of an existing version. If the property also affects linked-access or permission checks when present, that is additionally a **service behavior change** that should be reviewed as such. See the TypeSpec versioning guidance and Azure versioning guidance: [TypeSpec ARM versioning](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/versioning), [TypeSpec versioning guide](https://typespec.io/docs/libraries/versioning/guide), [Azure Versioning Guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/VersioningGuidelines.md).

Before doing that, the safer alternatives to consider first are:

- **Keep the old contract intact and model the new mode separately**, if you can, so existing clients do not see a formerly-required field become optional. Azure’s compatibility guidance prefers preserving prior shapes and introducing new behavior only via clearly versioned surface changes. See [Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines | API Versioning](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md) and [CPEX FAQ: When is a new API version required?](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/faq_breaking_changes).

- **If you need both “optional” and a default/replacement behavior, do not assume `@madeOptional` is enough.** The retrieved TypeSpec guidance says `@madeOptional` versions only the optionality change; it does **not** version adding a default. The recommended workaround is the **replace-property pattern**: remove/rename the old property in the new version and add a new optional property for the new semantics. See [TypeSpec versioning guide](https://typespec.io/docs/libraries/versioning/guide) and [TypeSpec ARM versioning](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/versioning).

- **Treat permission/linked-access implications as first-class review criteria.** Azure guidance explicitly calls out changing required permissions as a behavior change that must not be slipped into an existing customer-visible version. See [Azure Versioning Guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/VersioningGuidelines.md).

So the reusable answer is:

- **Yes, it can be justified in a new API version** when a new scenario makes the old required field meaningless.
- **No, it is not the first choice** if you can preserve the old contract through a separate modeled path.
- **Prefer alternatives that isolate the new semantics first**; if those are not viable, ship the optionality change in a new version and handle it as a breaking-change-reviewed design choice.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to suppress the TypeSpecValidation FolderStructure MustUseV2 check

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a resource provider needs to temporarily remain on folder structure v1 and migrate to v2 in a later PR, how should suppressions.yaml be configured to suppress the TypeSpecValidation FolderStructure/MustUseV2 check?

**Historical ground truth**

Add a suppressions.yaml entry for the TypeSpecValidation tool that suppresses the FolderStructure rule and MustUseV2 sub-rule, and list the affected service folder paths under paths. Use this structure:
- tool: TypeSpecValidation
  rules: [FolderStructure]
  sub-rules: [MustUseV2]
  reason: temporarily bypass the check; a later PR will refactor to v2
  paths:
    - <affected service folder path>
Set paths to the actual service folders reported by the tooling.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — configure `suppressions.yaml` as a **TypeSpecValidation** suppression for the **`FolderStructure`** rule and the **`MustUseV2`** sub-rule.

```yaml
- tool: TypeSpecValidation
  rules: [FolderStructure]
  sub-rules: [MustUseV2]
  reason: Temporarily remaining on folder structure v1; migration to v2 will happen in a follow-up PR.
  paths:
    - <TypeSpec project folder>
```

**What to put in `paths`:**
- Use the affected **TypeSpec project folder name(s)**, for example:
  - `Napster.CompanionAPI.Management`
  - `Discovery.Bookshelf`
  - `DBforPostgreSQL.Management`

**Where to put the file:**
- Put `suppressions.yaml` at the **root of the service spec folder**, for example `specification/<service>/suppressions.yaml`.
- Keep the suppression scoped as narrowly as possible.

**Example**
```yaml
- tool: TypeSpecValidation
  rules: [FolderStructure]
  sub-rules: [MustUseV2]
  reason: Temporarily remaining on folder structure v1; conversion to v2 is planned in a later PR.
  paths:
    - Contoso.Management
```

This matches repository examples and the validation logic that checks for `FolderStructure` plus sub-rule `MustUseV2`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Handle false-positive ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly in TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

In a TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI spec, LintDiff reports ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly even though provisioningState is already effectively readOnly. What is the preferred fix, and what should be done if the validator still fails after the spec is corrected?

**Historical ground truth**

For TypeSpec-generated specs, the preferred fix is to enable use-read-only-status-schema: true and re-emit the OpenAPI so provisioningState is represented explicitly as readOnly in the generated swagger. That accuracy fix should be preferred even if it causes minor updates in older swagger files by adding explicit readOnly annotations to fields that were already intended to be read-only. If the validator still reports ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly after the spec is correct, add a scoped LintDiff suppression for the exact reported path using the documented PR suppression process and a clear justification.

**Cached dev answer**

The preferred fix is to correct the **TypeSpec emitter output**, not to patch the generated OpenAPI by hand.

- **Preferred fix:** set `use-read-only-status-schema: true` in `tspconfig.yaml` for `@azure-tools/typespec-autorest`. That is the documented workaround for the known validator limitation around `$ref` siblings that can trigger `ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly` even when `provisioningState` is effectively read-only. See **Swagger LintDiff**: [Swagger-LintDiff](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-LintDiff).
- **Do not** work around this with OpenAPI-only decorators or `#suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/no-openapi"` just to change the emitted Swagger. The guidance says those can make the generated OpenAPI diverge from the TypeSpec semantic model.
- **If enabling `use-read-only-status-schema: true` would change already-published API versions:** keep the TypeSpec model unchanged and add a **narrowly scoped Swagger/LintDiff suppression** for the exact generated schema/version, with a descriptive reason. Use the documented scoped suppression process here: [Swagger-LintDiff](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-LintDiff).
- **If the validator still fails after the spec is correctly fixed:** treat it as a validator false positive and add that same **scoped suppression** rather than forcing more OpenAPI-only changes.

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to interpret a breaking-change tag that also appears on a no-op PR

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a minimal no-op PR that changes only whitespace or descriptive text still triggers a Go breaking-change tag, what does that imply about the source of the problem?

**Historical ground truth**

Use a minimal PR that changes only whitespace or descriptive text to isolate whether a reported Go breaking change is caused by your actual modification. If that no-op PR still reports the Go breaking-change tag, that indicates the problem is likely pre-existing in the spec on the main branch rather than introduced by your PR.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — that usually implies the **Go breaking-change signal is coming from the spec comparison context, not from the whitespace or descriptive-text edit itself**.

- A `BreakingChange-Go-Sdk` tag means the tooling detected a **generated Go SDK surface break** from the spec state being compared.
- If a **no-op PR** still triggers it, the meaningful difference is usually **already present in the compared API versions / repository state**; the trivial PR merely **caused the check to run and expose it**.
- In Azure spec validation, breaking-change automation reasons over the **published baseline and the versions present in the repo**, not just the exact hunks edited in the PR.
- A known case is when versions were merged **out of release order** or a branch is **out of sync**: then a later trivial PR can surface a breaking change that was effectively introduced earlier.
- So the right interpretation is: **“this PR exposed an existing comparison problem”**, not **“whitespace caused a Go SDK break.”**

If you need to act on a live PR, the reusable process is still to follow that PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** and the breaking-change flow at https://aka.ms/brch.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to model RPaaS provisioningState when services return additional states

question: For an RPaaS-managed ARM resource in TypeSpec, should provisioningState use Azure.ResourceManager.ResourceProvisioningState even if the service can return additional states such as Accepted? If extra states are needed, how should they be modeled?

**Historical ground truth**

Use the built-in Azure.ResourceManager.ResourceProvisioningState for an ARM provisioningState property, and keep the property optional and read-only. That built-in type represents the standard terminal states Succeeded, Failed, and Canceled; it is not intended to enumerate every non-terminal or service-specific state. It is acceptable for the standard type to cover only that subset. If the resource can return additional values such as Accepted, Provisioning, or Updating, model the property as a union that includes ResourceProvisioningState plus the extra literal values, and optionally string if future ad hoc values should also be allowed.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — for an RPaaS ARM resource, you should still base `provisioningState` on `Azure.ResourceManager.ResourceProvisioningState`. If your service returns extra values like `Accepted`, do **not** replace it with a completely separate enum; instead, define a custom `@lroStatus` union that **includes** `ResourceProvisioningState` and adds your extra states.

- **Use the built-in type directly** when you only need the standard ARM states.
- **Use a custom union** when your service returns additional non-terminal states such as `Accepted`, `Provisioning`, `Updating`, or other service-defined values.
- Keep `provisioningState` as a **read-only lifecycle property** with `@visibility(Lifecycle.Read)`.
- ARM requires the terminal states **Succeeded**, **Failed**, and **Canceled** to be present. Extra states are modeled as **non-terminal** states.

**If you only need standard states:**
```typespec
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager";
using Azure.ResourceManager;

model MyResourceProperties {
  ...DefaultProvisioningStateProperty;
}
```

**If you need extra states like `Accepted`:**
```typespec
import "@typespec/versioning";
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core";
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager";

using Azure.Core;
using Azure.ResourceManager;

@lroStatus
union ProvisioningState {
  ResourceProvisioningState,
  Provisioning: "Provisioning",
  Updating: "Updating",
  Deleting: "Deleting",
  Accepted: "Accepted",
  string,
}

model MyResourceProperties {
  @visibility(Lifecycle.Read)
  provisioningState?: ProvisioningState;
}
```

A few correctness notes:

- `Accepted` is fine as an **additional non-terminal** provisioning state.
- Including `string` keeps the union **open/extensible**, which matches current ARM guidance and TypeSpec samples.
- Do **not** use `provisioningState` to represent overall health/runtime state; it is only for the latest long-running PUT/PATCH/DELETE operation.

</details>

### spec-review-0131: Can an ARM list operation be made non-pageable by setting nextLinkName to null?

**Dataset:** `spec-review.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0147](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0147) | **GT basis:** expert | **Temporal scope:** mixed | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-05-18T22:45:42.648Z

**Assessment:** The answer matches the historical guidance: ARM collection/list GET operations are expected to be pageable, `nextLinkName: null` is not the correct fix, and the proper model is the standard list envelope with optional `nextLink`/`x-ms-pageable` using `nextLink`. It also correctly frames a failing followed `nextLink` as a service/runtime issue rather than a spec-shape fix.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that an ARM collection/list GET must follow ARM paging semantics rather than being converted to a non-pageable shape by setting `nextLinkName` to `null`.; Explain that the correct ARM/OpenAPI paging declaration for such list operations is paging metadata with `nextLinkName` set to `nextLink`, not `null`.; Clarify that `nextLink` is optional at runtime, so a single-page implementation can simply omit it when there are no more results.; Preserve the standard list response contract (`value` plus optional `nextLink`) instead of changing between pageable and non-pageable response shapes.; If a returned `nextLink` is populated but unusable, identify that as a service/platform/runtime defect rather than a reason to remove paging metadata from the spec.

**Frozen facts:** A GET list request returned 200 with a value array and a populated nextLink.; Following the returned nextLink produced a 502 response.; The 502 body reported ProviderError and said the resource provider failed to return collection response for type 'clusters'.; The proposed fix was to set nextLinkName to null so the operation would not appear pageable.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [spec-review-01-007](expert-knowledge-report.md#spec-review-01-007), [spec-review-01-008](expert-knowledge-report.md#spec-review-01-008)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can an ARM list operation be made non-pageable by setting nextLinkName to null?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

**Historical ground truth**

No. ARM list operations are required to be pageable, so setting nextLinkName to null is not the right way to address this behavior. If the response includes a populated nextLink that fails when followed, that points to the service or platform returning an invalid nextLink rather than a specification problem. Pageable behavior is part of the contract for list operations, and changing between pageable and non-pageable shapes is not an appropriate fix here.

**Cached dev answer**

No. For an **Azure Resource Manager collection `GET`**, you should **not** try to make it “non-pageable” by setting `nextLinkName` to `null`.

- **ARM rule:** collection/list `GET` operations **must use paging**. The required ARM pattern is a response with a `value` array and an **optional** `nextLink`; clients continue until `nextLink` is absent or `null`.
- **Why `nextLinkName: null` is wrong:** ARM list operations are expected to declare paging metadata using `x-ms-pageable` with `nextLinkName` set to **`nextLink`**. Using `null` would contradict the ARM list contract rather than express “single page only.”
- **Recommended modeling:** keep the operation as a normal ARM list operation and keep `nextLink` optional. If the service currently returns everything in one page, it can simply omit `nextLink` at runtime.
- **Historical migration guidance:** when teams had a similar pageable/non-pageable mismatch, the recommended fix was to **add optional `nextLink`**, because that preserves the standard ARM pattern and avoids a future breaking change.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Whether to suppress or fix Avocado MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG when deprecated operations still exist

question: When Avocado reports MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG because a generated OpenAPI still contains operations that are not covered by the default tag in readme.md, should this be handled by suppression or by updating the default tag/input-file configuration?

**Historical ground truth**

This should be fixed by updating the readme.md default tag configuration, not by suppressing Avocado. MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG means the generated OpenAPI contains operations that are not included in the default tag. Removing examples or marking models as removed does not remove the operations themselves, so the swagger files that define those paths still need to be included in the default tag's input-file list. Suppression is appropriate only for a genuine false positive or a rule that does not apply, not when the paths are actually present in the generated OpenAPI.

**Cached dev answer**

If the Avocado `MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG` is happening **only because deprecated operations are still present in the generated OpenAPI**, treat that as a **false positive and use the Avocado suppression path**, not as a reason to rewrite the default tag. The repo guidance explicitly lists `MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG` on deprecated APIs as a known Swagger-Avocado issue, with `Approved-Avocado` as the documented workaround.\

- **Use suppression** when:
  - the missing operations are **deprecated/legacy artifacts** still emitted in generated OpenAPI, and
  - your `readme.md` default tag is already correctly representing the intended/latest spec set.
- **Fix `readme.md` / `input-file`** only when the default tag is actually wrong — for example, it really is missing APIs that should belong to the current default/latest version set.
- **Do not expand the default tag just to silence this false positive.** The README default tag is supposed to point to the latest-version spec files used by tooling and docs, not to absorb deprecated leftovers from generated output.

A couple of specifics:
- Swagger Avocado does **not** have a permanent suppression path; the documented PR workaround is the reviewer-applied `Approved-Avocado` label in the [suppression guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).
- The Avocado wiki calls out `[MISSING_APIS_IN_DEFAULT_TAG] False positive on deprecated APIs` as a known issue in [Swagger-Avocado](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-Avocado).
- The docs also say the default tag should refer to the **latest API version’s** spec files for automatic refresh, which is another reason not to widen it just to include deprecated operations in generated output: [Publish REST API reference docs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-docs).

**Bottom line:** for **deprecated operations still lingering in generated OpenAPI**, prefer **suppression (`Approved-Avocado`)**; only change default tag / `input-file` config if the README is genuinely incorrect.

</details>

**Assessment:** The answer matches the historical guidance: use separate PRs, adding the new breaking api-version first and deleting older preview versions later. It also grounds the sequencing in durable repo-check behavior and retirement workflow evidence, without contradicting the frozen scenario.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that addition of the new api-version and removal of older preview api-versions should be done in separate PRs rather than combined.; Require the first PR to introduce a new dated api-version instead of modifying an existing published preview in place.; Require the removal/deletion PR to happen later, after the older preview versions are actually retired from the service.; Acknowledge that deleting retired preview specs follows its own breaking-change approval workflow and expected PR-check pattern.; Preserve the practical sequencing rule that smaller PRs focused on a single api-version change are preferred when feasible.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [repository-workflow-02-030](expert-knowledge-report.md#repository-workflow-02-030), [repository-workflow-02-032](expert-knowledge-report.md#repository-workflow-02-032)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Preferred PR sequencing when replacing older preview API versions with a new breaking version

question: When replacing older private preview API versions with a new API version that introduces breaking changes, what PR strategy should be used in Azure API specs: combine the addition and removal in one PR, or split them into separate PRs?

**Historical ground truth**

Use separate PRs: add the new API version in one PR, then remove the old API versions in a second PR. This works better with repository checks, and when possible it is generally best to change only a single API version per PR.

**Cached dev answer**

Use **separate PRs**.

- **PR 1: add the new API version** that contains the breaking changes. That is the supported way to evolve a published preview: **do not change the old preview in place**; create a newer dated version instead. If automation flags it, follow the PR’s **“Next steps to merge”** guidance and the breaking-change process at [aka.ms/brch](https://aka.ms/brch).
- **PR 2: remove the older preview version(s)** **later**, as a cleanup/retirement PR, **only after those old previews are fully retired from the service**. The repo guidance for preview retirement treats deletion as its own workflow: the PR is expected to fail `Swagger BreakingChange`, pass the other checks, and then go through normal breaking-change approval via [aka.ms/brch](https://aka.ms/brch).

So the practical rule is:

- **Do not combine “introduce new breaking version” and “delete old preview specs” in one PR.**
- **Add first; retire/delete later in a separate PR** once the old preview is actually retired.
- Replacing one preview with a newer preview/GA does **not** itself require the Azure retirement process for the service transition, but customers should still be notified that the old preview stops working in **90 days**.

</details>

**Replay question**

title: Separate private-to-public moves from FSV1-to-FSV2 migrations

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If an existing RP already exists in the private specs repo in FSV1, and moving it to the public repo would also require an FSV2 folder-structure migration, should the private-to-public move and the FSV1-to-FSV2 migration be done in one PR? What sequence is recommended?

**Historical ground truth**

Do not combine the private-to-public move and the FSV1-to-FSV2 migration in a single PR. Keep them as separate changes. The recommended sequences stated were either: (1) migrate the RP to FSV2 in the private RPSaaSMaster repo first, then merge that result to public/main; or (2) first merge the existing FSV1 spec to public/main, then do the FSV2 migration afterward. If the RP is in a gap between older standards and newer folder-structure requirements, the guidance was still to avoid solving both changes in one PR.

**Cached dev answer**

No — the reusable guidance points to **separating** them.

- **Do the private-to-public move first as its own public PR.** The documented move process says to open a **new PR** in the public repo, copy the files from private to public, and **preserve the source file paths** when copying.
- **Do the FSV1-to-FSV2 folder migration afterward in a separate follow-up PR.** Folder-migration guidance treats the structure refactor as its own change and tells authors to align subsequent PRs to folder structure v2 after rebasing/merging latest `main`.

**Recommended sequence**
- **Step 1:** Finish/merge the private-repo work that is ready to be published.
- **Step 2:** Open a **new** PR in the public repo that performs the **private-to-public copy only**, keeping the existing paths and linking the reviewed private PRs.
- **Step 3:** After that lands, open a second PR for the **FSV2 migration**.
- **If the public repo’s folder-migration PR has already merged by then:** base your follow-up PR on latest `main` and move the service into the FSV2 layout there.

That recommendation is an **inference from the documented process**: the move-to-public workflow is path-preserving, while folder-structure migration is a separate refactor with its own conflict-handling guidance. Combining them would blur review history and make the “copy to public” step no longer a straightforward move.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to update an existing ARM lease when async POST actions are flagged as new resource types

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If ARM Lease Validation flags new async POST actions on existing resources as inferred "new resource types," should a separate lease be created, or should the existing lease be updated, and what kind of lease changes are needed?

**Historical ground truth**

A separate lease is not needed solely because the operations are async POST actions. When the validator infers such actions as new modeled resource types, update the existing RP lease so it explicitly covers them. That means ensuring the lease includes the relevant API version if needed and adding entries for the new action operations using the same lease syntax and pattern already used for similar actions. After updating the lease, rerun validation. If the validator still flags the actions after the lease is updated, request a refresh or unblock from the ARM modeling owners and reference the updated lease.

**Cached dev answer**

You should **update the existing lease, not create a separate lease for a “new resource type.”**

- The key technical point is that **POST-only paths on an existing ARM resource are actions on that existing resource**, not a brand-new resource type.
- So if async `POST` actions are being interpreted as inferred “new resource types,” the lease response should be to **keep the lease scoped to the existing RP/service** and **refresh or extend that existing lease as needed**, rather than minting a second lease as if a new ARM resource type were being added.
- From the lease documentation I retrieved, leases are modeled at the **RP/service lease file level** and the public lease shape only exposes the normal lease metadata (`resource-provider`, `startdate`, `duration`, `reviewer`). I did **not** find evidence of a separate action-specific lease file format in the retrieved docs.
- Practically, that means the lease change is the **usual lease maintenance change**: update the existing lease entry’s timing/approval metadata if coverage needs to continue, instead of creating a parallel lease for a supposedly new type.

**Short version:** async `POST` actions on an existing resource should be treated as **existing-resource actions**; handle them under the **existing lease** and make a **lease extension/refresh** change, not a **new-resource-type lease**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to resolve CI TypeSpec validation mismatches after formatter or generator changes

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If CI TypeSpec validation fails even though running `npx tsp format **/*.tsp` locally reports no changes, how should the author troubleshoot and fix it when newer repo dependencies or a recent TypeSpec release may have changed formatting or generated output?

**Historical ground truth**

A local `tsp format` result of no changes does not by itself prove CI is wrong. A common cause is that CI is using newer repo state or pinned dependencies than the local environment, especially after a recent TypeSpec release that changed formatting behavior or generated output. The recommended fix is to update from the latest `main`, reinstall dependencies from the repo root with `npm ci`, rerun `tsp format` over the TypeSpec directory, run the repository's local TypeSpec validation workflow, and commit any regenerated or reformatted files. Needing to reformat or regenerate after TypeSpec releases is expected.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes: if CI fails but `npx typespec format "**/*.tsp"` reports no changes, treat that as a **validation/generation drift** problem, not proof that CI is wrong. In this case, the reliable fix is to reproduce the **full TypeSpec Validation** flow from the **repo root**, because CI checks generated artifacts after compile/validation, not just source-file formatting. Inline guidance is in [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation) and the formatter behavior is documented in [Formatter](https://typespec.io/docs/handbook/formatter).

- **First, sync to the same dependency baseline as CI.** Follow the repo-root “running locally” flow from [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation): merge the latest parent branch into your PR branch, then clean and reinstall dependencies at the repository root.
  ```bash
  git clean -xdf
  git pull
  pnpm ci
  pnpm tsv <your-typespec-project-folder>
  git status
  ```

- **Do not rely on `tsp format` alone.** The formatter only checks `.tsp` text layout. CI `tsv` also recompiles TypeSpec and compares checked-in generated Swagger/artifacts. The formatter itself is configurable and follows repo Prettier config when present, as described in [Formatter](https://typespec.io/docs/handbook/formatter).

- **If `git status` shows generated-file diffs after `tsv`, commit them.** When repo dependencies or a recent TypeSpec/emitter release changed output, the usual resolution is to **update forward** by accepting the newly generated output, unless you have a specific reason to believe the new output is incorrect.

- **If local still doesn’t match CI, eliminate environment skew.** Repeat the same [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation) steps in a fresh clone or on another machine. That helps confirm whether the mismatch is caused by stale local state.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to proceed with merging a PR after code owner review

question: After a PR has been reviewed by code owners, how should the author proceed to merge it?

**Historical ground truth**

Follow the instructions in the "next steps to merge" comment added to the PR.

**Cached dev answer**

After code owner review, the author should **not** treat that alone as “ready to merge.” In the Azure REST API specs process, the next action is to follow the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** comment; when that comment is satisfied, the **Automated merging requirements met** status is green, required approvals are present, and branch-policy requirements are met, the PR can be completed by someone with write access. ([github.com](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/API-Spec-Review-FAQ))

- **Use the PR’s `Next Steps to Merge` comment as the source of truth.** That comment tells you whether anything is still blocking merge in the specs repos. The FAQ explicitly tells authors to follow that comment rather than asking separately how to proceed. ([github.com](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/API-Spec-Review-FAQ))
- **Make sure merge requirements are actually green.** In specs PRs, the key signal is that both **`Next Steps to Merge`** and **`Automated merging requirements met`** are green. If they are, required automated blockers are cleared.\
- **Confirm approvals and unresolved feedback.** Required reviewers/code owners added by branch policy are part of merge requirements, and required review comments should be resolved before completion. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies-overview?view=azure-devops))
- **Then complete the PR merge.** Azure Repos guidance says that once required reviewers approve and branch-policy requirements are met, you can complete the PR and merge into the target branch. ([learn.microsoft.com](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/complete-pull-requests?view=azure-devops))
- **If you don’t have write access, ask someone on your team who does to complete it.** The specs guidance says at least one approver is generally another person from your team with write access, and write access is required to perform the merge.

**Specs-repo caveats**
- **Public `main`:** before merging, apply the **`PublishToCustomers`** label.
- **Private repo `main`:** it **cannot** be merged directly; use the move/publish flow instead.
- **Data-plane PRs:** if applicable, they also need **`data-plane-review-signoff`** before merge.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: What spec and approval steps are required to retire preview API versions in favor of GA

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

When retiring preview API versions in favor of an existing GA version, what spec changes are typically required, how should expected breaking-change validation failures be handled, and what approval process is needed before merge?

**Historical ground truth**

For a preview API retirement in favor of GA, the expected spec work is to remove the preview TypeSpec sources, generated OpenAPI files, examples, and associated readme tags for the retired preview versions. Deleting preview API versions is treated as an intentional breaking change, so Swagger breaking-change failures such as removed paths or removed definitions are expected and should be left as-is rather than suppressed by the author. The remaining work is to follow the breaking change review process: file the required intake with justification and migration details, notify the breaking change review channel identified by the process, and obtain the appropriate breaking-change approval label on the PR. After that approval label is applied, rerun checks and continue the normal merge workflow.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes. The usual pattern is:

- **Only remove the preview spec after the preview API is fully retired in the service.** The retirement guidance says the spec should stay in the repo until the API version is actually retired, then be removed so the repo matches what customers can still call.
- **In the retirement PR, delete all repo artifacts for that preview version**, typically:
  - the TypeSpec source files (`*.tsp`)
  - the nearby example source files
  - the generated OpenAPI/examples under `preview/YYYY-MM-DD-preview/**`
  - the corresponding `readme.md` tags that reference that preview version\
  See: [Deprecating Preview APIs](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Deprecating-Preview-APIs)

- **Validation expectation:** the PR is expected to **fail `Swagger BreakingChange`** and **pass the other checks**. That breaking-change failure is normal for deleting a published preview spec; it is not something you usually “fix” away in the retirement PR.
- **Handling the failure:** do **not** treat the expected `Swagger BreakingChange` failure as self-approving, and don’t rely on a casual suppression as the normal path. Instead, take the PR through the standard breaking-change approval flow at [aka.ms/brch](https://aka.ms/brch). The guidance also points to `[maintained contact alias]` for the approval path.
- **Approval needed before merge:** obtain the **normal breaking-change approval** before merging the deletion PR.

A useful distinction from the broader lifecycle guidance:

- Replacing a preview with a newer preview or GA service version generally means customers should be told the old preview will stop working after **90 days**.
- But the **repo cleanup PR** that actually removes the preview spec is still handled as a **breaking-change-reviewed deletion** once that preview has been fully retired from the service.

</details>

**Search evidence documents:** [`azure_rest_api_specs_docs/.github#arm-leases#README.md`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/main/.github/arm-leases/README.md)

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: After ARM modeling office-hours sign-off for a new RP or resource type, who adds the lease and what should the author do next?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

Historical context: for a PR that introduces a new Resource Provider namespace or a new resource type and has already received ARM API Modeling office-hours sign-off, who is allowed to add the required ARM lease file, and what should the PR author do after that lease is added while waiting for validation checks to recognize it?

**Historical ground truth**

For a PR that introduces a new Resource Provider namespace or a new resource type, office-hours sign-off does not by itself complete the ARM modeling requirement if a lease file is still needed. The lease file can be added only by the PM or certain designated engineers after the initial discussion; not every ARM reviewer is authorized to add it. If the reviewer who attended office hours is not on that allowed list, the PR author should have an authorized person add the lease rather than trying to add it themselves. After the lease is created in the public repo, the author should wait for it to sync to the private RPSaaSMaster branch used by the check. That sync was stated to take a few hours and sometimes up to 1–2 days, and during that wait there was nothing further required from the PR author.

**Cached dev answer**

Historically, the required ARM lease file was supposed to be added by a **Product Manager (PM)** after the ARM API Modeling office-hours discussion sign-off — not by the PR author or another engineer.

After that lease was added to public `main` in [Azure/azure-rest-api-specs](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/main/.github/arm-leases/README.md), the PR author’s next step was **not** to copy the lease into their own PR branch. Instead:

- **Wait for the ARM Modeling Review / validation to pick up the lease from public `main`.**
- **Do not sync the lease into `RPSaaSMaster`, `RPSaaSDev`, or the PR branch**, because the check reads leases only from public `main`, and lease files present only in the PR’s branch are ignored.
- In practice, once the PM-added lease is merged to public `main`, it applies to PRs across repos and branches; the author just needs to let the validation rerun or refresh against that state.

**Replay question**

title: Are ARM API reviewers expected to add the lease file for a new RP after modeling office-hours sign-off?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

For a PR that appears to introduce a new Resource Provider, are ARM API reviewers generally expected to add the ARM lease file themselves in order to unblock progress after modeling office-hours sign-off?

**Historical ground truth**

When the PR is for a new Resource Provider, the lease still needs to be added, but ARM API reviewers are not generally the ones expected to add it unless they are among the specifically authorized people. In the cited guidance, the lease addition was handled by an authorized owner rather than by the reviewer who provided office-hours sign-off.

**Cached dev answer**

No. Based on the documented ARM lease process, **ARM API reviewers are not generally expected to add the lease file themselves** to unblock a new RP after modeling office-hours sign-off.

- The documented rule is that **only Product Managers (PMs)** are authorized to add or modify `lease.yaml` files in the ARM leases area.
- Those lease files are supposed to be added **after office-hours discussions with the RP owner**, and the `reviewer` field must name the approving PM.
- Practically, that means the unblock path is to have the **authorized PM / lease owner** add the lease in the public repo’s ARM leases location described in [ARM Leases — Design Discussion Period](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/main/.github/arm-leases/README.md), not to expect an ARM reviewer to do it as part of PR review.
- Also, leases are read from **public `main`**, so a lease only in the PR branch would not be the effective fix.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Handling .NET SDK validation failures caused by a C# management emitter crash

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

When .NET SDK Validation fails because the TypeSpec C# management emitter crashes on an operation that combines @list with ArmResourceActionAsync, should the problem be treated as a spec issue or a generator bug, what escalation path should be used, and what temporary mitigations can unblock the PR while waiting for a fix?

**Historical ground truth**

Treat an internal emitter crash during .NET SDK Validation as a generator or emitter bug rather than a specification bug when the failure indicates the tooling crashed while generating code. Escalate the issue to the Azure SDK .NET code generation owners and include the failing PR identifier, pipeline failure details, stack trace, and a minimal repro of the TypeSpec pattern that triggers the crash. For management-plane SDK generation failures caused by tooling rather than the specification, the recommended path is to contact the Azure SDK team instead of continuing to debug the spec itself. If the PR must be unblocked before the emitter is fixed, a temporary mitigation is to avoid the crashing code path, such as removing pageable behavior from the long-running action or modeling the long-running action and pageable list as separate operations, subject to API design requirements. This kind of failure does not indicate a tspconfig.yaml or SDK validation infrastructure misconfiguration when the crash occurs only inside the emitter.

**Cached dev answer**

Treat it as a **generator-side bug first, not a spec-rule violation**, unless you can independently prove the TypeSpec is invalid for another reason.

- The strongest evidence I found is that the Azure specs repo already contains operations that use **`@list` together with `ArmResourceActionAsync`** on the same operation shape, so that pattern is not inherently invalid by itself.
- The .NET guidance also distinguishes **`spec change`** from **`emitter change`** / generator-side causes, and says not to classify a problem as spec-caused without supporting evidence.
- Because spec review and SDK generation are separate stages, a crash in the **C# management emitter** should be escalated through the **.NET/management SDK generation path**, not treated as a spec-review blocker by default.

**Recommended escalation path**

- Use the **Azure SDK Tools Agent** as the primary path for SDK-generation triage and reruns: [aka.ms/azsdk/agent](https://aka.ms/azsdk/agent).
- If the PR is blocked specifically by SDK Validation, use the SDK validation guidance to inspect logs and rerun the failing check: [SDK Validation wiki](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- Route the issue to the **.NET management generator / emitter owners**, with the failing operation and crash details, rather than trying to “fix” the spec blindly.

**Temporary mitigations while waiting for the fix**

- **Best temporary unblock:** rerun the failing **`.NET SDK Validation`** check after the generator-side fix lands, using the PR comment flow documented here: [SDK Validation wiki](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- **If this is a development-branch PR:** the retrieved guidance says not every SDK validation error must be fixed on development branches, so a temporary suppression / non-blocking treatment may be acceptable depending on branch policy.
- **Do not rewrite the spec just to satisfy a crashing emitter** unless you have a semantics-preserving alternative and can verify it. The .NET guidance explicitly warns against speculative fixes when the root cause is unresolved.
- If you do need a temporary workaround, prefer a **minimal, behavior-preserving modeling change** only if the service contract stays identical; otherwise wait for the emitter fix.

**Practical rule of thumb**

- **Spec invalid by rule?** Fix the spec.
- **Spec shape is valid, but the C# ARM emitter crashes?** Treat it as a **generator bug**, escalate to the .NET management generation path, and unblock with rerun / branch-policy handling rather than inventing a permanent spec workaround.

</details>

### spec-review-0143: Model PATCH payloads so ARM RPC rules do not treat them as top-level resources

**Dataset:** `authoring.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0160](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0160) | **GT basis:** bot_fallback | **Temporal scope:** mixed | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-05-09T19:39:58.97Z

**Assessment:** The answer correctly explains the core cause: a model used on a resource-shaped PATCH path that extends the ARM resource base can be inferred by ARM tooling as a top-level resource, which then triggers resource RPC expectations such as GET/list consistency. It gives the preferred fix from the historical ground truth: model partial-update payloads as non-resource patch DTOs and keep the actual resource model for the real resource/response. It also correctly points to recommended TypeSpec PATCH templates and avoids the non-preferred workaround of adding GET/list just for the patch model. Although it does not mention LintDiff/rebase behavior or suppression as fallback options, those are ancillary to the reusable authoring question rather than required to answer it.

**Acceptance criteria:** Explain that extending Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.Resource (or equivalent ARM resource base) gives a schema ARM resource-envelope semantics, so when that schema is used as a body or response on a resource-shaped path validators may classify it as a resource rather than a mere DTO.; State that once classified as a resource, standard ARM resource RPC rules can apply, including expectations around GET and, for top-level tracked resources, collection/list operations and schema consistency across CRUD operations.; Recommend the preferred remediation for a partial-update payload: author a separate plain non-resource patch model that does not inherit from the ARM resource base type.; Clarify that the actual independently addressable ARM resource type remains the model used by the existing GET/list operations and typically the PATCH success response.; Avoid prescribing adding GET or list operations solely to satisfy validation for a PATCH-only payload model; if mentioned, present that only as a fallback when the model must remain a resource.; For TypeSpec guidance, prefer custom PATCH/update modeling patterns that accept an explicit patch request model rather than deriving the PATCH payload from a resource type.

**Frozen facts:** A PATCH operation was added on the path subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/providers/Microsoft.Advisor/recommendations/{recommendationId}.; The PATCH payload/response model RecommendationsPatchPayload extends Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.Resource.; LintDiff later reported TopLevelResourcesListBySubscription after a subsequent PR update, although the PR had previously passed checks.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [authoring-01-023](expert-knowledge-report.md#authoring-01-023)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Model PATCH payloads so ARM RPC rules do not treat them as top-level resources

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

In TypeSpec/OpenAPI for ARM, if a PATCH operation on a resource-shaped path uses a payload or response model that extends Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.Resource, why can ARM RPC rules start treating that model as a new top-level resource, and how should the model be authored if it is only a partial-update payload rather than an independently retrievable resource?

**Historical ground truth**

ARM validation can infer that a model is a top-level resource when it both extends the ARM resource base type and is used as the body or response on a resource-shaped path. Once inferred as a resource, rules that require standard resource operations such as GET and list-by-subscription can apply even if the intended use was only a PATCH payload. A validation failure can appear after a later PR update because LintDiff compares the PR against the current main branch and current validator behavior, so rebasing or rerunning validation can surface rules that did not trigger earlier. If the type is only a partial-update payload or PATCH response and is not meant to be an independently addressable ARM resource, it should be modeled as a plain non-resource type and should not extend Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.Resource. The actual ARM resource type should remain the resource used by the existing GET and list operations. Adding GET or list operations just to satisfy the rule for the PATCH payload model is not the preferred fix. If resource inheritance must be retained, the remaining options are to satisfy the resource rules or request a scoped suppression with justification.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — if your PATCH body model extends `Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.Resource`, ARM tooling can start reading that schema as **a resource definition**, not just as an update DTO. That happens because `Resource` is an ARM **resource envelope** type: inheriting it gives the model resource-shaped top-level fields such as `id`, `name`, `type`, and other ARM envelope members, so validators and reviewers can apply **resource-scoped RPC expectations** to it. Those expectations include “PATCH is only a partial update,” “PATCH/GET/PUT/LIST must line up on the same resource schema,” and tracked-resource CRUD/list/tag rules.\

If the model is only a **partial-update payload**, author it as a **separate patch model** that contains only the **updatable** fields, usually all optional and using merge-patch semantics. In TypeSpec, the recommended pattern is to use [`ArmCustomPatchSync` / `ArmCustomPatchAsync`](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/resource-operations) with an explicit patch DTO, rather than making the patch DTO inherit `Resource`. The PATCH **response** should still be the **real resource model** for that resource, not a second resource-like wrapper.\

**What to avoid**

```typespec
model WidgetUpdate extends Azure.ResourceManager.Foundations.Resource {
  properties?: WidgetProperties;
}
```

- This is resource-shaped, so it can be interpreted as “another ARM resource model.”
- It also pushes PATCH toward a full resource envelope, which conflicts with ARM PATCH guidance that PATCH should only carry the fields being updated.

**Preferred TypeSpec pattern**

```typespec
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager";

using Azure.ResourceManager;

model WidgetProperties {
  color?: string;
  size?: int32;
}

model Widget is TrackedResource<WidgetProperties> {
  @key("widgetName")
  @segment("widgets")
  name: string;
}

model WidgetUpdateProperties {
  color?: string;
  size?: int32;
}

model WidgetUpdate {
  tags?: Record<string>;
  properties?: WidgetUpdateProperties;
}

@armResourceOperations
interface Widgets {
  get is ArmResourceRead<Widget>;
  createOrUpdate is ArmResourceCreateOrReplaceAsync<Widget>;
  update is ArmCustomPatchSync<Widget, WidgetUpdate>;
  delete is ArmResourceDeleteWithoutOkAsync<Widget>;
  listByResourceGroup is ArmResourceListByParent<Widget>;
}
```

**Practical rule**
- **Resource model**: use for GET/PUT/PATCH response of the real resource.
- **Patch model**: use for PATCH request only.
- **Do not** make the patch model inherit `Resource` unless it is truly an independently retrievable ARM resource, which a partial-update payload is not.

If you want a reusable helper shape, the [ARM library sample](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/samples/resource-manager/arm-library) shows a merge-patch-style update model pattern that omits non-updatable fields and makes the remaining updateable fields optional.

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to request an offline REST API review

question: How do I request an offline REST API review for a small API change?

**Historical ground truth**

To request an offline REST API review, follow the documented steps in the official offline REST API review request guidance.

**Cached dev answer**

For a **small data-plane API change**, request an **offline REST API review** by emailing **[maintained contact alias]** with a link to your spec PR. This path is specifically recommended for minor changes when the previous API version was already approved and your PR is ready for review.

- **Use offline review only if all of these are true:**
  - the **prior API version was already reviewed and approved**,
  - the new version has only **minor changes** like added response fields or added optional request fields,
  - **all PR pipeline checks are passing**, and
  - the **TypeSpec/OpenAPI APIViews** are generated and show the changes cleanly without noise. See [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).

- **How to request it:**
  - Email **[maintained contact alias]** with:
    - a link to your PR,
    - links to your design docs / hero scenarios,
    - a link to the prior API review if there was one,
    - a short description of the change.
  - Request it **at least 2 days before** you need sign-off. The same guidance is documented here: [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).

- **Also include on the request:**
  - the **CPEX PM/owner** responsible for Cloud Lifecycle updates, and
  - any **engineering team members** who will generate or update SDKs. See [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).

- **PR labels/sign-off:**
  - `data-plane-review-requested` is typically applied automatically for a new data-plane API version; if it is missing, you can add it on the PR to indicate review readiness.
  - Final approval is recorded with the protected `data-plane-review-signoff` label, which only API Stewardship reviewers can apply. See [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

- **Important distinction:** if your change is **management plane (ARM)**, this is **not** the offline path. ARM review happens through the normal PR review process instead. See [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).

</details>

Maintained docs confirm that TypeSpec `Record` emits OpenAPI `additionalProperties`, including `Record<unknown>` and `Record<string>`, and maintained Azure linter docs name the relevant Azure Core rules `no-unknown` and `bad-record-type`. Maintained Azure REST tooling docs also establish that inline `#suppress` and config suppressions are supported. However, the KB does not contain the full expert workflow: it does not state the normative 'use the narrowest type matching the contract' rule, does not explicitly recommend `Record<string>` over `Record<unknown>` for simple string metadata, does not provide the wrapper-model recommendation for opaque JSON object content in Azure guidance, and does not provide maintained authoritative documentation naming ARM-specific `arm-no-record`. The only evidence for exact-swagger-text equivalence and ARM-specific suppression naming comes from static Q&A or wiki material, which is not sufficient as maintained authoritative coverage for the whole pattern.

**Current-KB clarification hypothesis:** State that the model should use the narrowest type matching the contract, not default to arbitrary JSON.; If metadata is only simple key/value strings, recommend `Record<string>` rather than `Record<unknown>`.; If the contract truly requires an opaque JSON object, describe modeling it via a wrapper model that represents free-form additional properties.; Acknowledge that this arbitrary JSON object shape conflicts with Azure TypeSpec lint rules and requires targeted suppressions with justification.; Name the relevant suppressions for no-unknown and bad-record-type, with ARM-specific arm-no-record as applicable.; Clarify that emitting an OpenAPI object with additionalProperties is an acceptable equivalent and exact legacy Swagger text matching is not required.

**Potential fix (not validated by search alone):** When modeling JSON-object properties in TypeSpec, choose the narrowest schema that matches the service contract. Use `Record<string>` when the values are simple string metadata; avoid defaulting to `Record<unknown>` unless the contract truly permits arbitrary JSON object values. If the contract requires an opaque JSON object, model that shape explicitly with a dedicated wrapper model or record-based object so the emitted OpenAPI is an `object` with `additionalProperties`; exact textual matching to legacy Swagger is not required if the emitted schema is semantically equivalent. Because broad unknown/record shapes conflict with Azure lint guidance, use narrowly scoped suppressions with justification only where necessary, including Azure Core `no-unknown` and `bad-record-type`, and ARM-specific `arm-no-record` when applicable.

**Search evidence documents:** [`typespec_docs/getting-started#typespec-for-openapi-dev.md`](https://typespec.io/docs/getting-started/typespec-for-openapi-dev), [`typespec_azure_docs/libraries#azure-core#reference#linter.md`](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/libraries/azure-core/reference/linter), [`azure_rest_api_specs_docs/eng#tools#typespec-suppressions#README.md`](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/blob/main/eng/tools/typespec-suppressions/README.md)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Model an opaque JSON metadata property when `unknown` and `Record<unknown>` are disallowed

question: In Azure TypeSpec, how should a service model a metadata property that must remain an opaque JSON object rather than a well-defined schema, when `unknown` and `Record<unknown>` are flagged by the `no-unknown` and `bad-record-type` rules?

**Historical ground truth**

Use the narrowest type that matches the contract. If the metadata values are simple key/value strings, model the property as `Record<string>`. If the service truly needs arbitrary JSON object content, avoid a bare `unknown` property and instead use a wrapper model with additional properties to represent the free-form object. Because that arbitrary JSON shape still conflicts with the Azure TypeSpec lint rules, apply targeted suppressions for `@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/no-unknown` and `@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/bad-record-type` on that wrapper with a clear justification. Emitting this as an OpenAPI object with `additionalProperties` is an acceptable representation; exact legacy Swagger shape matching is not required.

**Cached dev answer**

Use a **targeted `Record<unknown>` property with targeted suppressions**.

Because your requirement is specifically **“opaque JSON object”** and not “well-defined schema,” `Record<unknown>` is the closest TypeSpec model of that contract. `unknown` is broader than you want because it allows any JSON value, not just an object. Azure lint rules discourage both patterns, so when the contract truly must stay opaque, the practical guidance is to **keep the open object type and suppress the rule(s) on that property only**.

```typespec
model MyModel {
  @doc("Opaque metadata bag. Keys and nested values are intentionally service-defined.")
  #suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/no-unknown" "This property must remain an opaque JSON object by contract."
  #suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/bad-record-type" "This property must remain an opaque JSON object by contract."
  metadata?: Record<unknown>;
}
```

A few important distinctions:

- **If it must be an object:** use `Record<unknown>`.
- **If it may be any JSON value:** use `unknown` instead.
- **If this is ARM/management-plane:** the record-specific rule may be `@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager/arm-no-record` instead of `bad-record-type`, so suppress that rule on the property in addition to `no-unknown`.

Also, don’t try to force the emitted OpenAPI to look like a “cleaner” bare `type: object`. For an opaque object, emitting unconstrained `additionalProperties` is considered an accurate representation. If your repo runs LintDiff, this shape can also require corresponding LintDiff suppressions.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Why intra-version breaking-change checks still fail despite ARM and versioning labels

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

A PR modifies an API version that already exists on main. The PR already has the labels ARMSignedOff, Versioning-Approved-BranchPolicyException, and PublishToCustomers. The Swagger BreakingChange intra-version check reports rules 1006 RemovedDefinition, 1017 ReferenceRedirection, and 1029 ReadonlyPropertyChanged. Why do these errors still occur, what do those rule failures mean, and what kinds of changes are required to resolve them?

**Historical ground truth**

Those labels do not bypass the intra-version Swagger BreakingChange check. They relate to ARM review and versioning-policy exceptions, but they do not authorize changing the contract of an existing API version that is already on main.

The reported failures mean:
- 1006 RemovedDefinition: a schema that previously existed was removed. Removing or renaming definitions within the same API version is treated as a breaking change.
- 1017 ReferenceRedirection: a $ref now points to a different schema than before. That changes request or response shapes within the same API version and is treated as a breaking change.
- 1029 ReadonlyPropertyChanged: a property changed from readOnly true to readOnly false. That changes the contract from service-set to client-settable and is treated as a breaking change.

To resolve the failures, either keep the existing API version logically compatible by restoring removed definitions, reverting redirected references, and restoring readOnly where the original contract must remain unchanged, or treat the changes as breaking changes and follow the breaking-change approval process. In many cases, intentional contract changes should be introduced in a new API version rather than by modifying the existing one.

A Versioning-Approved-BranchPolicyException does not override intra-version breaking-change validation for an already-existing API version.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — those errors can still occur. The key point is that `Swagger BreakingChange` evaluates the **actual wire-contract diff within the same API version**, and the labels you listed do **not** change that diff.

- `Swagger BreakingChange` checks for breaking or versioning-policy violations **within a single published API version**.
- Once an API version is published, it generally must not be changed in place, except for a spec correction that matches real service behavior under the `*-Approved-BugFix` path at [aka.ms/brch](https://aka.ms/brch).
- `Versioning-Approved-BranchPolicyException` is a **branch-policy exception**, not a waiver for specific OpenAPI-diff rule failures.
- `ARMSignedOff` is an ARM review outcome; breaking/versioning issues are a separate gate.
- `PublishToCustomers` is an acknowledgment required for public-main publication, not a suppression.

**What the failures mean**

- **`1006 RemovedDefinition`**\
  An existing schema/model definition was removed from the old spec. That is a breaking change.\
  **Fix:** restore the old definition, or move the removal to a **new API version**.

- **`1017 ReferenceRedirection`**\
  A `$ref` at an existing location now points to a different model. Even if the old model still exists, redirecting the reference is breaking.\
  **Fix:** keep the original `$ref` target at that location, or introduce the new shape in a **new API version**.

- **`1029 ReadonlyPropertyChanged`**\
  A property’s `readOnly` behavior changed. That is breaking because clients may send or consume it differently.\
  **Fix:** restore the previous `readOnly` setting, or move the change to a **new API version**. The documented exception is only when `readOnly` changes from `true` to `false`.

**Reusable resolution rule**

- If the goal is to preserve the existing published contract, **put the old shape back exactly**.
- If the goal is to change the contract, **create a newer dated `api-version`**.
- If the old spec was simply wrong and the service already behaves differently, use the **bug-fix approval path** at [aka.ms/brch](https://aka.ms/brch), not a branch-policy-exception label.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: What to do when the breaking-change check crashes because a TypeSpec model name conflicts with common types

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

In a management-plane Azure REST API spec after a Swagger-to-TypeSpec conversion, the cross-version breaking-change check crashes because a model named `Resource` conflicts with a name from common types. What is the correct resolution, and can a PR be unblocked by applying a breaking-change approval label when the checker is crashing?

**Historical ground truth**

A PR should not be merged while the breaking-change checker is crashing, and a breaking-change approval label is not an acceptable way to bypass a crash. If the crash is caused by a duplicate model name such as `Resource` conflicting with common types, the spec should be changed so the checker can analyze it, for example by renaming the conflicting model. If that change then produces an actual breaking-change result, that result must be handled through the normal breaking-change process rather than leaving the checker unusable.

**Cached dev answer**

The correct resolution is to **fix the spec/generation issue**, not to use the breaking-change approval process as a bypass.

- In this scenario, the cross-version checker is **crashing** because the emitted management-plane OpenAPI hits an AutoRest/runtime problem. For crashes, the guidance is to determine whether the failure exists on the target branch or was introduced by your PR, and then **fix the spec** in the appropriate branch; if it is introduced by your PR, fix it in your PR. In your stated case, that means resolving the `Resource` name collision with ARM common types in the converted TypeSpec/OpenAPI output rather than leaving the conflicting model as-is.\
- A breaking-change approval label is for PRs where the tooling **successfully detects** a breaking change or branch-policy/versioning issue. It is **not** the right mechanism when the checker is crashing instead of producing a reviewable breaking-change result. So **no**—you should not expect a PR to be unblocked just by applying a breaking-change approval label when the checker itself is crashing.
- Put differently: **possibility** — a PR can be unblocked by an approval label when there is an actual reviewed breaking-change finding; **rejection reason here** — a crash is a tooling/spec failure, not an approved-review outcome; **recommendation** — resolve the TypeSpec/common-types collision first, then rerun the breaking-change checks.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to resolve `ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly` lint-diff failures in a TypeSpec ARM spec

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

In a TypeSpec-based ARM spec, lint-diff reports `ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly`, and the same problem may already exist in an earlier API version. What is the correct way to handle this rule violation?

**Historical ground truth**

An existing occurrence in an earlier version is not, by itself, a reason to ignore the rule. The correct resolution is to either fix the spec so it complies with `ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly` or add a scoped suppression with a justification when suppression is the better choice. For TypeSpec ARM specs, the documented remediation guidance for this rule should be followed, and fixing the issue is generally preferred over suppression.

**Cached dev answer**

The correct handling is:

- **Prefer a real fix first:** if turning on `use-read-only-status-schema: true` in `tspconfig.yaml` will **not** change any previously published OpenAPI, use that workaround. The guidance says this is the preferred fix for `ProvisioningStateMustBeReadOnly` because the failure comes from a validator limitation around `$ref` siblings, not from the intended TypeSpec semantics.
- **If older/published API versions would change, do not apply that setting project-wide.** In that case, keep the TypeSpec model as-is and add a **narrowly scoped Swagger/LintDiff suppression** for the exact generated schema/version that fails, following the [Swagger LintDiff guidance](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-LintDiff).
- **Do not “fix” this with OpenAPI-only decorators** such as `@typespec/openapi`, `@azure-tools/typespec-autorest`, or `#suppress "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core/no-openapi"` on the TypeSpec side. The guidance explicitly says not to use those because they change only generated OpenAPI and can diverge from the TypeSpec semantic model.
- **If the same problem already exists in an earlier API version, that does not justify widening the change.** The safe reusable process is:
  1. Use `use-read-only-status-schema: true` only when it won’t alter published contract output.
  2. Otherwise, suppress the LintDiff violation only for the affected generated artifact/version with a descriptive reason, per [Swagger LintDiff](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-LintDiff).

So, in short: **fix with `use-read-only-status-schema` when contract-safe; otherwise use a narrowly scoped LintDiff suppression, not OpenAPI-only TypeSpec workarounds.**

</details>
