title: How to handle MULTIPLE_API_VERSION blocking a spec PR

question: What is the standard way to handle a MULTIPLE_API_VERSION Avocado error that blocks a spec PR?

**Historical ground truth**

A MULTIPLE_API_VERSION Avocado result is a blocking error. The preferred fix is to update the readme or tag configuration so each default tag references only a single API version. If that cannot be completed immediately, a one-time Approved-Avocado suppression may be used only when there is an active plan to resolve the uniform versioning problem and alignment with the owners of that effort; if that is unclear, contact the uniform versioning contacts before using the suppression.

**Cached dev answer**

The standard path is: **fix the uniform-versioning violation**, not suppress it. `MULTIPLE_API_VERSION` became an **error on July 1, 2025**, so it now blocks spec PRs, and the documented first step is to follow the **Uniform Versioning Violation Guide**.

- **Preferred resolution:** use the [Uniform Versioning Violation Guide](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Uniform-Versioning-Violation-Guide) to make the service’s default tag use a uniform API version instead of mixing multiple API versions.
- **If you think your service needs an exception:** follow the same [Uniform Versioning Violation Guide](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Uniform-Versioning-Violation-Guide) and check with `[maintained contact alias]`. The documented temporary unblock is a **one-time** PR bypass via the `Approved-Avocado` label, but only when there is an **ongoing discussion**, plus a **clear resolution plan and timeline**.
- **Do not plan on a permanent suppression:** for **Swagger Avocado**, the PR suppression path is the `Approved-Avocado` label; the docs say **permanent suppression is not available** in the normal suppression table at [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).

So, in short: **fix it via the violation guide; use `Approved-Avocado` only as an approved one-time escape hatch, not as the standard long-term solution.**

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to proceed when .NET and Python SDK validation report breaking changes

question: If .NET and Python SDK validation fail on a spec PR because of reported SDK breaking changes, what is the standard remediation and approval workflow?

**Historical ground truth**

When SDK validation reports breaking changes, first inspect the detailed build logs to identify the exact reported changes. If the changes are real and intended, add an sdk-suppressions.yaml file in the TypeSpec project root describing each breaking change under the appropriate language section, commit it in the same PR, and let the automation apply the SDK suppression labels. The PR remains blocked until the corresponding SDK reviewers approve those suppressions and the approval labels are present. If the logs instead show a tooling issue unrelated to the spec changes, capture the relevant error details and contact the language support channels referenced by the validation guidance.

**Cached dev answer**

Short answer: **the default remediation is to change the spec so the generated SDKs are no longer breaking**. If the break is truly unavoidable, **Python has a suppression-and-review path, but .NET does not** based on the current spec-PR suppression guidance.

- **Start with the PR’s merge guidance and treat each language separately.** The overall PR workflow is: resolve any REST/API breaking-change or versioning blockers first, then ARM/data-plane review if applicable, then SDK breaking-change review. See [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep) and [SDK Breaking Changes](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Breaking-Changes).

- **Standard remediation is to remove the SDK break in the spec.** The SDK-breaking-changes guidance says authors are strongly encouraged to update the API spec to eliminate the reported break, then rerun validation. Use [SDK Breaking Changes](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Breaking-Changes).

- **For .NET:** there is **no supported suppression path** for `SDK azure-sdk-for-net` / `azure-sdk-for-net-track2`. In practice, that means you must fix the spec/service shape so the .NET SDK validation no longer reports a breaking change. See [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).

- **For Python:** if it is specifically an SDK **breaking-change** finding, you can use `sdk-suppressions.yaml`, add the reported entries, and let the bot apply the suppression label. Then SDK reviewers evaluate it and, if accepted, add `BreakingChange-Python-Sdk-Suppression-Approved`. See [SDK Breaking Changes](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Breaking-Changes) and [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).

- **Approval workflow:** after earlier PR blockers are cleared, SDK reviewers proactively review `BreakingChange-[Language]-Sdk` / suppression labels; the documented expectation is about **48 business hours**. The PR moves forward only after those SDK breaking changes or suppressions are approved. See [SDK Breaking Changes](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Breaking-Changes).

- **If the reported SDK break reflects a real product/service breaking change, not just generation noise:** that is a broader Azure breaking-change governance issue and needs formal review through the Azure breaking-change process, not just a PR suppression. See [Azure Breaking Change Process](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/azurebreakingchangeplaybook).

So for a PR failing in **both .NET and Python**:
- **Fix the .NET break** in the spec.
- **Fix or suppress the Python break**.
- Then rerun the PR and wait for the required SDK approvals.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Required permissions and org visibility for PR authors

question: What permissions, membership, and GitHub organization visibility settings does a PR author need to successfully run and merge PR checks in the Azure REST API specs repository?

**Historical ground truth**

If a PR author lacks the necessary repository permissions, PR checks and merge flow can be blocked. The author should follow the Azure SDK access process, ensure their Azure GitHub organization membership is public rather than private, and join the Azure SDK Partners path that grants membership in the Azure SDK write group, with manager approval where required. After changing org membership visibility to public, pushing an empty commit can be used to re-run checks.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — for a PR author in the Azure REST API specs flow, the practical minimum is:

- a **GitHub account linked to a Microsoft account** and **access to the relevant repo/org**; see [Create a PR against main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish) and [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).
- membership in the **Azure GitHub organization**, and that membership should be **public, not private**, or some checks may not appear/run; see [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).
- **write access** if you expect to trigger all gated checks and merge the PR yourself; see [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

**What the PR author needs**

- **Identity/access**
  - Your GitHub account must be **linked with your Microsoft account**. The spec PR docs list that as a prerequisite in [Create a PR against main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish).
  - You must have **permission to the repository you are using**. For public work that is [Azure/azure-rest-api-specs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-repos); for private work it is `azure-rest-api-specs-pr`, which also requires access to the Azure org/private repo as described in [Azure REST API specs repositories on GitHub](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-repos).

- **GitHub organization membership**
  - You may need to **join the Azure GitHub organization** to access the PR and related review flow; that prerequisite is called out in [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).

- **Organization visibility setting**
  - Your membership in the **Azure** GitHub org should be set to **Public**. The SDK validation guidance says that if `SDK Validation - {Language}` checks do not appear, it usually means you lack the needed permission, and it explicitly says to make Azure org membership public in [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).

- **Permission level for checks**
  - If the SDK validation checks are missing from the PR, treat that as a **permissions/write-access issue** and use the access process referenced from [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).

- **Permission level for merge**
  - To merge, the docs say the PR must have a green **`Automated merging requirements met`** check, **at least one approval** from another person with **write access**, and **you must also have write access** if you want to merge it yourself; see [Get your PR merged](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).
  - If the PR targets public `main`, you must also apply the **`PublishToCustomers`** label before merge, per [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

**Bottom line**

- **Required:** Microsoft-linked GitHub account, Azure org membership, repo access.
- **Visibility:** Azure org membership should be **public**.
- **To merge yourself:** **write access** to the repo.
- **To complete merge:** green required checks + approval from someone with write access.

I could **not verify an authoritative single doc in this turn that names the exact GitHub team/group to request** for access; the retrieved docs consistently describe the requirement as having the needed repo/org access and write permission.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: What to do when two open PRs share the same commit SHA

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

**Historical ground truth**

Checks are associated with commit SHAs rather than PRs, so having multiple open PRs with the same source commit SHA can confuse GitHub check behavior and repository automation. In that situation, close the other open PR so that only one PR remains associated with that commit SHA before proceeding.

**Cached dev answer**

The reusable answer is: **don’t keep two open PRs on the same head commit SHA if you can avoid it**. Based on the documented behavior of spec validation and trusted PR-routing, the safe practice is to make each live PR resolve to a **unique head commit**; otherwise commit-to-PR mapping can become ambiguous, and some automation is designed to stop rather than guess.

- **Preferred fix:** keep **one branch / one open PR / one head SHA**. If you accidentally opened a duplicate PR for the same exact commit, close one PR and continue with the other, following the normal PR flow in [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).
- **If both PRs must stay open:** make them diverge by pushing a small follow-up commit to one branch (even a no-op commit if needed), so each PR has a different head SHA. That fits how spec checks reason about a PR: they compare the PR’s **base** and **head** commits, as described in [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).
- **After you separate the SHAs:** let CI rerun from the new push. If a required build does not retrigger and stays in an “Expected / waiting for status” state, use the retry guidance in [Azure DevOps Pipeline Guidance](https://dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/internal/_wiki/wikis/internal.wiki?wikiVersion=GBwikiMaster&pagePath=/Engineering-System/Pipelines/Azure-DevOps-Pipeline-Guidance).

**Why this is the reusable rule:** the retrieved docs show that spec validation is commit-based, and the PR-review routing guidance explicitly treats **ambiguous commit-to-PR matches** as something to stop on rather than dispatch through. So the process answer is to remove the ambiguity by giving each open PR its own head commit.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to fix a failing TypeSpec validation check

question: If a PR cannot merge because the TypeSpec validation check is failing, what should be updated and how can the validation be run locally?

**Historical ground truth**

A PR cannot merge while the required TypeSpec validation check is failing. To fix it, update the generated swagger produced from the TypeSpec changes and run TypeSpec validation locally using the documented local workflow, then push the corrected outputs so the check can pass.

**Cached dev answer**

If the **TypeSpec Validation** check is blocking merge, the usual fix is to update the **checked-in outputs and config that `tsv` validates**, not just the `.tsp` files. In practice that means: sync your branch with the latest target branch, reinstall repo dependencies, rerun validation from the repo root, and commit any generated Swagger/examples/config changes it produces. The current repo guidance is in [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).

**What to update**
- **Update your PR branch to the latest parent branch** (`main`, `RPSaaSMaster`, etc.) and reinstall dependencies from the repo root, because mismatches between CI and local runs are commonly caused by stale branch state or stale dependencies. See [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).
- **Update and commit generated artifacts** if `tsv` or `tsp compile` changes them. The check fails if compiling TypeSpec leaves uncommitted changes in generated Swagger or copied example files. See [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).
- If the failure is specifically **`SdkTspConfigValidation`**, update **`tspconfig.yaml`** with the required emitter options/parameters. If the missing config is for an SDK language that is intentionally out of scope, you can suppress the specific **sub-rules** in **`suppressions.yaml`** instead of suppressing the whole check. The rule and suppression format are documented in [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).
- **Do not expect a PR-level suppression for the overall `TypeSpec Validation` check.** The suppression matrix says that check itself is not suppressible as a PR check. See [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).

**Run the validation locally**
- From the **repository root**, the repo wiki’s recommended flow is:

```bash
git clean -xdf
git pull
pnpm ci
pnpm tsv specification/<service>/<TypeSpecProject>
git status
```

- If `git status` shows changes, **commit and push those files** so the PR matches what CI generates. The repo’s local-run instructions are in [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).
- If you only need to regenerate from inside the TypeSpec project folder, you can also run:

```bash
pnpm tsp compile .
```

- Some PR logs still print the equivalent npm form:

```bash
npm ci
npx tsv specification/<service>/<TypeSpecProject>
```

**Rule of thumb**
- **Compile/output drift** → regenerate and commit changed files.
- **`SdkTspConfigValidation`** → fix `tspconfig.yaml`, or add a targeted `suppressions.yaml` entry for only the unsupported emitter option(s).
- **Still repro mismatch vs CI** → reclone or test in a clean folder/machine, per [TypeSpec Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/TypeSpec-Validation).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Whether to fix generated SDK breaking changes in SDK repos or in TypeSpec

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

A TypeSpec change altered a PATCH operation to use a different request body model, and autogenerated SDK PRs in multiple languages now show breaking-change failures because an existing update method signature changed. In this situation, should the fix be made manually in each SDK repo or in TypeSpec? What are the main options for preserving compatibility versus intentionally accepting the breaking change across languages?

**Historical ground truth**

Do not rely on hand-editing each generated SDK repo for this kind of issue. Generated SDK code is derived from the TypeSpec or OpenAPI description, so manual fixes to generated surfaces are expected to be overwritten by future generations if the underlying TypeSpec still defines the changed request body shape.

The preferred place to address the issue is the TypeSpec definition so the change is handled consistently across languages.

There are two main approaches:

1. Preserve the existing SDK contract.
If the prior SDK method signature must remain compatible, model the change in TypeSpec so the older operation shape is preserved while the newer API version introduces its different PATCH shape through versioning. This can be done with versioned operations and route-sharing or rename patterns so the wire route remains the same while the SDK surface stays compatible where needed.

2. Intentionally accept the SDK breaking change.
If changing the public SDK method signature is deliberate, keep the TypeSpec change and add SDK breaking-change suppressions for the affected languages in the TypeSpec project, such as through sdk-suppressions.yaml, so regenerated SDK PRs can proceed consistently.

In short, cross-language remediation should be centralized in TypeSpec by correcting the model, applying versioning or customization patterns, or adding approved suppressions, rather than patching each SDK independently.

**Cached dev answer**

Usually **fix it at the TypeSpec layer first**, not by hand in every SDK repo. For generated Azure SDKs, the preferred mitigation is a TypeSpec-side customization in `client.tsp` and sometimes `tspconfig.yaml`, because that drives generation across languages and survives regeneration ([Modular SDK Customization Guide | Before You Customize](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-js/blob/main/documentation/modular-customization.md); [TypeSpec-to-SDK Release Workflow Spec | Definitions](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-tools/blob/main/tools/azsdk-cli/docs/specs/typespec-to-sdk-release-workflow.spec.md)).

**Main options:**

- **Best option: preserve compatibility in TypeSpec.**\
  If the old update method shape still represents the same wire behavior, restore the stable SDK surface with TypeSpec customizations in `client.tsp` or generator config in `tspconfig.yaml`, then regenerate all languages ([Spec: Customizing Clients | Background / Problem Statement](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-tools/blob/main/tools/azsdk-cli/docs/specs/3-customizing-client-tsp.spec.md); [Modular SDK Customization Guide | Before You Customize](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-for-js/blob/main/documentation/modular-customization.md)).

- **Fallback: use language-specific SDK customization layers.**\
  If TypeSpec cannot express the compatibility shape, then fix it in each SDK’s supported customization layer, not as ad hoc edits to regenerated files. Those are handwritten customizations in the SDK repos and must be preserved across regeneration ([Spec: Customizing Clients | Background / Problem Statement](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-tools/blob/main/tools/azsdk-cli/docs/specs/3-customizing-client-tsp.spec.md); [TypeSpec-to-SDK Release Workflow Spec | Definitions](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-tools/blob/main/tools/azsdk-cli/docs/specs/typespec-to-sdk-release-workflow.spec.md)).

- **Intentional break: accept it rather than hiding it.**\
  If the PATCH body change is a real service-contract change and no faithful compatibility shape exists, the SDK owners may choose to **accept** the breaking change instead of manually “fixing” every language. In the spec-PR workflow, accepted or otherwise unmitigated SDK breaking changes are handled via suppression/approval rather than forcing a cross-language manual patch campaign ([Spec: [SDK Breaking Change Detecting] - [SDK Breaking Change Detector Tool] | Design Proposal | Scenarios for Using the Tool](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-tools/blob/main/tools/azsdk-cli/docs/specs/sdk-breaking-change-detect.spec.md)).

**Important nuance:** a generated signature difference is only a **potential** SDK breaking change until you confirm the affected API was actually shipped in a released SDK. The docs explicitly say TypeSpec-based detection is not fully authoritative by itself ([Spec: [SDK Breaking Change Detecting] - [SDK Breaking Change Detector Tool] | Background / Problem Statement | Detect SDK breaking changes from TypeSpec is not 100% reliable](https://github.com/Azure/azure-sdk-tools/blob/main/tools/azsdk-cli/docs/specs/sdk-breaking-change-detect.spec.md)).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Recommended way to update protected release-* branches

question: What is the recommended process for updating a protected release-* branch with changes from its parent branch, and what are the git-history tradeoffs compared with alternatives?

**Historical ground truth**

Branches named release-* are a known special case: they get branch protection, but that makes updating them harder. The recommended process is to use the documented branch-update workflow, which creates a PR to merge the parent branch into the release branch. Using that process is the recommended way to update the branch. It may add extra merge commits and clutter the branch history, but it does not break the intended PR flow; when a later PR is opened from the release branch to RPSaaSMaster, that clutter should fall out of the final comparison. If cleaner history is preferred, an alternative is to create a new release-* branch from RPSaaSMaster and cherry-pick the desired commits. A feature-* branch allows normal git merge updates more easily, but it does not provide the same branch protection as release-* naming.

**Cached dev answer**

The recommended approach for a **protected `release-*` branch** is to **update the branch through a PR**, not by pushing a direct merge. If you only need repo infrastructure/tooling updates, the preferred path is the helper pipeline **[tools - update-release-branch-in-specs](https://dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/internal/_build?definitionId=7487)**, which creates a PR with a **selective merge** from `main` that excludes files under `specifications`. That is the documented workaround specifically for protected branches because a full merge into an old `release-*` branch can pull in lots of unrelated changes and break checks. For normal, unprotected branches, the docs say to just use `git merge main`.\

**Recommended process**
- **If the protected `release-*` branch only needs infra/shared-tooling updates:** run **[tools - update-release-branch-in-specs](https://dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/internal/_build?definitionId=7487)**, set `BranchToMergeTo` to your `release-*` branch, review the PR it creates, and merge it after checks pass.
- **If you truly need all parent-branch changes:** create a **PR into the protected `release-*` branch** containing the merge, instead of trying to update it directly.
- **If the branch is very stale:** the guidance says to first try updating it from `main`; if it is too old for that to work reliably, **recreate the release branch**.
- **For day-to-day feature work:** create topic branches from the release branch and PR back to it; the docs explicitly say **do not merge `main` into your topic branch**. If you only need a few upstream fixes, **cherry-pick** them or copy the changes manually.

**Git-history tradeoffs**
- **Selective-merge helper pipeline — recommended for protected release branches when only infra is needed**
  - **Pros:** keeps unrelated spec changes out of the release branch; lower risk of noisy diffs and broken checks; best fit for branch-protection constraints.
  - **Cons:** history is **not a full content sync** with the parent branch’s specs, because `specifications/**` is intentionally excluded.

- **Full merge from parent branch via PR**
  - **Pros:** preserves the real merge relationship in Git history and brings over the complete upstream state.
  - **Cons:** on an older `release-*` branch, it can import many unwanted changes, especially outside your service area, and may cause validation/check failures.

- **Cherry-pick specific commits**
  - **Pros:** very clean, targeted history; avoids unrelated upstream changes.
  - **Cons:** you lose the “this branch was merged from parent” history edge, and it does not truly synchronize the branch.

- **Recreate the release branch**
  - **Pros:** cleanest branch state when the existing one is too far behind.
  - **Cons:** you give up continuity on the old branch and may need to move or re-home in-flight work.

So in short: **for protected `release-*` branches, prefer the helper pipeline for infra-only refreshes; use a PR-based full merge only when you actually need the whole parent-branch state; use cherry-picks for a few targeted fixes.**

</details>

**Cached dev answer**

- **Get the required access** by following [aka.ms/azsdk/access](https://aka.ms/azsdk/access). The guidance says missing `SDK Validation - {Language}` checks usually means the author does **not** have the permission needed to trigger them.
- **Make Azure GitHub org membership public** on the [Azure organization people page](https://github.com/orgs/Azure/people?query=). A private membership can prevent the PR gateway/SDK validation workflows from starting correctly.
- **Join the Azure SDK Partners group** using the instructions linked from [aka.ms/azsdk/access](https://aka.ms/azsdk/access).
- **After access is fixed, rerun the SDK validation check**. Re-running any `SDK Validation - {Language}` check will automatically re-evaluate the aggregate `SDK Validation Status` check. If needed, comment:
  ```text
  /azp run SDK Validation - {Language}
  ```
- If the PR is still stuck after access is corrected, use the Azure SDK Tools Agent guidance page at [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review) and ask the Agent: **“What’s the status of my spec PR?”**

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Requirements to approve Azure API spec PRs

question: What access and repository configuration are required for service team members to be able to approve Azure API spec PRs, and do they need to be added to CODEOWNERS?

**Historical ground truth**

To approve Azure API spec PRs, reviewers need the required repository write access through the documented access process, and they must be listed in CODEOWNERS for the relevant spec paths so their approvals count. If the service team is not yet included in CODEOWNERS for those paths, update CODEOWNERS, and make that CODEOWNERS change in a separate PR.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — service team members generally need **repository write access** to the relevant specs repo to give the approval that counts for merge, plus the usual repo/org access setup. **Being in `CODEOWNERS` is not what gives someone permission to approve**, but `CODEOWNERS` *does* matter if the PR touches paths that require code-owner review.

- **Minimum access for an approver**
  - A **GitHub account linked with their Microsoft account** and access to the relevant repo/org, as described in [Create a PR against main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish) and [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).
  - **Write access** to the target repository. The merge guidance says a PR needs at least one approval, generally from another person on the team who has write access, and a user with write access can merge once the required checks are green. See [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

- **Branch/repo-specific nuance**
  - For **`azure-rest-api-specs-pr` → `RPSaaSDev`**, the approver must be a member of the **RP platform Users** group; the ARM guidance calls that out explicitly in [REST API specifications (either OpenAPIv2 or TypeSpec)](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/swaggeronboarding.html).
  - For **data-plane PRs**, service-team approval alone may still not be enough: the protected `data-plane-review-signoff` label must be applied by the API Stewardship reviewer pool, per [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review).

- **Do they need to be added to `CODEOWNERS`?**
  - **Not just to click Approve.**
  - **Yes, if you want their review to satisfy required code-owner review for the changed paths.** If the touched folder is covered by `CODEOWNERS`, GitHub requests those owners and at least one matching code-owner approval is needed for merge.
  - If your service already has a `CODEOWNERS` entry covering that area, you usually **do not** need a new entry for every PR. Add/update `CODEOWNERS` when your service’s folder ownership is not already represented.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Handle HTTP 403 when pushing Azure API spec changes

question: When contributing Azure API spec changes, if pushing to the upstream repo or branch returns HTTP 403, should the changes be made from a fork, and when should repo access be requested instead?

**Historical ground truth**

An HTTP 403 when pushing to the Azure specs repository usually means the account does not have write permission to that repository or branch. The standard contribution workflow is to fork the appropriate specs repository, clone the fork, create a feature branch there, push to the fork, and open a pull request to the upstream repository. If direct write access is expected for the contributor, the correct next step is to follow the Azure SDK access request process to obtain the required permissions.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **an HTTP 403 when pushing to the upstream Azure API specs repo usually means you should push to your own fork instead**, then open a PR back to the upstream repo/branch. The Azure API spec workflow docs explicitly tell contributors to **fork** `Azure/azure-rest-api-specs` or `Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr`, work in their fork, and submit the PR against the upstream branch. See [Work against the release branch](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-2-update) and [Convert OpenAPI specs to TypeSpec](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs/api-typespec-conversion).

**Request repo access instead** when you actually need permissions that a fork does not provide, for example:
- You need to work directly on branches in the main Azure repo rather than only in your fork. Follow [Access](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/onboard/access).
- You need **write access** for repo operations such as applying/dismissing labels, creating or modifying issues, assigning issues, or similar upstream-repo tasks. The access guidance says those scenarios require write access; start from [Access](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/onboard/access).
- You need to work in the **private** repo `Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr`, which requires permission to that repository. See [Azure REST API specs repositories on GitHub](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-repos) and [Access](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/onboard/access).

**Before requesting access**, make sure the basics are satisfied:
- Join the Microsoft and Azure GitHub organizations and make those memberships public, as required by [Access](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/onboard/access).

So the short rule is:
- **403 on push to upstream:** use your **fork** for commits.
- **Need private-repo access or direct upstream write capabilities:** **request access**.

</details>

### spec-review-0187: Should ARM PATCH request models expose id, name, and type as writable properties?

**Dataset:** `versioning.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0213](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0213) | **GT basis:** expert_plus_bot | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-04-09T19:42:43.301Z

**Assessment:** The answer aligns with the cited ARM PATCH guidance that id/name/type/location/provisioningState are not updatable in PATCH and, if present, must be readOnly or immutable. It also correctly recommends a PATCH-specific model/custom patch template when inheritance from Resource/TrackedResource/ProxyResource would otherwise expose those fields. On change classification, it appropriately treats removing or marking such non-updatable fields as a spec bug fix/contract correction rather than a real backend breaking change, while preserving the valid caveat that if a service truly supported updating such fields, changing that would be breaking.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that ARM PATCH request bodies should expose only actually updateable properties.; State that top-level ARM envelope fields such as id, name, and type are not valid writable PATCH inputs for normal ARM resources.; Acknowledge that if such fields appear in PATCH due to inheriting from Resource, TrackedResource, or ProxyResource, the fix is to use a PATCH-specific model or otherwise ensure those fields are readOnly/immutable in the PATCH shape.; Classify removing those accidentally writable non-updateable fields, or marking them readOnly, as a spec bug fix/contract correction rather than a backend API change, conditioned on the service never truly supporting updates to them.; Note the conditional exception that if the backend genuinely honors PATCH updates to one of those fields, then changing that behavior would be a real breaking change.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [authoring-01-023](expert-knowledge-report.md#authoring-01-023)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Should ARM PATCH request models expose id, name, and type as writable properties?

question: For an ARM resource PATCH request model, should top-level ARM properties like id, name, and type be modeled as writable request-body properties? If they appear because the PATCH model inherits from Resource, TrackedResource, or ProxyResource, is removing them from writable PATCH input or marking them readOnly treated as a breaking change or as a spec bug fix?

**Historical ground truth**

ARM PATCH request bodies should contain only properties that are actually updatable. Top-level ARM fields such as id, name, and type are not appropriate writable PATCH input and should not be exposed as writable properties in the PATCH model. If those fields appear only because the PATCH schema inherits from Resource, TrackedResource, or ProxyResource, the correct fix is to use a PATCH-specific model or otherwise make those fields readOnly in the request shape. Treating this as a correction to an inaccurate specification is appropriate; it is not a backend API change. This guidance assumes those fields are not truly updateable, and changing an ARM resource name via PATCH is not a valid general pattern because the name is part of the resource ID.

**Cached dev answer**

No. For an ARM resource `PATCH`, top-level ARM envelope properties like `id`, `name`, and `type` should **not** be modeled as writable request-body properties.

- ARM’s PATCH rules explicitly say a `Patch` operation **must not update** `id`, `name`, `type`, `location`, or `properties.provisioningState`. If any of those properties appear in the PATCH body, they must be modeled as **readOnly** or **immutable**, not writable.
- In TypeSpec guidance, the PATCH model should generally **exclude** service-generated and create-only fields such as `id`, `name`, `type`, `systemData`, and `location`. If those fields are showing up only because the PATCH type inherits from `Resource`, `TrackedResource`, or `ProxyResource`, the preferred fix is to use a **custom PATCH model** rather than inheriting the full resource shape; see [ARM Resource Operations](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/resource-operations).

On the breaking-change question:

- If those properties were never actually valid PATCH inputs at runtime, then changing the spec to remove them from writable PATCH input, or marking them `readOnly`, is best treated as a **spec bug fix / contract correction**, not as a true breaking API change.
- That conclusion follows from the ARM rule that such properties are **not updatable** in PATCH in the first place, so a writable schema is describing invalid behavior.
- The only caveat is: if your service really did honor PATCH updates to one of those fields, then changing that behavior would be a **real breaking change**. For normal ARM resources, though, `id`/`name`/`type` are identifiers or immutable envelope fields, so the expected treatment is **bug fix**.

So the short answer is:

- **Should they be writable in PATCH?** No.
- **If inherited accidentally, should you remove or mark readOnly?** Yes.
- **Is that usually a breaking change?** Usually **no** — it is typically a **spec bug fix**.

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Should an AFEC-gated preview API be published to the public specs repo before rolling out private resource manifests?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

For an ARM API version that is still AFEC-gated and therefore in private preview, should the team first roll out private resource manifests or first publish the OpenAPI spec to the public azure-rest-api-specs repository?

**Historical ground truth**

If an ARM API version is still AFEC-gated, it should remain private and should not be published to the public azure-rest-api-specs main branch yet. The correct sequence is to roll out the resource manifests in the private specs flow first while the API remains AFEC-controlled. Publish the OpenAPI spec to the public azure-rest-api-specs repository only when the API is ready to move from private preview to public preview and no longer requires AFEC gating.

**Cached dev answer**

No — if the ARM API version is still **AFEC-gated**, it is still treated as **private preview**, so the team should **keep the spec in the private repo and roll out the private resource manifests first**. Publishing that spec to public `azure-rest-api-specs` would effectively move it to **public preview**, which the guidance says should happen only after the private-preview requirements are no longer in effect.

- **Private preview means not public yet.** The process guidance says a private-preview API version must **not be present in the public specs repo**, and for ARM it belongs in private `RPSaaSMaster` behind AFEC.
- **Publishing to the public repo changes the lifecycle stage.** The guidance in [Move private specs to public](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/pr-move-private-to-public) says copying specs from private to public effectively converts the API from **private preview** to **public preview**.
- **So the order is:** private manifests / private rollout first, then public spec publication later.
- **Only publish publicly when you are ready for public preview**, including the related readiness work called out in [Move private specs to public](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/pr-move-private-to-public) and the lifecycle rules in [API versions and branches](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches).

</details>

**Acceptance criteria:** State that if TypeSpec Validation is a required check on the target branch and is failing, the PR is not mergeable until the blocker is resolved.; Ground mergeability in required-check status such as Automated merging requirements met / Next Steps to Merge, without implying non-required failures always block merge.; State that TypeSpec Validation does not have a PR-only suppression path that would allow merging past the failure.; If resolving the validation issue would require a cross-version breaking change, direct the author to the normal breaking-change or versioning approval process rather than merging with the failing validation check.; Make clear that customer-impacting breaking changes must receive the appropriate review/approval before shipping.; Allow branch-specific nuance: this applies when the check is actually required for the PR target branch, not universally on every branch.; If discussing versioning policy, preserve the distinction that new preview versions may break prior preview versions, but new preview or GA versions must remain compatible with the latest prior GA version.; If discussing already-published API versions, note that fixes should generally be made via a new API version rather than editing the published version in place, unless an approved bug-fix exception applies.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can a preview spec PR merge if TypeSpec Validation is failing?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If an Azure REST API spec PR for a new preview API version has a failing required TypeSpec Validation check, can it be merged anyway? If fixing the validation issue would require a cross-version breaking change, what process should be followed instead?

**Historical ground truth**

No. A spec PR should not be merged while the required TypeSpec Validation check is failing. If resolving the validation issue requires a cross-version breaking change, handle that through the normal breaking-change approval or exception process rather than merging with the failing validation check. Customer-facing breaking changes should not be shipped without that review.

**Cached dev answer**

No. If `TypeSpec Validation` is **required** for the PR’s target branch and it is failing, the PR is **not mergeable** until that blocker is resolved. In the spec PR process, merge readiness is determined by the **`Automated merging requirements met`** status and the **`Next Steps to Merge`** guidance; a required failing check blocks merge. `TypeSpec Validation` also does **not** have a check-level PR suppression path you can use to merge past it.

If the only way to “fix” the validation failure would introduce a **cross-version breaking change**, don’t merge through the failure. Follow the normal **breaking-change review/approval** process instead via [aka.ms/brch](https://aka.ms/brch). For spec PRs, breaking/versioning blockers are represented by labels such as `BreakingChangeReviewRequired` or `VersioningReviewRequired`; those must be addressed first, then the PR is rerun (for example with `/azp run`) and only proceeds once the blockers are cleared.

Two important distinctions from the policy:

- A **new preview** version does **not** have to stay compatible with the **previous preview** version.
- But a **new preview or GA** version **must** remain backward compatible with the **latest previous GA** version. If your fix breaks that contract, it needs the breaking-change process rather than an exception to merge.

Also, once an API version is published, you generally should **not change that same version in place** just to resolve the issue. If the needed correction is itself a breaking change within an already-published preview version, the documented path is to create a **new preview API version** and, if that new version breaks the latest GA, take it through the same [breaking-change review flow](https://aka.ms/brch).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Which repo to use for release planning and SDK generation when specs are still private

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If an API spec change is still in the private azure-rest-api-specs-pr repo and release-plan tooling says the PR is not in the public repo, should standard release planning and SDK release generation be done from azure-rest-api-specs-pr or from the public azure-rest-api-specs repo? What is the expected workflow for private preview versus public preview or GA?

**Historical ground truth**

Use azure-rest-api-specs-pr for private, pre-announcement work, but use the public azure-rest-api-specs repo for the standard release-planning and SDK release flow. A PR that exists only in azure-rest-api-specs-pr is not the expected input for the normal public release-plan tooling. For private preview, staying in azure-rest-api-specs-pr is appropriate and SDK generation should use the private-preview agent or MCP-based flow rather than the standard public release process. For public preview or GA, move or copy the spec changes into a PR in the public azure-rest-api-specs repo and create the standard release plan from that public PR.

**Cached dev answer**

Use the **private** repo only for the **Private Preview** phase. Use the **public** repo for the **standard Public Preview / GA release workflow**. So if the spec is still only in `azure-rest-api-specs-pr`, that is **not** the normal public release-planning / public SDK-generation path yet.

- **Private Preview**
  - Merge the spec PR into **`Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr`**.
  - That merge generates a **Private Preview release plan**, but it is expected to be **completed immediately**; there is no ongoing standard public SDK release workflow attached to it.
  - If you want SDKs during private preview, that is **optional and nonstandard**: use the **[Azure SDK Tools Agent](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/plan/release-plan-create)** against the **private spec repo** and **private SDK repos** for internal use. The docs say there is **no formal public SDK release process** for private-preview SDKs, and those changes should stay in private branches/private feeds rather than public mainline release flow.

- **Public Preview or GA**
  - Merge the spec PR into **`Azure/azure-rest-api-specs`**.
  - That public merge is what generates the **active** release plan used for the normal SDK workflow.
  - For management-plane TypeSpec, the public merge is also the trigger for the standard automated SDK generation flow; the resulting SDK PRs are tracked from that release plan.

- **Expected transition**
  - A **Private Preview** plan is **not reused** for **Public Preview** or **GA**.
  - When you move from private preview to public preview/GA, the expected workflow is: publish the spec in the **public repo**, then let automation create a **new** release plan for that release type and plane.

So the reusable rule is:

- **Private Preview** → `azure-rest-api-specs-pr`
- **Public Preview / GA** → `azure-rest-api-specs`

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to bootstrap the first default tag in a README when lint-diff fails on the base branch

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If lint-diff fails because the base branch README has no default tag and a PR is introducing the first default tag, what is the recommended way to bootstrap that default tag? Historical facts: the base branch had no default tag, lint-diff reported "No default tag found for readme ... in before state", and the proposed change added `tag: release_2026-05-01`.

**Historical ground truth**

Bootstrap the first default tag by making the smallest possible spec change in main that adds a valid default tag to the README. That default tag should be a proper README/AutoRest default tag that covers the latest API-version files intended to be exposed. If lint-diff still fails solely because the base branch previously had no default tag, use a one-time Swagger LintDiff suppression for that bootstrap PR under the PR suppression process. Once that minimal bootstrap change is merged, later PRs can change or extend the default tag normally because both before and after states will resolve a valid default tag.

**Cached dev answer**

The recommended bootstrap is a **two-step change**:

- **First, submit a small README-only PR to the base branch** that adds the first default tag there.
- **Then rebase or retarget the real PR** on top of that change and continue with the substantive spec update.

Why this is the reusable fix:

- `Swagger LintDiff` compares the spec **before** and **after** the PR. The docs and Q&A both indicate that if the **before state is invalid**, the PR that tries to fix it can still fail because LintDiff must evaluate both sides. That matches the reported error: **“No default tag found for readme ... in before state.”**
- A default tag is an expected README construct and should point to **all spec files for the latest API version**. See [Publish REST API reference docs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-docs) and [Create or update an Azure REST API spec](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs/api-specs).

So in your historical example, the right bootstrap pattern would be:

```yaml
tag: release_2026-05-01
```

added first as the **initial default tag on the base branch**, assuming that tag is the intended latest-version tag and its `input-file` list is version-uniform.

### spec-review-0192: Can preview-only properties be omitted from a first GA ARM API version?

**Dataset:** `versioning.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0221](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0221) | **GT basis:** bot_fallback | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-04-14T14:46:46.36Z

**Assessment:** The answer matches the historical guidance and retrieved evidence: for a first GA ARM version, preview-only properties may be omitted because only changes promoted to stable remain in GA, and preview-only changes should be reversed/removed from the stable version. It also correctly describes the ARM-specific TypeSpec patterns for either replacing the preview with the first stable version or introducing a subsequent preview when some features remain preview-only.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that omitting properties that existed only in preview is acceptable when producing the first GA ARM API version, because there is no prior GA contract to preserve.; Explain that this is preview-to-GA hardening rather than a breaking change against an existing GA surface.; Describe TypeSpec modeling for stable-after-preview: keep only changes promoted to stable in the GA version and remove or reverse preview-only changes from the stable contract.; If only the first GA version is being produced, indicate that the old preview version can be replaced by the new stable version and preview-only properties omitted from the stable model.; If some features must remain preview after GA for ARM, describe the ARM-specific pattern of adding a new stable version plus a subsequent preview version, marking only the later preview with `@previewVersion`.; Explain how to scope preview-only properties so they appear only in the preview version, e.g. by adding them in the subsequent preview version rather than including them in GA.; Avoid claiming that preview-only properties must be preserved in the first GA solely because they existed in preview.; Avoid suggesting in-place mutation of an already published API version; contract differences should be represented through a new API version.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [versioning-01-002](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-002)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can preview-only properties be omitted from a first GA ARM API version?

question: When introducing the first stable ARM API version for a resource provider, is it acceptable to omit properties that existed only in preview API versions and were never part of any prior GA API version? If so, how should that be represented in TypeSpec versioning?

**Historical ground truth**

Yes. For a first stable API version, properties that existed only in preview versions and were never part of any GA API version may be omitted from the stable contract. That is treated as normal preview-to-GA hardening rather than a breaking change to an existing GA contract, because there is no prior GA surface to preserve. In TypeSpec, keep preview versions marked as preview, add the new stable version as the GA baseline, and scope preview-only properties so they are not included in the stable version.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes.

For a **first GA ARM API version**, it is acceptable to **leave out properties that existed only in preview** and were **never part of any earlier GA contract**. The TypeSpec guidance for “stable after preview” says to keep only the changes that are being promoted to stable, and to **reverse/remove preview-only changes** from the new stable version.

**How to model it in TypeSpec**

- **If you are producing only the first GA version:** replace the old preview version with the new stable version, remove `@previewVersion`, and simply **omit the preview-only property** from the stable model. Use the “stable after preview” pattern from [Adding a Stable Version when the Last Version was Preview](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/versioning/03-stable-after-preview).
- **If some features must remain preview after GA:** for ARM, create a **new preview after the new stable**. The guidance is to remove preview `A`, add stable `A+1`, add preview `A+2`, and mark only `A+2` with `@previewVersion`. Put the preview-only property behind `@added(Versions.\`A+2\`)`, so it exists only in the new preview, not in GA. That is the ARM-specific pattern in [ARM: Managing a Single Active Preview When Some Features Always Remain in Preview](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/versioning/uncommon-scenarios/02-perpetual-preview).

**Recommended shape**

```tsp
import "@typespec/versioning";
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-core";
import "@azure-tools/typespec-azure-resource-manager";

using TypeSpec.Versioning;
using Azure.Core;

@versioned(Versions)
namespace Contoso.Employees;

enum Versions {
  `2026-01-01`,
  @previewVersion
  `2026-02-01-preview`,
}

model EmployeeProperties {
  /** GA property */
  displayName?: string;

  /** Still preview-only, so not in 2026-01-01 */
  @added(Versions.`2026-02-01-preview`)
  experimentalProfile?: string;
}
```

**What not to do**

- Don’t keep the preview-only property in the GA model and try to “explain” it away.
- Don’t alternate the same property with repeated stable-remove / preview-add patterns unless you truly need the ARM perpetual-preview flow; the guidance says that pattern is error-prone.
- Don’t modify the existing preview version in place; publish the contract difference through a new API version, consistent with [Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines | Common API Patterns | API Versioning](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md).

**Rule of thumb**

- **Promoted to GA** → present in the stable version.
- **Not promoted to GA** → absent from the stable version.
- **Still needs preview** → reintroduced or kept only in the **next preview version**, not in the first GA.

</details>

### spec-review-0193: How to handle service-level and server-level @doc text in a versioned TypeSpec API

**Dataset:** `versioning.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0222](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0222) | **GT basis:** bot_fallback | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-04-14T04:52:44.612Z

**Assessment:** The answer aligns with the historical guidance and retrieved evidence: TypeSpec versioning decorators are documented for API surface elements, not for independently versioning `@doc` on shared `@service`/`@server` symbols. It correctly concludes that shared top-level docs should be updated in place and that version-specific details belong on versioned API elements or external per-version artifacts. Its extra suggestion to keep top-level docs generic/stable is a reasonable optional pattern, not a contradiction.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that `@doc` attached to shared `@service`/`@server` symbols is not independently versioned by the documented TypeSpec versioning mechanism.; Explain that updating shared symbol documentation affects all emitted API versions that include those symbols.; Recommend updating the shared `@doc` text in place rather than duplicating service/server symbols solely to vary documentation by API version.; Clarify that actual contract differences must be represented through versioned API surface constructs such as versioned operations, models, properties, or parameters.; If older-version-specific narrative must be preserved, direct that content to versioned elements or external per-version artifacts rather than attempting to version top-level `@doc` separately.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [authoring-02-010](expert-knowledge-report.md#authoring-02-010)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to handle service-level and server-level @doc text in a versioned TypeSpec API

question: In a versioned TypeSpec API, if a new API version changes the functionality and the shared @service or @server @doc text needs to be updated to remove deprecated features and describe new capabilities, how should that documentation be maintained? Can @doc content be versioned separately, or should it be updated in place on the shared symbols?

**Historical ground truth**

Update the @doc text directly on the existing shared @service and @server symbols. In TypeSpec, documentation comments are attached to symbols and are not versioned independently. Versioning decorators are intended for API surface elements such as operations, models, and properties, not for maintaining separate documentation text per API version.

As a result, changing the documentation on a shared symbol affects every emitted API version that includes that symbol. That is acceptable for documentation-only updates, provided the actual contract changes are represented through the versioned API surface itself. Avoid duplicating symbols solely to produce different docs for different versions, because that adds unnecessary complexity.

Keep the existing versioned namespace and API version enum, add the new API version normally, and revise the shared service/server documentation in place.

**Cached dev answer**

Short answer: **update the shared `@doc` text in place**. Based on the retrieved TypeSpec versioning guidance, I did **not** find a documented mechanism to version `@doc` independently on shared `@service` or `@server` metadata.

- TypeSpec versioning is documented around **API surface changes** on declarations and members — e.g. `@added`, `@removed`, `@madeOptional`, `@madeRequired`, `@renamedFrom`, and `@typeChangedFrom`.
- The guidance also says that after you define versions, you **adapt the TypeSpec code for the latest version while preserving earlier API surfaces**.
- Service-level description metadata is attached to the namespace via decorators like `@service` and `@doc`, so if that metadata is shared, it is effectively **shared metadata**, not independently versioned content.

So for your case:

- **If the `@service` / `@server` description is meant to describe the current service as a whole**, update it in place.
- **If older-version behavior needs to remain documented**, don’t rely on versioning `@doc` itself. Instead:
  - keep the shared description **generic/stable**, and
  - put version-specific details on the **versioned operations/models/properties** or in per-version emitted specs/examples/release notes.

A practical pattern is:

```typespec
import "@typespec/http";
import "@typespec/versioning";

using Http;
using TypeSpec.Versioning;

@doc("Contoso service for managing widgets.")
@service(#{ title: "Contoso Widget Service" })
@server("{endpoint}", "Service endpoint", {
  @doc("The service endpoint.")
  endpoint: url,
})
@versioned(Versions)
namespace Contoso.Widgets;

enum Versions {
  v2024_01_01: "2024-01-01",
  v2025_01_01: "2025-01-01",
}

model Widget {
  id: string;

  @added(Versions.v2025_01_01)
  @doc("New capability introduced in 2025-01-01.")
  advancedFeature: string;
}
```

That keeps top-level docs stable, while version-specific documentation lives on the elements that actually changed.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Adding an enum value to an unpublished preview API version without changing api-version

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

Can an added enum value in an unpublished preview API version proceed without changing the api-version, and if so what approval workflow applies?

**Historical ground truth**

Adding an enum value changes the contract, so keeping the same api-version normally requires a versioning-policy exception rather than being automatically allowed. For an unpublished preview API version that has not been rolled out to customers, the change can proceed as an exception if it is treated as a breaking-change/versioning review case and the required approval labels and sign-off are obtained. If that exception is not approved, the safe fallback is to introduce a new preview api-version with the updated enum instead of modifying the existing one in place.

**Cached dev answer**

Short answer: **not via the private-preview same-version exception**. An added enum value is treated by OpenAPI diff rule [`1020 - AddedEnumValue`](https://github.com/Azure/openapi-diff/blob/main/docs/rules/1020.md) as a **breaking change in the same `api-version`**, even though it is allowed in a **newer** `api-version`. So the reusable guidance is:

- **If the preview API version is already published** to a production branch, **do not keep the same `api-version`** for this change. Create a **new preview `api-version`** instead, per the [Breaking Changes FAQ](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/faq_breaking_changes) and [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).
- The **same-version private-preview approval path** is only for **non-breaking** changes, using `Versioning-Approved-PrivatePreview` as described in [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep). An added enum value does **not** fit that exception.
- **If you move the change into a newer preview `api-version`**, that preview-to-preview replacement generally does **not** need the Azure Breaking Change or Retirement process; however, if the **new preview** is breaking relative to the **latest GA**, then the **full breaking-change process** applies, per the [Breaking Changes FAQ](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/faq_breaking_changes).
- If by **“unpublished”** you mean truly **`in development`** with **no customers**, the retrieved policy implies the hard “don’t change in place” rule starts **once the version is published**. The docs I found do **not** describe a separate special approval workflow for that pre-publication case; they only spell out the published/private-preview/public-preview rules in [API versions and branches](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches).

</details>

It also documents a general exception for fixing the spec to match actual implementation. However, the supplied maintained guidance does not explicitly connect the AddedPath same-version exception to Breaking Change Board approval, and it does not explicitly say that recent merge timing or limited rollout are not valid reasons to suppress/override the AddedPath finding for a published version. One passage mentions a branch-policy exception for not-yet-released APIs, but that is not framed as an AddedPath exception workflow and should not be substituted for the requested rule.

**Current-KB clarification hypothesis:** Reject recency of merge or limited rollout as valid reasons to override/suppress the AddedPath failure for that published version.; If discussing exceptions, include the condition that a same-version correction is only possible when the spec is being updated to match already implemented service behavior, and that this requires Breaking Change Board approval rather than a local override/suppression.

**Potential fix (not validated by search alone):** Add to the maintained PR breaking-change/versioning guidance a rule such as: 'For policy purposes, an API version becomes published/existing once merged to a production branch. Adding a new path, including a nested resource path, in that same api-version is an AddedPath/versioning violation and requires a new dated api-version. Recent merge timing, partial rollout, or limited customer exposure are not by themselves grounds to suppress or locally override this finding. The only same-version correction case is when the spec is being updated to match service behavior already implemented under that api-version; that case must go through the documented breaking-change approval path (Approved-BugFix / aka.ms/brch), not an ad hoc suppression.'

**Search evidence documents:** [`azure-sdk-docs-eng/docs#design#specs-pr-guides#pr-brch-deep.md`](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep), [`azure_openapi_diff_docs/docs#rules#1038.md`](https://github.com/Azure/openapi-diff/blob/main/docs/rules/1038.md), [`static_cpex_docs/faq_breaking_changes.md`](https://eng.ms/docs/cloud-ai-platform/azure-core/azure-core-product/azure-product-lifecycle-management-plm/azure-product-lifecycle-management/cpex/media/faq_breaking_changes)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can you modify an API version after it is merged to main without creating a new version?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a PR adds a new nested resource path in the same API version as a spec that has already been merged to main, and the author says that version was merged only recently and is not yet broadly released, can the breaking-change AddedPath failure be overridden for that file, or is a new API version required?

**Historical ground truth**

After an API version is merged to main, it is treated as an existing published version for spec policy purposes. Changes such as adding new paths to that existing version require an API version update rather than an override based on how recently it was merged or whether rollout is still limited. An exception exists only when the spec is being corrected to match behavior the service already implements; keeping the same API version in that case requires Breaking Change Board approval rather than a local suppression or simple override.

**Cached dev answer**

No — if that API version has already been merged to `main`, you should treat it as published and **not** add the nested resource path in place. In this case, **`AddedPath` is only allowed in a new API version**; in the **same** API version it is classified as a breaking/versioning violation, not something you normally override just because the merge was recent or the feature is not yet broadly released.

- **Why:** Azure versioning policy says that once an API version is merged to a production branch, you must not change its on-the-wire contract in place — even for additive changes — because that creates “two versions of the same version.”
- **For this specific scenario:** a new nested resource path is a new path, and `AddedPath` explicitly treats that as:
  - **additive in a new API version**
  - **breaking in the same API version**
- **Expected fix:** create a **new dated API version** and add the new nested resource there.
- **Narrow exception:** some **private preview** cases can keep certain **non-breaking** changes in the same API version, but that exception does **not** generally apply to specs already merged to public `main`.

</details>

**Replay question**

title: Who can apply ARM signoff and suppression approval labels on a PR that needs suppressions reviewed

question: For an API spec PR that requires suppressions to be reviewed, who is authorized to apply ARM signoff and suppression approval labels, and can contributors add labels like ARMSignedOff themselves?

**Historical ground truth**

If a PR requires suppressions to be approved, the ARM reviewer should add the Approved-Suppressions label when they add ARMSignedOff. A PR that needs suppressions reviewed does not qualify for ARM auto signoff. Contributors should not add labels such as ARMSignedOff themselves; those labels are intended to be applied only by authorized reviewers. **Cached dev answer**

No — contributors should **not** self-apply `ARMSignedOff`, and in general the labels for ARM signoff / suppression approval are applied by the **reviewing authority**, not by the PR author.

- **`ARMSignedOff`**: this comes from the **ARM review step**. If a PR has `ARMReview`, it must be **reviewed by an ARM reviewer** and then receive `ARMSignedOff`. That means the signoff is tied to ARM reviewer approval, not contributor self-labeling.
- **`Approved-Suppression`**: when a PR gets `SuppressionReviewRequired`, you wait for the suppression to be reviewed; if approved, **the approver adds `Approved-Suppression`**.
- **Temporary PR-only suppression**: the guidance says to **comment on the PR and ask the PR assignee to apply the suppression**, with justification.
- The docs explicitly call out a few labels that **PR authors are allowed to apply themselves** for specific breaking-change/versioning cases, which is a useful contrast: `ARMSignedOff` is **not** one of those self-service labels. So the safe rule is: **don’t add `ARMSignedOff` yourself; follow the PR’s Next Steps to Merge and wait for the ARM reviewer / suppression approver.**

</details>

### spec-review-0199: Whether ARM resource properties may use Record or unknown for forwarded policy parameters

**Dataset:** `authoring.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0231](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0231) | **GT basis:** bot_fallback | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-03-31T09:15:21.345Z

**Assessment:** The answer aligns with the historical guidance and retrieved ARM TypeSpec docs: first-class ARM resource properties should be explicitly specified, `Record`/open-ended bags are discouraged by `arm-no-record`, and forwarding to a downstream service does not justify loosening the ARM resource contract. It also correctly notes a backward-compatibility suppression exception for already released contracts. The answer does not overclaim a reusable Azure Policy parameter type and stays within frozen evidence.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that for a management-plane first-class ARM resource, policy-related parameter properties should use an explicit schema rather than `Record`, `unknown`, or other open-ended object modeling.; Explain that ARM resource `properties` are RP-defined and should be completely specified/self-describing for ARM tooling and validation, even if values are forwarded downstream unchanged.; Make clear that downstream Azure Policy accepting loosely typed input is not, by itself, sufficient justification for an open-ended bag on the main resource surface.; Reference durable ARM/TypeSpec guidance that `Record` on ARM resources is disallowed or flagged (for example `arm-no-record` / avoidance of `additionalProperties` in resource properties).; Allow the compatibility exception conditionally: suppressing the rule may be acceptable only when preserving an already released contract, not as the preferred design for new modeling.; Prefer explicit evolution guidance when supported parameters change over time, such as adding optional properties or introducing a new API version.; If discussing unavoidable opaque input, constrain that advice to an alternative surface pattern rather than recommending it on first-class resource properties.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [authoring-01-029](expert-knowledge-report.md#authoring-01-029)

**Coverage boundary:** The cached answer passed its substantive criteria. Additional unmapped expert context is not treated as a required answer gap; its knowledge coverage is retained in the expert report.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Whether ARM resource properties may use Record or unknown for forwarded policy parameters

question: For an ARM management-plane first-class resource, may properties that carry policy initiative or policy assignment parameters be modeled as Record/unknown because the RP only forwards them to Azure Policy, or should the RP define an explicit schema for the parameters it supports?

**Historical ground truth**

For an ARM management-plane first-class resource, do not model such properties as a generic Record or unknown bag merely because a downstream API accepts loosely typed input. There is no shared standard policy-parameter type to reuse for this purpose. The resource provider should define an explicit schema for the parameter shapes its feature supports so the resource contract remains self-describing and compatible with ARM tooling and validation. If the supported parameter set changes over time, evolve the contract by adding optional properties or by versioning the API. If truly arbitrary opaque input is unavoidable, that pattern is more appropriate on a second-class surface such as an action or child resource than on the main resource properties.

**Cached dev answer**

No — for a **management-plane first-class ARM resource**, those properties should be modeled with an **explicit schema**, even if your RP only forwards the values to Azure Policy.

- ARM guidance says the resource’s RP-specific `properties` bag is **defined by the resource provider** and its properties should be **completely specified**.
- The ARM RPC guidance also says that inside the `properties` envelope, use of **`additionalProperties` must be avoided**, even though ARM passes those values to the RP unmodified.
- In TypeSpec, the ARM linter rule **`arm-no-record`** exists specifically because ARM resource properties and parameters should not be modeled as open-ended `Record<...>` dictionaries; the stated reason is that ARM expects RPs to **define types explicitly**.

So in your case, “we only forward this to Azure Policy” is **not** a reason to use `Record`/open-ended object modeling on a first-class ARM resource. The RP surface should still declare the contract it supports.

**Important distinction**
- **TypeSpec language** can represent open-ended objects/dictionaries.
- But **ARM resource modeling** is stricter: for ARM resource properties, open-ended dictionary-style modeling is generally not the compliant choice.

**Only notable exception**
- If you are preserving an **already released** ARM contract for backward compatibility, the ARM `arm-no-record` rule can be **suppressed** in that specific legacy case. That is an exception for compatibility, not the recommended model for a new or newly-defined ARM resource surface.

**What to model instead**
- Define a concrete parameters model for the subset of policy parameters your RP accepts or forwards.
- If values vary by parameter, model that variability explicitly in the schema rather than exposing an unbounded bag.

</details>
