**Acceptance criteria:** Explain that ARM review is gated behind earlier required validation/policy checks and does not proceed while required blockers remain unresolved.; State that breaking-change/versioning blockers on public `main` and private `RPSaaSMaster` block further review, including ARM review.; Clarify that only required checks are authoritative for this gate, typically reflected by the `Automated merging requirements met` status; non-required failures alone do not block review/merge.; Describe the needed remediation before ARM review can proceed: fix the validation issue or obtain the documented formal suppression/approval path, then rerun validation/CI.; Indicate that once step-1 blockers are cleared, the PR can re-enter or resume the ARM review queue/state.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [review-process-03-034](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-03-034), [review-process-01-021](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-01-021)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Why waitForArmReview is removed when required PR checks are failing

question: In azure-rest-api-specs, why does automation remove waitForArmReview and apply notReadyForReview when required checks such as breaking-change validation or Swagger LintDiff are failing, and what must be done before ARM review can proceed?

**Historical ground truth**

In azure-rest-api-specs, ARM review does not begin until required validation and breaking-change checks are addressed. When required checks are failing, automation removes waitForArmReview and marks the PR not ready for review. To proceed, fix the validation issues or add an allowed formal suppression, rerun CI, and then reapply waitForArmReview after the required checks are passing or neutrally suppressed.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — in `azure-rest-api-specs`, that behavior is intentional. ARM review is a later stage in the spec PR workflow, and a PR is **not eligible to stay in the ARM-review queue** while it still has **required merge blockers**. For public `main`, checks like **breaking-change validation** and **OpenAPI LintDiff** are required branch-protection checks, so if they fail, automation marks the PR as **not ready for review** and removes the waiting-for-ARM state until those blockers are cleared.

What this means in practice:

- **ARM review does not start until step 1 blockers are resolved.** The docs say PRs with `BreakingChangeReviewRequired` or `VersioningReviewRequired` are **blocked from any further review, including ARM review** on public `main` and private `RPSaaSMaster`. See [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).
- **Only required checks matter for this gating.** The authoritative signal is the **`Automated merging requirements met`** status. If that status is not green, the PR is still blocked; if it is green, non-required failing checks do not stop merge/review. See [Create a pull request with your Azure REST API spec update](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).
- **Before ARM review can proceed, you must clear the required blockers** by following the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** guidance, fixing the validation issue or completing the required approval/suppression path, and then rerunning validation (for breaking-change issues, the guidance says to comment `/azp run` after addressing the issue). See [Deep-dive into breaking changes on spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).
- **After step 1 is resolved**, the ARM queueing state can resume. The ARM-review doc says that once earlier blockers are handled and `ARMChangesRequested` is removed, automation should add `WaitForARMFeedback`. See [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).

So the short answer is: automation removes `waitForArmReview` because the PR is **not reviewable yet**; ARM reviewers should only spend time on PRs whose **required CI and policy gates are already satisfied**.

</details>

- If they **do not** add it, then the suppression review is **not reflected as complete in the PR workflow**. In practice, the PR remains blocked in the suppression-review state and **does not move forward to the next stage**, even if the reviewer informally agreed.

**Replay question**

title: What access prerequisites should a PR author verify if required specs PR checks never start?

question: If required checks on an Azure REST API specs PR remain pending and never start, what access or permission prerequisites should the PR author verify?

**Historical ground truth**

If required checks on an Azure REST API specs PR never start, verify that the PR author has completed the required Azure SDK access setup, that their Azure GitHub organization membership is public rather than private, and that the PR author is a member of the "Azure SDK Partners" security group. Missing one or more of these prerequisites can prevent required checks from running.

**Cached dev answer**

If required spec PR checks stay **pending and never start**, the PR author should first verify **access prerequisites**, not the spec content.

- **Verify your GitHub account is linked to your Microsoft account** and that you have access to the relevant repo workflow described in [Work against the release branch](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-2-update) and [Create a PR against main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish).
- **Verify you have access to the Azure GitHub organization** by joining it through [Request a data plane REST API spec review](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-review). The docs explicitly call out Azure org membership as a prerequisite for spec PR work.
- **Verify you have permission to the correct repository**:
  - public work: [`Azure/azure-rest-api-specs`](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-repos)
  - private work: [`Azure/azure-rest-api-specs-pr`](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-repos)
- If the missing checks are specifically **`SDK Validation - {Language}`** checks, verify you have the required **write access**, make your **Azure org membership visibility public**, and join the **Azure SDK Partners** group as described in [SDK Validation](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation). That guidance says if those language checks do not appear at all, it usually means you lack permission to trigger them.
- If all of the above is already correct and checks still never start, the retrieved guidance indicates it may be an **automation/workflow issue**, in which case an `azure-rest-api-specs` maintainer may need to rerun or repair the workflow.

**Short version:** check **MSA-linked GitHub account**, **Azure org membership**, **repo access**, and for **SDK validation**, also **public org visibility + write access + Azure SDK Partners membership**.

**Replay question**

title: Do not manually remove automation-added PR labels

question: If a spec PR has labels added by repository automation, should contributors manually remove those labels to try to fix the PR state?

**Historical ground truth**

No. Contributors should not manually remove labels that were added by repository automation. If the PR state appears incorrect, leave the automation-added labels in place and ask maintainers to investigate or correct the workflow instead of editing those labels manually.

**Cached dev answer**

See [ARM review process](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).
- Related distinction: some labels are **protected**, such as `data-plane-review-signoff`; contributors should not apply those themselves, and automation removes them if applied by the wrong person. See [Get your PR merged](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

**Short rule:** don’t manually remove automation labels unless the process docs for that exact label explicitly tell you to.

### spec-review-0204: Supporting gzip-compressed request bodies in an ARM management-plane API

**Dataset:** `spec-review.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0238](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0238) | **GT basis:** expert_plus_bot | **Temporal scope:** durable | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-03-18T18:58:50.57Z

**Assessment:** The answer aligns with the historical guidance: gzip request compression is acceptable as optional HTTP content-coding for ARM management-plane APIs, the 4 MB ARM request-body limit still applies, and compression should be represented via standard Content-Encoding rather than a custom gzip-specific contract shape. It also correctly advises not to rely on compression instead of designing smaller request payloads.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that ARM management-plane APIs may support gzip-compressed request bodies as an optional optimization, not a requirement for all clients.; State that ordinary uncompressed JSON requests must still be accepted when they fit within ARM limits.; State that ARM's maximum request body size remains 4 MB even when gzip is supported.; Clarify that oversized requests are rejected by ARM before reaching the resource provider.; Represent compression using the standard HTTP Content-Encoding: gzip mechanism rather than a custom gzip-specific header parameter or alternate resource model.; Keep the API contract's request body modeled normally as JSON/application/json rather than treating compression as a different semantic payload type.; Advise that API design should keep common scenarios within the ARM size limit instead of depending on gzip to enable arbitrarily large payloads.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [spec-review-01-014](expert-knowledge-report.md#spec-review-01-014)

**Coverage boundary:** The cached answer passed its substantive criteria. Additional unmapped expert context is not treated as a required answer gap; its knowledge coverage is retained in the expert report.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Supporting gzip-compressed request bodies in an ARM management-plane API

question: For an ARM management-plane API whose request body may be large, is it acceptable to support gzip-compressed request bodies, what request-size limit still applies, and how should request compression be represented in the API contract?

**Historical ground truth**

An ARM management-plane API may support `Content-Encoding: gzip` on requests as an optional optimization, but compression does not remove ARM's request body size limit. ARM still enforces a 4 MB maximum request size based on the uncompressed body, so requests larger than that are rejected before reaching the resource provider.

Request compression should not be modeled as a custom gzip-specific header parameter in the API contract. Instead, the request body should be described normally and the service may document support for the standard HTTP `Content-Encoding: gzip` header. Clients must still be able to send ordinary uncompressed JSON bodies that fit within the ARM limit.

The API shape should be designed so typical scenarios stay within the size limit rather than depending on gzip to allow arbitrarily large payloads.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — supporting `gzip`-compressed request bodies is compatible with an ARM management-plane API **as an HTTP content-coding**, as long as the request body is still modeled as JSON. In HTTP, compression is indicated with `Content-Encoding` and is separate from `Content-Type`; request content-codings such as `gzip` are allowed. ([httpwg.org](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html))

**The size limit to keep assuming is still 4 MB.** The ARM resource-provider contract says ARM accepts request bodies up to **4 MB** and returns **413 Payload Too Large** for larger ones. The contract does **not** document a larger allowance for compressed requests, so you should not treat gzip as a way to exceed the ARM request-size limit. ([github.com](https://github.com/cloud-and-ai-microsoft/resource-provider-contract/blob/master/v1.0/common-api-details.md))

**How to represent it in the contract**
- Keep the request body schema/content type as **`application/json`** for ARM.
- If your service supports compressed requests, represent that support through the **`Content-Encoding` request header** (for example, `gzip`), not by defining a different body media type.
- In other words, compression is transport metadata, not part of the JSON resource model.

**Practical recommendation**
- It is acceptable to support gzip for unusually large JSON payloads, but ARM management-plane APIs should still avoid routinely large request bodies.
- If the payload is often near the limit, that is usually a sign to revisit the API shape rather than rely on compression.

</details>

### spec-review-0205: How to interpret LintDiff when validation crashes on the baseline spec

**Dataset:** `spec-review.jsonl` | **Automated:** pass | **Reaudit:** pass

**Historical provenance:** [T0240](expert-knowledge-report.md#t0240) | **GT basis:** expert | **Temporal scope:** mixed | **Latest cited GT reply:** 2026-03-30T20:28:33.943Z

**Assessment:** The answer correctly interprets a fatal validator crash on the baseline ('before') spec as invalidating LintDiff’s comparison, so reported failures should not be treated as reliable new violations from the PR. It also gives the correct next step: investigate/fix the validator or baseline-processing failure and rerun LintDiff before acting on findings. This matches the supplied historical guidance and retrieved evidence that LintDiff must process both revisions successfully.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that LintDiff compares validation results for both the before and after revisions of the spec.; Explain that a fatal error while validating the baseline/before revision compromises the comparison and makes reported 'new' violations unreliable.; Conclude that such failures should be treated as a tooling or baseline-validation problem first, not as proof the PR introduced real spec violations.; Recommend investigating and fixing the validator/baseline crash, then rerunning validation/LintDiff.; Only treat reported violations as actionable after validation succeeds on both sides of the comparison.; Do not recommend suppression as the primary response when the baseline scan itself crashes.

**Frozen facts:** The validator emitted a fatal error while validating the before-state spec: `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.; The failing command used AutoRest with `@microsoft.azure/openapi-validator` against the before readme.; Human responders concluded the validator was crashing on the baseline spec.; Human responders identified the crash as a tool bug and said investigation should focus on the tool crash first.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [review-process-03-033](expert-knowledge-report.md#review-process-03-033)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to interpret LintDiff when validation crashes on the baseline spec

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If LintDiff reports failures for a PR, but the validator log shows a fatal error while scanning the baseline ('before') spec, such as `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, how should that result be interpreted? Should the reported failures be treated as real new spec violations, or as a tooling problem, and what is the appropriate next step?

**Historical ground truth**

A fatal validator error while scanning the baseline ('before') spec means the LintDiff result should be treated as a tooling problem, not as reliable evidence that the PR introduced real new violations. When the before-state validation fails with an error such as `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, the comparison is compromised because the tool cannot correctly establish the baseline. The right next step is to investigate and fix the validator failure first, then rerun LintDiff. Only after validation succeeds on both the before and after specs should any reported violations be treated as actionable spec issues.

**Cached dev answer**

Treat that outcome as a **tooling/baseline-processing problem first**, **not** as proof that the PR introduced real new LintDiff violations.

- **Why:** LintDiff works by linting the spec **before** and **after** the PR and then comparing the results. The guidance explicitly says that if the copy already on the target branch crashes, a bug-fix PR can still fail because LintDiff must process both revisions successfully.
- **So if the validator log shows a fatal error while scanning the baseline** — for example `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in the **before** spec — then the reported LintDiff failures are **not trustworthy as “new violations introduced by this PR.”**
- **Appropriate next step:** investigate and fix the **baseline crash / validator crash** first, then rerun validation. Don’t treat the listed LintDiff findings as real regressions until LintDiff can successfully analyze both sides of the comparison.
- **Also:** this is **not** the normal case for adding a suppression. Suppressions are for real or accepted findings; a fatal crash in the baseline means the comparison itself is invalid.

For general LintDiff guidance, see [Swagger LintDiff](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Swagger-LintDiff). For validation-process context, see [API Spec Review FAQ](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/API-Spec-Review-FAQ).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Why a PR may not be reviewed when breaking changes are unresolved

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

In the API specs review process, why might a PR not be assigned a reviewer yet, and what should the author do first if the PR is blocked on breaking changes?

**Historical ground truth**

A PR may not be reviewed yet if it is blocked on breaking changes. In that situation, the author should first follow the PR's "next steps to merge" instructions and address the breaking-change issues before expecting review.

**Cached dev answer**

A PR may not be assigned a reviewer yet because **breaking-change review is the first gate** in the spec PR workflow. If the PR has `BreakingChangeReviewRequired` or `VersioningReviewRequired`, it is treated as **blocked from further review** on production branches until that step is resolved, so ARM/data-plane review may not start yet.

What the author should do first:

- **Use the PR’s “Next Steps to Merge” comment as the source of truth.** The workflow and FAQ both say to follow that comment first, rather than waiting for a reviewer.
- **If the block is breaking changes or versioning, start with the breaking-change process** documented here: [Deep-dive into Breaking Changes on Spec PRs](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep).
- **After addressing the issue, rerun PR processing** by commenting `/azp run` on the PR, as described in the workflow guidance.
- **Only after step 1 is cleared** should the PR move into ARM/data-plane review; if it still does not appear in the review flow after that, check the ARM review guidance here: [Get your PR reviewed by ARM](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-arm-review).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can a PR still merge if a failing .NET SDK validation check is not required?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a PR has a failing .NET SDK validation check, but the checklist shows that the .NET check is not required for that PR, does that failure block merge, and what should the author do next?

**Historical ground truth**

No. A failing .NET SDK validation check does not block merge when that check is not required for the PR. In that situation, the author should proceed by following the PR's Next Steps to Merge guidance and completing the normal merge requirements.

**Cached dev answer**

No — if the `.NET` SDK validation check is **not required** for that PR, its failure does **not** block merge. The deciding signal is whether **`Automated merging requirements met`** is green; if that status is green, required automation is satisfied even if a non-required check is failing.

- **Does it block merge?**\
  No. Non-required checks are informational and do not prevent merge. See [Get your PR merged](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr) and [API versions and branches](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches).

- **What should the author do next?**\
  Follow the PR’s **Next Steps to Merge** guidance and confirm **both** the **Next Steps to Merge** comment and **`Automated merging requirements met`** are green before requesting/doing the merge. See [Get your PR merged](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

- **Should the failure still be ignored completely?**\
  Not really. It is still recommended to investigate and fix the failing non-required check if possible, because it may point to a real spec problem, but it is not a merge blocker by itself. See [Get your PR merged](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-specs-pr).

- **Should they try to suppress the .NET SDK failure?**\
  For `.NET` SDK validation, suppression is documented as **not possible**. Practically, if the check is non-required, the right move is usually to proceed with merge readiness checks rather than trying to suppress it. See [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Choose the base API version for new private-preview work when RPSaaSMaster and main diverge

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a resource provider's private-preview specs in RPSaaSMaster and public-preview specs in main have diverged, and the latest version in RPSaaSMaster contains internal changes that are not present in a newer public-preview version in main, which version should be used as the base for a new private-preview API version that adds a new resource type?

**Historical ground truth**

For a new private-preview API version in RPSaaSMaster, start from the latest private-preview version that already exists in RPSaaSMaster and create a new later-dated preview version from it. Do not add a new resource type by modifying an existing published API version. Published API versions should only receive bug-fix alignment with the implementation; new features require a new API version. During preview, the new preview version does not need to remain compatible with earlier preview versions, so the correct base is the most recent internal contract you want to carry forward in RPSaaSMaster. If main has a different public-preview version, reconcile that branch divergence later in a subsequent version rather than using it as the base for the new private-preview work.

**Cached dev answer**

Use the **latest private-preview version in `RPSaaSMaster`** as the **content baseline** for the new private-preview API version, then carry forward anything needed from the newer public-preview version in `main`.

- **Why:** ARM private-preview specs live in **`RPSaaSMaster`**, and teams are expected to keep that branch synchronized with public `main`, not treat `main` as the source of truth for private-preview-only changes.
- **In this exact scenario:** because the latest `RPSaaSMaster` version contains internal changes that are missing from the newer public preview in `main`, basing the new private-preview version on `main` would risk dropping those internal changes.
- **Important distinction:** this is the right **baseline for the spec contents**. Separately, the **new `api-version` value** still needs to be **newer than the previous preview or GA version**, since new versions must advance monotonically.

That last conclusion is an inference from the branch/lifecycle and versioning rules: **use `RPSaaSMaster` for the private-preview contract state, but choose a new later `api-version` date that stays ahead of the existing version timeline.**

</details>

**Acceptance criteria:** State that omission of `x-ms-azure-resource: true` after TypeSpec conversion is typically not a semantic ARM behavior change when the model still inherits from the correct ARM common resource base (`TrackedResource`, `ProxyResource`, or `Resource`/equivalent common ARM base as applicable).; Explain that TypeSpec migration commonly produces textual OpenAPI differences and that ARM resource identity/semantics are inferred from the standard ARM resource shape and common-types inheritance rather than requiring the legacy extension on the concrete schema.; Condition the conclusion on the resource still being modeled as the correct ARM resource kind and retaining the expected ARM envelope/properties supplied by the inherited base.; Identify that the substantive risk is misclassification of resource kind (for example tracked vs extension/proxy/child), not mere absence of the legacy extension.; Mention the plausible downstream caveat that custom or legacy tooling may depend specifically on `x-ms-azure-resource` and therefore should be validated separately.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Does omitting x-ms-azure-resource after TypeSpec conversion change ARM resource behavior?

question: When converting an ARM Swagger resource to TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI, what is the implication if the old Swagger had `x-ms-azure-resource: true` but the generated OpenAPI no longer emits that extension, while the model still inherits from ARM common-types such as `TrackedResource`?

**Historical ground truth**

If a model still inherits from ARM common resource bases such as `TrackedResource`, `ProxyResource`, or `Resource`, omitting `x-ms-azure-resource: true` after TypeSpec conversion is expected and should not change ARM or SDK behavior. ARM resource semantics are inferred from the standard resource shape and common-types inheritance rather than requiring that extension explicitly. The main potential impact would be on custom tooling that was written to look only for `x-ms-azure-resource` instead of recognizing the common ARM resource bases.

**Cached dev answer**

Short answer: **usually no, by itself this does not change ARM resource behavior**. In TypeSpec ARM modeling, the important contract is that the model is represented as the correct ARM resource kind and extends the right ARM base type, such as `TrackedResource`; the generated OpenAPI is expected to look textually different from the old Swagger after migration.

- The migration guidance says that if your model already extends an ARM common-types resource model, you should treat that as the resource representation and accept generated OpenAPI differences that come from aligning to ARM conventions.
- The TypeSpec ARM docs model tracked resources as `model X is TrackedResource<...>`, and the emitted Swagger examples show the concrete resource schema referencing `TrackedResource` through `allOf` rather than re-declaring every old Swagger detail on the concrete model.
- So if your converted model still represents the **same ARM resource kind** and still has the expected ARM envelope (`id`/`name`/`type`, plus tracked-resource fields like `location` and `tags` through `TrackedResource`), omitting `x-ms-azure-resource` on the concrete emitted schema is typically just a **serialization difference**, not a behavioral change.

**What actually would be risky**
- If the conversion changed the resource from the wrong kind to the wrong kind — for example, it should really be an `ExtensionResource`, `ProxyResource`, or child resource instead of `TrackedResource`.
- That distinction matters more than matching the old extension literally. Retrieved guidance explicitly calls out that **resource kind matters** even when shapes look similar.

**Practical conclusion for your case**
- If the old resource was a normal top-level tracked ARM resource and the TypeSpec version still uses `TrackedResource` correctly, I would treat the missing emitted `x-ms-azure-resource: true` as **not a semantic ARM behavior regression**.
- I would only investigate further if:
  - ARM validation/checks started failing,
  - downstream tooling explicitly keys off the old concrete-schema extension,
  - or the migrated model may actually be the wrong ARM resource kind.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI lead to stricter ARM template preflight validation even when name and type are not in the properties bag?

question: For an ARM resource that still inherits from common-types `TrackedResource`, can migrating from handwritten Swagger to TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI lead to stricter ARM template preflight validation, including errors involving read-only envelope properties like `name` and `type`, even when the resource-specific `properties` model does not define those fields?

**Historical ground truth**

Removing `x-ms-azure-resource` is not itself expected to cause ARM template preflight failures involving `name` and `type` when the resource still inherits from `TrackedResource`. However, TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI can lead downstream ARM or Bicep schema tooling to validate more strictly if the emitted schema changes how `required` and `readOnly` are represented and those combinations are interpreted against the writable request shape. A known pattern is that server-set or read-only properties emitted as non-optional can be treated as required in a writable view, producing confusing validation errors even though the API semantics did not change. If the resource-specific `properties` model does not define `name` or `type` and the resource still inherits from ARM common resource bases, the likely investigation points are differences in emitted `required` arrays, `readOnly` flags, or schema-tooling interpretation rather than the absence of `x-ms-azure-resource`.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **it can**, but the key point is **why**.

- In ARM, a `TrackedResource` is split into two layers: an outer **ARM envelope** and the inner RP-specific **`properties` bag**. The docs explicitly say the envelope is processed by ARM, while the resource-specific `properties` model must **not duplicate** envelope fields. So `name` and `type` can still be validated even if they are absent from your `properties` model, because they belong to the inherited ARM envelope, not to `properties`.\
- TypeSpec ARM resource templates emit resources by extending ARM/common-types resource bases such as `TrackedResource`, and migration guidance says this can introduce **textual OpenAPI differences** and should generally be accepted to align with ARM conventions. That means a migration can expose or normalize the resource shape in a way that ARM/template tooling interprets more strictly than the handwritten Swagger did.
- So the answer is **yes, potentially**: not because TypeSpec secretly adds `name`/`type` into the RP `properties` bag, but because the generated OpenAPI may model the **standard ARM envelope** more faithfully, and preflight validation can reason over that full resource contract.

What I’d use as the decision rule:

- **If the generated spec is still a true standard ARM `TrackedResource`**, treat `name`/`type` validation as expected envelope-level behavior, not evidence that your `properties` schema is wrong.
- **If brownfield compatibility matters more than normalization**, compare old and new emitted OpenAPI with the migration workflow at [Getting started with TypeSpec migration](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/01-get-started). If the new shape changes runtime/template behavior, the migration FAQ says you can preserve the original resource definition with [`@customAzureResource`](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/migrate-swagger/faq/mustread) instead of forcing the standard resource base.
- For the ARM resource split itself, the clearest reference is [ARM Resource Types](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/howtos/arm/resource-type), which states that envelope properties are separate from RP-specific `properties`.

**Bottom line:** `name` and `type` errors during template preflight are fully compatible with a `properties` model that does **not** define those fields. The likely cause is that ARM is validating the inherited **resource envelope**, and TypeSpec migration may make that contract more explicit.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How can you distinguish schema-caused ARM preflight regressions from later validator or manifest rollouts?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If ARM template preflight errors begin weeks after a TypeSpec-generated OpenAPI change was merged, how can you distinguish whether the failures are caused by the schema change itself versus a later ARM/Bicep/schema-validator or manifest rollout?

**Historical ground truth**

To distinguish a schema-caused validation regression from a later validator or manifest rollout, first confirm the actual generated OpenAPI shape and compare it with the checked-in version. Then correlate the merge date of the schema change with when failures first appeared. If the schema had already been stable for weeks before errors started, that points away from the TypeSpec conversion itself and toward downstream validator, template-schema, ARM, or manifest rollout behavior. Comparing behavior across API versions also helps: if only the new API version fails, the new schema is implicated; if older and newer versions fail similarly, the validator or manifest behavior is more likely responsible. When diffing the old and new OpenAPI, focus on `required` arrays and `readOnly` flags, especially combinations that can cause writable-view validation quirks. If timing and cross-version checks remain inconclusive, confirmation requires help from the owners of the validator or manifest pipeline because external observation may not reveal exactly when a new schema or validator version was picked up.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes: use **activation timing** and **rollout scope** as your primary discriminator.

- Under **Swagger SDP**, a merged TypeSpec/OpenAPI PR does **not** become active by itself. The spec is **captured at RP manifest rollout start** and then promoted ring-by-ring for ARM validation. So if preflight failures start **weeks after merge**, first ask: **what manifest rollout started around the first failure?** If there was no rollout that could have captured that spec, the merge itself was not the activation event. See [OpenAPI Specifications SDP Rollout](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/openapispec_sdp_rollout.html) and [RP platform integration](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/swaggeronboarding.html).

- A **schema-caused regression** should line up with the **specific rollout that captured that schema**:
  - failures begin when that rollout reaches **Canary** or the next ring,
  - the same captured spec stays in effect for that rollout,
  - unaffected higher rings keep using the prior baseline until promotion.\
  That ring-by-ring progression is the expected signature of a schema rollout. See [OpenAPI Specifications SDP Rollout](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/openapispec_sdp_rollout.html).

- A **later validator / manifest / schema-validator rollout** is more likely when:
  - failures begin **without** a matching spec-capturing manifest rollout,
  - onset timing matches a **later platform change** rather than the original spec merge,
  - impact pattern does **not** follow the spec rollout rings or also affects APIs whose OpenAPI did not change.\
  Swagger SDP explicitly says the spec snapshot is fixed at rollout start, which helps separate spec activation from later platform behavior changes. See [OpenAPI Specifications SDP Rollout](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/openapispec_sdp_rollout.html).

- A practical reusable process:
  1. Identify whether the incident happened in the **pre-SDP** or **Swagger SDP** model. Before Swagger SDP, spec activation came from periodic GitHub refreshes (about every 30 minutes), so timing analysis is less rollout-centric. See [OpenAPI Specifications SDP Rollout](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/openapispec_sdp_rollout.html).
  2. For Swagger SDP incidents, find the **first failing timestamp** and match it to the **manifest rollout start** and **ring promotion**.
  3. Confirm which spec snapshot the rollout captured.
  4. Compare blast radius: **ring-by-ring, spec-specific** suggests schema; **later broad platform behavior change** suggests validator/manifest rollout.
  5. If needed, rerun or compare against the **previous baseline** behavior in unaffected rings, because each ring keeps its last-known-good baseline until promoted. See [OpenAPI Specifications SDP Rollout](https://armwiki.azurewebsites.net/rpaas/openapispec_sdp_rollout.html).

**Bottom line:** in the Swagger SDP model, a failure that appears only **weeks after merge** is **not enough** to blame the schema change. You need evidence that a later RP manifest rollout actually **captured and activated** that schema in the failing ring; otherwise a later ARM/Bicep/schema-validator or manifest rollout is the stronger explanation.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can TypeSpec files be organized in nested folders under a service folder?

question: Under the Azure REST API specs v2 service folder structure, can TypeSpec files be organized in nested subfolders under the service folder, or must all .tsp files be flat at the service root? Are there any constraints on where tspconfig.yaml can live?

**Historical ground truth**

Yes. Under the v2 service folder structure, additional nested subfolders may be used to organize .tsp files within the service folder. The key constraint is that the service is identified by the tspconfig.yaml, so tspconfig.yaml should remain at the service root rather than inside nested organizing folders.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — under **Folder Structure v2**, your TypeSpec sources do **not** have to be flat at the service root.

- **Nested subfolders for `.tsp` files are allowed** inside a service folder. The guidance explicitly says that a service must have `examples`, `preview`, and `stable` subfolders, and that **additional subfolders may be used to organize `*.tsp` files**.
- **Do not add extra service-grouping levels above the service folder.**
  - **ARM:** use `specification/<org>/resource-manager/<RPNS>/<service>/...`
  - **Data plane:** use `specification/<org>/data-plane/<service>/...`
  - Once you are **inside** `<service>/`, organizing TypeSpec into nested folders is fine.
- **`tspconfig.yaml` is expected at the service folder root**, alongside `main.tsp`, other top-level `*.tsp` files, and `readme.md`. I would **not** place `tspconfig.yaml` in a nested subfolder.
- The normal service subfolders still apply:
  - `examples/<apiVersion>/` for TypeSpec examples
  - `preview/<apiVersion>/` and `stable/<apiVersion>/` for emitted OpenAPI
- If multiple services want to use the same TypeSpec/OpenAPI content, the guidance says **do not point multiple services at one shared contract location**; copy it into each consuming service folder instead.

A compliant example looks like:

```text
specification/<org>/resource-manager/<RPNS>/<service>/
  tspconfig.yaml
  main.tsp
  readme.md
  models/
    common.tsp
    resources.tsp
  operations/
    widget.tsp
    admin.tsp
  examples/
    2026-01-01/
      Widget_Create.json
  preview/
    2026-01-01-preview/
      openapi.json
  stable/
    2026-06-01/
      openapi.json
```

**Bottom line:**\
- **Nested `.tsp` folders:** allowed\
- **All `.tsp` flat at root:** not required\
- **`tspconfig.yaml` location:** keep it at the **service root**

</details>

**Acceptance criteria:** State that management-plane specs use the nested path `specification/<org>/resource-manager/<RPNamespace>/<ServiceName>/` for new services, not a flat RP-only folder.; Explain that `ServiceName` should correspond to a real control-plane service boundary within the RP namespace, i.e., a set of operations that versions together and owns its contract/docs/examples/SDK lifecycle.; Confirm that when an RP effectively has a single service, a repeated-name pattern such as `Microsoft.Foo/Foo` is acceptable.; Clarify that if an RP contains multiple independently versioned services, they should be modeled as separate sibling service folders under the same RP namespace.; Prefer durable customer-facing service identity/service boundaries over transient marketing or branding names when choosing `ServiceName`.

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to choose the ServiceName folder under an RP namespace

question: For a management-plane spec, how should the ServiceName folder be chosen under an RP namespace? If an RP effectively has a single service, is using a pattern like Microsoft.Foo/Foo acceptable, and should ServiceName follow stable service boundaries rather than marketing names?

**Historical ground truth**

For management-plane specs, ServiceName should represent the service boundary within the RP namespace. If the RP effectively contains a single service, using a pattern like Microsoft.Foo/Foo is acceptable and is expected to be common. The distinction between RP namespace and service name becomes more important when a namespace contains multiple services, so naming should follow durable service boundaries rather than transient branding.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — for a management-plane spec, the `ServiceName` folder should represent a **real ARM service boundary**, not just mirror the RP namespace mechanically.

- **Use the required ARM path shape:**\
  `specification/<org>/resource-manager/<RPNamespace>/<ServiceName>/`\
  Even if the RP has only one service, new specs should still use the nested `<RPNS>/<ServiceName>` layout rather than a flat `resource-manager/<RPNS>` structure.

- **Choose `ServiceName` by stable service boundary:**\
  The guidance defines a service as a set of operations that **version together over time** and own their own contract, docs, examples, and SDK lifecycle. So the folder should follow that durable boundary, not a transient marketing label.

- **So is `Microsoft.Foo/Foo` acceptable?**\
  **Yes, if `Foo` is genuinely the single customer-facing control-plane service** under `Microsoft.Foo` and you expect it to version as one unit. In that case, `resource-manager/Microsoft.Foo/Foo/` is fine.

- **But don’t use `Foo` just because the RP is single-service today.**\
  If the RP really contains multiple independently versioned surfaces, or likely will, those should be separate sibling service folders under the same RP namespace.

- **Practical rule:**\
  Pick the folder name that matches the long-lived service identity customers and SDK/docs will recognize, and keep that mapping stable across versions.

**Example**
```text
specification/contoso/resource-manager/Microsoft.Foo/Foo/
```

Use that only when `Foo` is the actual service boundary. If later you have independently versioned services, prefer:
```text
specification/contoso/resource-manager/Microsoft.Foo/Widgets/
specification/contoso/resource-manager/Microsoft.Foo/Policies/
```

</details>

Its extra detail about versioning/SDK impact is consistent with the retrieved versioning guidance and does not contradict the frozen historical answer.

**Acceptance criteria:** State that a single service folder may later be split into multiple ServiceName folders when the resulting services are genuinely independent and need independent versioning lifecycles.; Explain that service boundaries should ideally be chosen before the first GA release because a service is expected to version uniformly over its lifetime.; Ground the rationale in durable versioning guidance: one service corresponds to a uniform versioning stream and its own contract/docs/SDK lifecycle.; Acknowledge that refactoring an existing service into multiple services is possible but is a restructuring decision that should be discussed with the appropriate review/design board when needed.; Do not claim there is authoritative durable guidance endorsing later merging/recombining previously separated independent services back together; if uncertain, say no supported process was established in the evidence.

**Canonical knowledge / repeat links:** [versioning-01-031](expert-knowledge-report.md#versioning-01-031)

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Can a single service later be split into multiple ServiceName folders?

question: Can an RP start with a single ServiceName and later refactor into multiple ServiceName folders for independent versioning? Should this ideally be decided before first GA, and what durable guidance exists about later recombining services?

**Historical ground truth**

Services should be factored so they can exist independently for the duration of the service lifetime. It is best to decide those boundaries before the first GA release. If an existing service needs to be refactored into multiple services, that can be discussed with the appropriate design board, such as the data-plane or resource-manager board. No authoritative guidance in this discussion establishes a supported process for later merging previously separated services back together.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — an RP can start with one service folder and later split into multiple sibling `ServiceName` folders **if those are truly independent services with independent versioning lifecycles**. But the guidance strongly suggests you should choose that boundary **before first GA** if you can, because Azure defines a service as a set of operations that version uniformly **“in perpetuity,”** and the folder boundary is meant to align with that durable service boundary.

- **When a split is appropriate**
  - Split when parts of the API need to version independently.
  - The recommended end state is multiple sibling service folders, each with its own API contract, docs, examples, and SDK package/versioning lifecycle.
  - The guidance explicitly lists “split into multiple independent services” as the fix when a single service folder violates uniform versioning.

- **Why deciding before first GA is better**
  - The durable rule is: one service = one uniform versioning stream over time.
  - Each service version is expected to map 1:1 to its API contract, documentation, and SDK package lifecycle.
  - So after GA, changing the boundary is not forbidden, but it becomes a **restructuring event** with downstream customer and SDK impact rather than a routine refactor.

- **What the current guidance says about splitting later**
  - Later splitting is recognized as possible, and even the SDK guidance discusses splitting a monolithic package into service-specific packages as a **one-time break** to get to a sustainable long-term model.
  - That is a strong signal that **late correction is allowed**, but not ideal.

- **What the current guidance says about recombining later**
  - I did **not** find durable guidance that endorses later recombining previously separated services back into one service folder.
  - The retrieved guidance points the other way: once services are independent, they should remain independently versioned; multiple services must not share one mutable contract copy; and combining independently versioning services is called out as problematic for versioning, SDK packaging, and customer choice.
  - So the best evidence-backed answer is: **treat a split as durable**, and only consider recombination if the pieces were never truly independent services in the first place.

- **Practical rule of thumb**
  - If you expect independent cadence, independent contract evolution, or separate SDK/documentation ownership, use **multiple `ServiceName` folders from the start**.
  - If everything will always ship and version together, one service folder is fine.

</details>

**Replay question**

title: What to try first when azure-rest-api-specs PR checks appear stuck

question: If checks on an azure-rest-api-specs pull request appear stuck in a pending state, what should the PR author try first?

**Historical ground truth**

If PR checks appear stuck, first try pushing another commit to the pull request to retrigger the checks.

**Cached dev answer**

If PR checks look stuck, **the first thing to try is updating your branch with the latest infrastructure from `main`**, because older branches can cause spec PR checks to stop functioning correctly.

- **If your branch is not protected:** merge `main` into your branch normally, then push. Guidance: [Create a PR against main / Update your branch with changes from main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish)
- **If your branch is protected** (for example `release-*`): use the helper pipeline **tools - update-release-branch-in-specs** to bring over only infrastructure changes: [Run pipeline](https://dev.azure.com/azure-sdk/internal/_build?definitionId=7487)
- **After updating the branch:** retrigger the checks. The documented easiest way is to **close and reopen the PR**. Same guidance page: [Update your branch with changes from main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish)

A nearby variant: if **SDK Validation checks are missing entirely** rather than just pending, that usually points to **permissions/org membership**, not a stuck run. In that case, check access guidance: [SDK Validation wiki](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Cadence for publishing public REST API reference docs

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

After REST API spec changes are merged to Azure/azure-rest-api-specs, how often is the public REST API reference on learn.microsoft.com refreshed, and when does it require a manual publishing request instead of automatic refresh?

**Historical ground truth**

After REST API spec changes are merged to Azure/azure-rest-api-specs, public REST API reference documentation on learn.microsoft.com is refreshed weekly on Tuesdays for services that are onboarded with the proper README publishing configuration. Services using the alternative direct-path publishing configuration are not updated by an automatic time-based refresh; they require a manual configuration change and a publishing request.

**Cached dev answer**

If the service is already onboarded for **automatic refresh** and uses the **README-based publishing configuration** correctly, changes merged to `Azure/azure-rest-api-specs` are picked up by the public REST API reference on Microsoft Learn **weekly, on Tuesdays**.

A **manual publishing request** is needed instead of relying on that automatic refresh in either of these cases:
- **You need an out-of-band publish** rather than waiting for the next Tuesday refresh.
- **Your service uses the alternative publishing configuration** that points directly to OpenAPI spec file paths instead of the recommended README/default-tag setup. In that model, API changes are **not** automatically picked up; the publishing configuration must be manually updated via a publishing request.

A related prerequisite: automatic refresh only applies **after first-time onboarding** and requires a README whose **default tag includes all spec files for the latest API version**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: When a folder-structure v2 suppression is acceptable for an in-flight PR

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

For an Azure REST API specs PR that was already in flight before the v2 folder-structure requirement was enforced, is a temporary suppression acceptable when the service already has related specs in the repository using the v1 layout, even though guidance says v1 and v2 should not be mixed?

**Historical ground truth**

Yes. A temporary suppression is considered valid when a PR was already open and the service already has related specs using the v1 folder structure. In that situation, the in-flight PR can be allowed to proceed under a suppression instead of requiring an immediate migration to v2, and broader folder-structure updates can be handled later.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — **historically, a temporary suppression was an acceptable exception for an already in-flight PR** when the PR belonged to an existing service that still had related specs in the repository using the legacy v1 layout.

- **Why this was acceptable:** the repo guidance says existing v1 specs were not all forced to convert immediately when v2 became required for new specs; instead, **existing v1 specs received root-level suppressions**. That shows the policy distinguished **new specs** from **legacy/in-flight existing specs**.
- **Why this does not conflict with “don’t mix v1 and v2”:** “do not mix” is the **target repository structure**, not proof that every legacy PR had to be blocked immediately. The folder-migration guidance explicitly treats **ongoing PRs** as a transition case and tells authors to reconcile with the migration.
- **What the exception means in practice:** a temporary suppression is reasonable as a **bridge** for pre-existing work, especially when the service already had v1 material in repo. It is **not** a blanket approval to keep expanding the old layout indefinitely.
- **Important boundary:** if the PR is rebased after the migration and can reasonably be moved, the guidance says the resolved PR should **align the new change to v2** and clean up old folders where applicable. So the historical answer is:
  - **In-flight legacy PR:** temporary suppression can be acceptable.
  - **New PR started after enforcement / after migration landed:** it should use **v2 directly**, not rely on suppression to keep adding to v1.
- **If you need to apply the temporary suppression process:** the documented path is to request a **PR-only suppression** from the PR assignee and justify it per the suppression guidance at [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Was Folder Structure v2 required for new specs, and how could an existing spec suppress MustUseV2?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

When TSV reports FolderStructure/MustUseV2 for an existing Azure REST API spec, was Folder Structure v2 required for new specs at that time, and how could a single spec suppress that rule if it could not migrate immediately?

**Historical ground truth**

At that time, Folder Structure v2 had been made mandatory for new specs, although exceptions could be granted for pull requests already in progress. For an existing spec that could not migrate immediately, the rule could be suppressed at the spec level by adding a suppressions.yaml file in that spec's own folder instead of editing a root suppressions file. The suppression example used tool TypeSpecValidation, rule FolderStructure, sub-rule MustUseV2, a reason, and the affected spec paths.

**Cached dev answer**

No—at the time Folder Structure v2 first appeared, it was **not yet required** for all new specs. The retrieved guidance says **v2 was introduced in June 2025**, when new specs were **encouraged** to start with v2 and existing specs were encouraged to migrate when convenient; it became **mandatory for new specs on March 23, 2026**.

For an **existing** spec that hit `FolderStructure/MustUseV2` and could not migrate immediately, the supported path was to add a **narrowly scoped** `suppressions.yaml` in the spec/service root and suppress only the affected folders. The examples in the guidance use `tool: TypeSpecRequirement` with scoped paths and a reason, for example:

```yaml
- tool: TypeSpecRequirement
  paths:
    - ./preview/2022-01-01-preview/*.json
  reason: Brownfield service not ready to migrate

- tool: TypeSpecRequirement
  paths:
    - ./stable/2025-01-01/*.json
  reason: Brownfield service not ready to migrate
```

A few important details from the docs:

- Put `suppressions.yaml` at the **root of the spec folder**; the tooling walks up the directory tree and uses the first one it finds. See [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).
- Scope the suppression **as narrowly as possible** to the specific version/folder, not the whole service, unless that broader scope is truly needed. See [Suppress validation failures on a PR](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-suppressions).
- Historically, broader **root-level suppressions** were later added for existing v1 specs in `main` and `RPSaaSMaster`, but for a **single spec**, the documented mechanism was the per-spec `suppressions.yaml` approach. See [Folder Structure](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Folder-Structure) and [Resolving Folder Migration Conflicts: A Guide for PR Authors](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Resolving-Folder-Migration-Conflicts:-A-Guide-for-PR-Authors).

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: For an existing RPaaS registration, does moving Swagger from v1 to v2 require manifest changes or cause downtime?

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

For an existing RPaaS spec whose registration already points to the RP namespace folder, if a folder structure v1 to v2 migration moves Swagger files one level deeper into the service folder, does that require changing the manifest or RT registration, and does the migration cause service downtime?

**Historical ground truth**

For an existing RPaaS registration that already points to the RP namespace folder, moving Swagger files from the RP namespace folder layout into the deeper service-folder layout during a v1-to-v2 migration does not by itself cause service downtime. In that scenario, no manifest or RT registration change is needed just for the folder refactor, because RPaaS was described as searching specs recursively from the RP namespace folder as long as the readme.md there contains openapi-type: arm and openapi-subtype: rpaas. When creating a new RT registration for new resource types, the registration must instead point to the actual service-layer folder path. Older Swagger versions should also be moved into that service folder during the migration.

**Cached dev answer**

No — **if the existing RPaaS registration already points `swaggerSpecFolderUri` at the RP namespace root** (`.../resource-manager/<RPNS>/`), then moving OpenAPI from folder-structure v1 to v2 **does not require changing the manifest path or RT registration just because the files moved one level deeper into a service folder**. RPaaS discovery is rooted at the **RP namespace folder**, not at the child service/stable/preview/version folders. The v2 layout is explicitly `resource-manager/<RPNS>/<service>/...`, and the registration is expected to stay at `<RPNS>`, not move down with the files.\

It also **does not inherently cause service downtime**. For an already onboarded managed RP, spec changes are picked up through the normal **OpenAPI SDP rollout** during **RP manifest rollout**; they are activated progressively through traffic rings rather than flipping globally at once. If a rollout fails or is stopped, higher rings keep using the **last-known-good** specification.\

**Practical takeaway**
- **Manifest / RT registration path:** **No change needed** if it already points to the RP namespace root.
- **Service availability:** **No expected downtime** from the repo-layout migration itself.
- **What still happens:** after the spec move is merged, the updated spec is picked up on the next **manifest rollout**; don’t change the referenced spec again after rollout starts because rollout uses the snapshot captured at start.

</details>

<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to get Go and JavaScript SDK breaking changes reviewed when SDK breaking-change labels appear

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a spec PR shows SDK breaking-change labels for Go and JavaScript in the merge steps, how should the author get those SDK breaking changes reviewed and approved?

**Historical ground truth**

When a spec PR shows SDK breaking changes for Go or JavaScript, the author should contact the owners for the affected SDKs individually instead of asking in the API Spec Review channel. Use the documented SDK breaking-change review process to identify the appropriate owners and obtain their review.

**Cached dev answer**

If a spec PR shows `BreakingChange-Go-Sdk` and/or `BreakingChange-JavaScript-Sdk`, the author generally does **not** need to manually find Go or JavaScript reviewers. The reusable process is:

- **Follow the PR’s Step 1 and Step 2 first** using the guidance in [Spec PR Review Workflow](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/specs-pr-guides/pr-brch-deep). SDK breaking-change review happens **after** the earlier merge steps are complete.
- **Try to remove the SDK breaking changes in the spec first.** The documented expectation is to avoid the SDK break if the spec can be adjusted.
- **If the SDK break is unavoidable, add SDK suppressions** using the process in [SDK Breaking Changes](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Breaking-Changes). The author adds the `sdk-suppressions.yaml` entries for the affected languages to the spec PR.
- Once those suppressions are in the PR, **SDK reviewers monitor the PR proactively** and review them. Approval is reflected by language-specific suppression approval labels such as `BreakingChange-Go-Sdk-Suppression-Approved`.
- So, for Go and JavaScript specifically, the author’s job is usually to **either eliminate the break or add the suppressions correctly, then wait for SDK reviewers**. There is no separate manual approval flow described beyond that.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: How to troubleshoot a .NET SDK validation failure that appears to resolve common-types with the wrong path

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If an Azure REST API specs PR fails the ".NET SDK Validation" check and the generation appears to resolve a shared common-types file using an incorrect path prefix such as inserting a service folder before `specification/common-types/resource-management/v2/types.json`, how should the author troubleshoot it from the specs side, and when should it be escalated as a .NET-specific code generation issue?

**Historical ground truth**

First inspect the detailed Azure Pipelines job behind the failing .NET SDK validation check, because the GitHub check summary may not show the actual generation error. Use the pipeline log to determine whether the failure is caused by spec configuration or by the .NET generator.

From the specs side, validate the configuration locally based on what the detailed error shows:
- If it is a TypeSpec import-resolution problem, check the relevant `tspconfig.yaml` and ensure required shared-type directories are included through `additionalDirectories` using paths relative to that config file.
- If it is an AutoRest/OpenAPI configuration problem, check the service `readme.md` and verify that `input-file` and `require` entries use valid relative paths and that references to shared `common-types` resolve correctly.
- Reproduce locally with commands such as `npx tsp compile .` for the TypeSpec project and `autorest readme.md` for the OpenAPI configuration before re-running validation.

If the failure appears only in .NET generation and the resolved path incorrectly inserts the service folder before `specification/common-types/...`, treat that as likely a .NET-specific code generation bug and escalate it to the .NET code generation/support channel with the exact generation error and relevant PR context.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes: treat this as a **specs-first triage**, and escalate only after you prove the spec inputs are already correct.

- Start with the [SDK Validation troubleshooting guide](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation) and inspect the failing .NET validation run’s logs/artifacts/HTML report. The goal is to determine **where the bad path first appears**: in the emitted OpenAPI / generation config, or only later during .NET generation.

- On the specs side, verify that your project is using the **canonical ARM common-types location**, not a service-relative override. For TypeSpec, the documented default `arm-types-dir` is `${project-root}/../../common-types/resource-management` in the [TypeSpec emitter reference](https://azure.github.io/typespec-azure/docs/emitters/typespec-autorest/reference/emitter). If your project overrides that setting, fix or remove the override.

- Also verify the project follows the normal Azure REST API specs folder layout from the [TypeSpec project structure guidance](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/Azure-REST-API,-SDK-development-process-with-TypeSpec). A misplaced project root or incorrect service-folder layout can make a relative common-types path resolve incorrectly.

- If your emitted spec/config already points to the expected repo-level path such as `specification/common-types/resource-management/v2/types.json`, but the .NET validation output still inserts an extra service-folder prefix, **that is the practical cutoff where this should be treated as a .NET-specific code generation issue**. That conclusion is an inference from the documented canonical path behavior plus the SDK-validation troubleshooting flow: once the spec input is correct, a later path rewrite is no longer a specs-side defect.

- At that point, use the [Azure SDK Tools Agent](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/develop/azsdk-tools-mcp) as the primary escalation path for SDK generation/validation troubleshooting. If you escalate manually, include the emitted spec/config evidence showing the canonical common-types path is already correct, so the .NET team can focus on generator path resolution rather than spec authoring.

- If the wrong prefixed path is already present in the emitted OpenAPI or language config, keep the fix in the specs PR: correct the TypeSpec/OpenAPI reference or CSharp generation configuration using the documented [SDK generation configuration guidance](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-spec-gen-sdk-config), then rerun the SDK validation process from the [SDK Validation guide](https://github.com/Azure/azure-rest-api-specs/wiki/SDK-Validation).

**Short rule of thumb**

- **Fix in specs PR** if the bad path exists in emitted spec/config.
- **Escalate to .NET codegen** if the spec/config is already correct and the bad path is introduced only during .NET generation.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Replay question, historical ground truth, and cached dev answer</summary>

**Replay question**

title: Why GitHub shows an approving-review requirement next to Swagger PrettierCheck

question: Why can GitHub show "At least 1 approving review is required by reviewers with write access" next to Swagger PrettierCheck?

**Historical ground truth**

That message is from GitHub branch protection and pull request merge requirements, not from the Swagger PrettierCheck job itself. GitHub can display the approval requirement alongside a required check to indicate that merging requires both the required checks to pass and at least one approving review from someone with write access.

**Cached dev answer**

GitHub shows that message there because it is surfacing a **branch protection / merge requirement**, not saying that **`Open API PrettierCheck` itself requires a human approval**.

- In the spec repos, merge requirements are a combination of:
  - **required automated checks** such as `PrettierCheck`, and
  - a separate **approver requirement** / team-member approval rule on protected branches.
- The docs explicitly distinguish these: required checks roll up into **`Automated merging requirements met`**, and even after that is green, the PR may still need **an approving review from someone with write access** before it can merge.
- The branch-protection table also lists **`PrettierCheck`** and **`approver`** as separate required items on protected branches such as public `main`, private `RPSaaSMaster`, and `release-*`.

So the short answer is: **GitHub is attaching the review requirement message to the checks area in a slightly confusing way. It does not mean PrettierCheck is a review gate; it means your PR still has a separate approval gate in addition to the check.**

What to look at instead:

- Check **`Automated merging requirements met`** first. If it is green, your automated required checks are satisfied.
- If GitHub still says an approval is required, then the remaining blocker is **review approval**, not `PrettierCheck`.
- On protected branches, you may also need the right reviewer / code owner approval depending on the changed paths.

</details>

**Replay question**

title: How to retrigger a Prettier check that did not run on an API specs PR

question: Historical context: Answer the reusable process or technical question from the facts stated below. Do not infer the current status of any linked PR, issue, check, dashboard, or document.

If a Prettier check did not run and is blocking an Azure REST API specs PR, how can that check be retriggered?

**Historical ground truth**

Prettier cannot be rerun by itself; it runs as part of the PR CI workflow, so the way to run it again is to retrigger the PR checks. One way is to push a no-op commit to the PR branch, which reruns all checks including Prettier. If you have write access to the repository, you can also open the PR's Checks tab and choose to rerun all jobs for the workflow. For a protected release branch with outdated infrastructure, first update the branch from main using the documented release-branch update helper process, then retrigger the checks. On protected branches, Prettier is a required check, so the PR remains blocked until the workflow reruns and that check completes successfully.

**Cached dev answer**

Yes — the documented way to retrigger a PR check that did not run is to **close the PR and then reopen it**. The API specs guidance says this is the **easiest way to retrigger all checks**, which includes `PrettierCheck` when it is one of the PR checks on that branch.

- **Retrigger the check:** close the PR, then reopen the same PR. See [Create a PR against main | Update your branch with changes from main | Updating only the infrastructure changes from main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish).
- **If checks still do not run:** update the branch with the latest infrastructure changes from `main`, then retrigger the checks again. The same guidance explains when to merge `main` normally versus using the helper flow for protected `release-*` branches: [Create a PR against main | Update your branch with changes from main | Updating only the infrastructure changes from main](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-tutorial/api-tutorial-3-publish).
- **Why this can matter:** `PrettierCheck` is a required check on several protected API specs branches, including public `main`, private `RPSaaSMaster`, and `release-*` branches. See [API versions and branches | Branch protection rules table](https://eng.ms/docs/products/azure-developer-experience/design/api-specs-pr/api-versions-and-branches).

</details>
